title: splice is enabled only in tests: flush_node is a silent no-op in every shipped build, so mount writes never reproject
description:
Traced 2026-07-27 from ley-line-open-f327e1's observation that `splice` is tested but never shipped. It is worse than a packaging wart.

## The finding

`grep -c leyline-fs/splice` in BOTH CLI manifests returns 0. No feature reaches it:

- leyline-fs default = ["validate", "fuse", "nfs"] — no splice
- cli-lib default = ["lsp", "validate", "hdc", "cdc"] — no splice
- cli-lib mount = ["leyline-fs/nfs", "leyline-fs/fuse", "leyline-fs/validate"] — no splice
- cli all  = ["lsp", "vec", "validate", "hdc", "text-search", "cdc"] — no splice
- cli full = ["lsp", "mount", "vec", "validate", "hdc", "text-search", "cdc"] — no splice

`splice` is enabled ONLY by the Taskfile's test and mutants targets (`--features cdc,splice,validate`). It is in no build that ships.

## What that compiles to

graph.rs `flush_node` is entirely wrapped in `#[cfg(feature = "splice")]`, with a bare fallthrough:

    fn flush_node(&self, id: &str) -> Result<()> {
        #[cfg(feature = "splice")]
        { ...lookup record, splice_and_reproject, invalidate manifests... }
        let _ = id;
        Ok(())
    }

Without the feature it is `let _ = id; Ok(())` — a SILENT SUCCESS. Same for `batch_splice` and `pending_splice`, which do not exist at all.

## Consequence

The mount write path is the intended splice flow — leyline-ts/src/splice.rs's own header says it "Enables LLMs to edit individual AST nodes via mounted files." In every shipped build, writing to a mounted file lands bytes in `nodes.record` via `write_content`, and then `flush_node` returns Ok(()) having done nothing. No reproject. `_ast` and `_source` never update, and the caller is told it succeeded.

`cmd_splice` (cli-lib/src/cmd_splice.rs:9) calls `leyline_ts::splice::splice_and_reproject` DIRECTLY, bypassing leyline-fs — so the `leyline splice` subcommand does reproject, but it also bypasses leyline-fs's manifest invalidation entirely. With CDC enabled that is a second question worth checking: reproject rewrites `nodes.record` for every node of the source, and splice.rs never touches `nodes.mtime`, so whether the freshness witness catches it depends on the size changing.

## Why nobody noticed

graph.rs:1967 `splice_write_and_flush_triggers_reproject` PASSES — because the test target enables `splice`. The test proves a capability the shipped binary does not have. This is ley-line-open-f327e1's "tested configuration is not the shipped one", with a concrete consequence rather than a hygiene concern.

It is also the day's recurring shape one more time: the failure is silent AND returns the success value.

## Decide, do not patch around

Either mount-edit reprojection is a real capability — in which case a shipped feature must enable it and a test must assert the SHIPPED feature set — or it is not, in which case `flush_node` should fail loudly rather than returning Ok(), the `splice` feature should be removed per the remove-don't-deprecate policy, and splice.rs's header claim should go.

Do not simply add `splice` to a feature list without checking the CDC interaction above.

## Close condition

cargo test -p leyline-fs with the SHIPPED feature set, plus the mount round-trip in acceptance_criteria.

comments.text:
DECISION 2026-07-27: FINISH IT, do not remove.

Direction confirmed by jamestexas. splice gets wired into a shipping configuration and mount becomes a tested, supported path.

## What finishing requires

1. Wire `splice` into a shipping config in rs/ll-open/cli{,-lib}/Cargo.toml so it is reachable from a declared release build. Today it is enabled ONLY by test targets, which is why flush_node degrades to `let _ = id; Ok(())` in every shipped binary.
2. A mount ROUND-TRIP test proving a write reprojects — not a build check. Two build checks exist today and neither proves a mount serves correct bytes.
3. Remove the not-shipping ledger entry in tools/check_feature_reachability.sh (ll-open/fs/splice) AND the coverage ledger entry for cli-lib/mount (ley-line-open-aed167). Both exist only because this is unfinished; leaving either behind would mean the gate still records a defect we have decided to close.

## Why the two are one job

aed167 says cli-lib/mount ships with zero test files gated on it at any level. 918a75 says splice is compiled out of every build. Together they mean the mount WRITE path is unproven end to end: the feature that would reproject is absent, and nothing tests the surface that would expose it. Finishing one without the other leaves the round-trip unverified, so the acceptance criterion above is deliberately a round-trip rather than a compile.

## Note for whoever takes it

The gate will tell you when it is done: deleting the ledger line and having lint:feature-reachability still pass IS the completion condition. Do not delete the line to make the gate quiet — that inverts it.
comments.author: rsry-cli

acceptance_criteria: Either (a) a shipped feature enables `leyline-fs/splice` so mount writes reproject, verified by mounting an `install:full` binary, editing a file, and confirming `_ast`/`_source` update; or (b) `flush_node` fails loudly rather than returning Ok(()) when compiled without splice, and the docs stop claiming mount-edit reprojection. A test must assert the SHIPPED feature set, not a test-only one.

title: Bump GHA action SHA pins to Node.js 24-supporting versions
description:
Filed 2026-05-10. Fast-follow to PR #3 (`ae0cf9f`).

GitHub flagged a deprecation warning during the PR #3 CI run on `Check + Clippy + Test (task ci)`:

> Node.js 20 actions are deprecated. The following actions are running on Node.js 20 and may not work as expected: `actions/checkout@34e114876b0b11c390a56381ad16ebd13914f8d5`, `arduino/setup-task@b91d5d2c96a56797b48ac1e0e89220bf64044611`. Actions will be forced to run with Node.js 24 by default starting June 2nd, 2026. Node.js 20 will be removed from the runner on September 16th, 2026.
> https://github.blog/changelog/2025-09-19-deprecation-of-node-20-on-github-actions-runners/

## Action inventory (across both workflows)

```
.github/workflows/ci.yml:21               actions/checkout@34e114876b0b... (v4.3.1, Node 20) ⚠️
.github/workflows/ci.yml:23               dtolnay/rust-toolchain@3c5f7ea2...
.github/workflows/ci.yml:35               arduino/setup-task@b91d5d2c... (v2.0.0, Node 20) ⚠️
.github/workflows/leyline-schema-go.yml:36  actions/checkout@34e114876b0b... (v4.3.1, Node 20) ⚠️
.github/workflows/leyline-schema-go.yml:39  actions/setup-go@0aaccfd1...
```

## Work

For each `uses:` line, find the latest tag whose action.yml declares `runs.using: node24` (or `composite` / `docker`, which are unaffected). Repin the SHA to that tag's commit SHA. Keep a `# tag = vX.Y.Z` comment next to each pin so future readers know what was resolved.

Practical: `gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/releases/latest` to find the latest tag, then `gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/contents/action.yml?ref=<tag>` to confirm `runs.using`. Or check release notes for "Node.js 24" mentions.

Specifically known to need a bump (per the deprecation warning):
- `actions/checkout` — needs ≥ v4.4.0 / v5 (Node 24)
- `arduino/setup-task` — check for newer release; if upstream hasn't shipped Node 24 yet, file an upstream issue and add a TODO comment

Probably also worth re-checking:
- `dtolnay/rust-toolchain` — appears to be a composite/script action, may not be Node-based at all
- `actions/setup-go` — confirm latest is Node 24

## Acceptance

- All `uses:` SHAs in both workflows point to Node 24-supporting tags (or are composite/docker)
- A re-run of either workflow shows no Node 20 deprecation warning in the job log
- Each pin has a `# tag = vX.Y.Z` comment for human readability

## Why this is a separate bead

Mechanical maintenance, not gated on any release. PR #3 was already long; splitting leaves a clean audit trail: `[ley-line-open-XXXXXX] ci: bump action pins to Node 24` is one focused commit.

title: epic: HDC hypervectors as structural stalks (LLO HdcPass + sheaf-cache integration)
description:
## Why this exists

Hyperdimensional Computing (HDC) gives us a third coordinate system alongside the structural AST tables (`_ast`, `nodes`) and the dense semantic VectorIndex (sqlite-vec sidecar). It uniquely fills a gap none of those handle well: **structural fuzzy match under α-renames** ("find every function that has *this shape* even if variable names changed").

But the strategic insight isn't just AST search. HDC hypervectors are **richer stalks** for the existing sheaf machinery:

- ADR-011 (sheaf cache) defines stalks as "content hash (Merkle root) summarizing a topological region's current state" — but explicitly says "any data structure that can be hashed can produce a stalk." Merkle stalks only give *equality* (changed / unchanged). HDC stalks give *continuous structural similarity* via Hamming distance.
- ADR-012 (merkle sheaf sync) per-community stalks today drive sync decisions binarily. HDC stalks let us measure *how much* a community drifted, not just whether — informing partial sync, weighted restriction maps, and the defect vector `||d⁰(stalks)||²` continuously rather than 0-or-large.

So the actual scope is: ship the HdcPass in LLO; the private LL crate then wires HDC stalks into the sheaf-cache and merkle-sync layers as a richer alternative to (or complement of) plain Merkle roots.

## Math foundation (vetted)

Theoretical-foundations review confirmed:
- For binary MAP-B with D=8192 (byte-aligned popcount), capacity bound `D ≥ 2·N·log(M/ε)` handles N≈250 items per flat bundle cleanly.
- Most function ASTs exceed N=300 → **flat bundling fails** (your initial proposal). Need **hierarchical/recursive** encoding (Plate 1994, Schlegel 2022): each subtree → its own hypervector → XOR-bound with ρ-permuted child slot into parent → bundled. XOR is bijective, depth doesn't lose info; Schlegel showed D=10k handles depth 5–7 cleanly, matches typical AST.
- Edit fidelity: one leaf rename → ΔH/D ≈ 1/(2√N). Sqrt-scaled, not linear. Threshold tuning has to use the curve.
- Genuinely orthogonal to dense embeddings (lexical) and AST tables (rigid). Not dominated.

## Subordinate beads (to file separately)

1. `hdc-1`: `_hdc` sidecar table + storage layout (BLOB column, parse_version basis).
2. `hdc-2`: codebook — random base vectors per AST node-kind + ρ permutation for child position. Seeded RNG, persisted alongside parse_version so different daemon instances produce comparable vectors.
3. `hdc-3`: `HdcPass` enrichment pass — recursive hierarchical encoding, function granularity. Bottom-up bundling capped at local fanout. Memoize by subtree content-hash.
4. `hdc-4`: `op_hdc_search` — bottom-k by `popcount(query_hv XOR row.hv)`. SQL UDF for hamming distance (or reuse sqlite-vec's bit-mode if available).
5. `hdc-5`: feature flag `hdc` (cfg-gated like `vec`), default-off. Documented.
6. `hdc-6`: integration tests — clone detection (rename one var, expect Hamming d/D ≈ 1/(2√N)), structural pattern search (find all `if-then-return` shapes), and a drift-guard that random-pair Hamming distance stays near 0.5.

## Scope, this epic

LLO-side only. The LL-side wiring (HDC stalks in sheaf cache, weighted restrictions, continuous defect) is a separate epic in the LL repo. This epic's deliverable: `_hdc` table populated correctly, `op_hdc_search` returns the documented Hamming-rank, all behind `hdc` feature flag.

## Files (anticipated)

- NEW: `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/daemon/hdc.rs` — codebook + encoder + HdcPass + op_hdc_search.
- `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/daemon/mod.rs` — register `pub mod hdc;` under cfg.
- `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/daemon/ops.rs` — wire `op_hdc_search` into handle_base_op + tool_registry + base_op_names.
- `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/Cargo.toml` — `hdc` feature flag.
- `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/tests/integration.rs` — integration tests.

## Math friend's recipe (for sub-beads to follow)

- D = 8192 bits (byte-aligned, fast popcount, ~18% smaller than 10k with negligible capacity loss)
- Binary MAP-B: XOR-bind `kind ⊕ position`, majority-bundle locally, ρ-permute for child order
- Hierarchical: bottom-up recursive; cache per-subtree by content-hash
- Threshold (starting point, tune empirically): `d/D < 0.42` for "match". Expect <10⁻⁶ FP, ~90–95% recall for k=1–3 leaf edits at function sizes 30–150 nodes.

## Connection to existing work

- ADR-011 (`docs/design/011-sheaf-cache.md` in ley-line repo) — HDC stalks slot in as richer Merkle alternatives.
- ADR-012 (`docs/design/012-merkle-sheaf-sync.md` in ley-line repo) — HDC enables continuous sync decisions.
- Existing `EnrichmentPass` framework (`daemon/enrichment.rs`) — HdcPass slots in downstream of TreeSitterPass, parallel to EmbeddingPass.
- Existing SSOT pattern (`base_op_names`, `tool_registry`, `STATE_CHANGING_OPS`) — `op_hdc_search` registers the same way as `op_vec_search`.

## Gearbox / logogram lead — codebook design

User redirected: see `../x-ray/internal/cartographer/cairn_*.go` (Cairn cartographer "Semantic Gearbox") and the "logogram" framing.

x-ray's gearbox is a multi-resolution coding-theory pipeline for visual zone tokenization:
- Gear 1: Tetracode [4,2,3] — 4D ternary, 9 codewords (coarsest)
- Gear 3: Ternary Golay [12,6,6] — 12D, 729 codewords
- Gear 5: Leech lattice Λ₂₄ — 24D continuous (default)
- Gear 6: Barnes-Wall BW₃₂ — 32D, finest

Each visual zone gets quantized to *one discrete codeword* in a richly-structured lattice. That's the "logogram" framing: **a unit of meaning encoded as a single symbol in a richly-structured space**, where distance is meaningful.

### Three concrete links to HDC

1. **Codebook design** — the math friend's recipe used random Bernoulli base vectors per AST node-kind (textbook HDC). Replace with **Leech/Golay/Tetracode codewords** as base vectors. Same XOR-bind / majority-bundle algebra; better properties:
   - Provably better minimum Hamming distance between distinct kinds (no accidental collisions among ~200 tree-sitter node-kinds)
   - Lattice quantization for nearest-codeword cleanup (more robust than raw popcount-threshold)
   - Closed-form analysis of capacity bounds (lattice codes have known sphere-packing density)

2. **Multi-resolution recursive encoding** — the gearbox's progressive Gear1→Gear5 stages mirror HDC's hierarchical/recursive bundling depth. We can use *coarse* lattice codes for shallow subtrees and *fine* lattice codes for deep ones, controlling capacity per depth. Maps directly onto Schlegel 2022's hierarchical VSA approach but with lattice base vectors instead of random ones.

3. **Cross-modal logograms — the strategic insight.** If both code-LLO and visual-x-ray use the *same* lattice base vectors, then their hypervectors live in the same space. You can literally bind a code-AST hypervector with a visual-screenshot hypervector and ask "which functions correspond to which UI zones." This is the unified "logogram" representation across art's ecosystem — code, visual, document zones, all in one coordinate system.

### Updated sub-bead recipe

`hdc-2` (codebook) should pick **Leech-derived base vectors** by default, not Bernoulli random:
- 196,560 minimum-norm Leech vectors → plenty of distinct codewords for ~200 AST node-kinds with huge headroom
- Maps to D=8192 by lifting/embedding (Leech is naturally D=24 but tensor products into higher-D codes preserve minimum-distance properties)
- Alternative: Barnes-Wall BW₃₂ for byte-aligned ops with provable minimum distance

`hdc-3` (HdcPass) stays the same algorithmically — still bind+bundle hierarchically — but base vectors come from the lattice codebook instead of an RNG.

### Files to read for codebook implementation

- `internal/cartographer/cairn_leech.go` — `ProjectToLeech` and Λ₂₄ generator matrix
- `internal/cartographer/cairn_tetracode.go` — `QuantizeTetracode` and the [4,2,3] generator matrix at lines 16-27
- `internal/cartographer/cairn_m12.go` — Mathieu group M₁₂ for Golay code automorphisms
- `internal/cartographer/cairn_pipeline.go` — how the gearbox stages compose

### Updated bead title (mental note)

The epic isn't quite "HDC hypervectors as structural stalks" anymore — it's **"Lattice-coded logograms as structural stalks"**. HDC algebra (bind + bundle) is the operator; lattice codes (Leech, Golay, BW32) are the representation.

comments.text:
## Correction: bidi is the goal, quantization is wrong frame

The previous comment talked about "lattice quantization for cleanup" — that was sloppy. AST node-kinds are already discrete (`IfStatement` is `IfStatement`); there's nothing analog to quantize. x-ray's gearbox quantizes *continuous* visual features (luminance, edge density) to nearest lattice points — that's the right move for analog signals. For our use case, the lattice's role is **codebook with provable minimum-distance**, not quantizer.

The actual goal is **bidirectional (invertible) encoding**, and HDC's bind/bundle/cleanup algebra is built for it:

```
encode:    H(node) = base[kind(node)] ⊕ ρ⁰·H(child₀) ⊕ ρ¹·H(child₁) ⊕ ...
unbind:    H ⊕ ρ⁰  → noisy estimate of H(child₀)
cleanup:   nearest-neighbor in codebook → recover kind
recurse:   query subtree-hypervector cache keyed on content-hash
```

XOR-bind is bijective. With a cleanup memory (the codebook) + cached subtree hypervectors (content-hash keyed), the encoding becomes **walkable both directions**: encode bottom-up, recover top-down by repeatedly unbinding ρⁱ and cleaning up.

### Why this beats plain Merkle stalks for sheaf cache

| Property | Merkle hash | HDC bidi vector |
|----------|-------------|-----------------|
| Equality detection | ✓ | ✓ (popcount = 0) |
| Continuous similarity | ✗ | ✓ (small popcount) |
| Partial reconstruction | ✗ | ✓ (unbind + cleanup) |
| Restriction-map weights | trivial 0/1 | continuous via Hamming distance |
| Defect vector `||d⁰||²` | 0 or large | continuous structural defect |

### Bidi cost (be honest)

Recovery at depth D requires D successful cleanups, each with small failure probability `p`. Per-cleanup error at D=8192 with ~200-entry codebook is ~10⁻⁶ — fine for typical AST function depth 5-7. Past depth ~12 it compounds (~(1-10⁻⁶)¹² ≈ 99.999%). For function granularity (the target), bidi works. For whole-file granularity, it doesn't.

### Updated sub-bead recipe (supersedes previous)

- `hdc-2` (codebook): Leech/Golay/BW32 **base vectors** (not quantizers). Chosen for minimum-distance properties — gives reliable cleanup memory.
- `hdc-3` (HdcPass): hierarchical bind+bundle, **cache every subtree hypervector** keyed on content-hash. The cache is what makes bidi work — without it, bundle is one-way.
- `hdc-4` was `op_hdc_search`, now becomes **two ops**:
  - `op_hdc_search` — popcount-rank for similarity queries (fast).
  - `op_hdc_unbind` — recover structural info from a function-level vector (slow but bidi).
- `hdc-7` (new): subtree-hypervector cache layer. parse_version-versioned, content-hash-keyed BLOB store. This is the structure that makes bidi tractable.

### Lattice codes vs Bernoulli — independent of bidi choice

Bernoulli random vectors *also* support bidi via cleanup memory; the algebra doesn't care. Lattice codes give better SNR margin for cleanup at deeper trees (quantitative win), but they're not strictly required for bidi to function. So `hdc-2` can ship with Bernoulli first and upgrade to lattice codebook later — bidi works on day one.

The strategic value of the lattice route remains the **cross-modal logogram** angle: if x-ray and LLO share lattice base vectors, code hypervectors and visual hypervectors live in the same space. That's a separate decision, downstream of getting bidi working.

comments.text:
## Unifying frame: HDC as continuity-equipped logogram, alongside tokenizers/ASTs/CAS/CDC

User's lens: tokenizing, ASTs/CSTs, CAS, CDC, HDC, sheaf stalks are all instances of one pattern. Capturing it because it informs the integration design.

| System | Symbols | Composition algebra | Cleanup store | Bidi via |
|--------|---------|--------------------|--------------:|----------|
| Tokenizers (BPE) | subwords | concatenation | vocabulary | `decode ∘ encode ≈ id` |
| ASTs/CSTs | node-kinds | tree containment | grammar | re-print from CST |
| CAS | blobs | hash-of-bytes | content store | hash → blob lookup |
| CDC | chunks | hash-of-chunks | chunk store | rolling-hash boundaries |
| HDC | base vectors | XOR-bind + bundle | codebook + subtree cache | unbind + cleanup |
| Merkle stalks | regions | restriction maps | Merkle tree | equality only (today) |

The triple in every row: **discrete signature + composable algebra + cleanup memory ⇒ bidi**.

### What this changes about the LLO design

1. **`_hdc` is a CAS for hypervectors, not a separate sidecar.** Content-hash key → hypervector → constituent kind+children (via subtree cache). Plug into ley-line's existing CAS layer — same primitive, different payload.

2. **Hierarchical HDC encoding *is* CDC chunking, structurally.** Top-level hypervector = bind of child-permuted child hypervectors; CDC top-hash = hash of chunk hashes. Same identity, different algebra (XOR-bind+bundle vs. concatenate-and-hash). Implication: ley-line's existing CDC chunk store can host the hypervector cache without redesign.

3. **The unique thing HDC adds**: continuous structural similarity *in the symbol space itself* (popcount), without a downstream embedder. Tokenizers need a learned embedding to get continuity. CAS/CDC/Merkle have no continuity. HDC bakes it in.

4. **Therefore: HDC stalks ≠ replacement for Merkle stalks.** They're a *richer* stalk class. Merkle stalks answer "is this region the same?" (binary). HDC stalks answer that *plus* "how similar?" (continuous). The sheaf cache's defect operator `||d⁰||²` becomes continuous; restriction-map weights become principled instead of trivially 0/1.

### Implementation reuse

- Subtree-hypervector cache (`hdc-7`): use ley-line's CAS infrastructure as the storage backend. Don't reinvent.
- Content-hash keying: same Merkle-style hash as the existing arena layer.
- Versioning: parse_version basis, identical to other enrichment passes.

### Position relative to dense embeddings

Dense embeddings (existing `VectorIndex`) get continuity through *learned semantic distribution* — they capture what tokens *mean* in context. They have **no structural awareness**. HDC vectors get continuity through *structural composition* — they capture what tokens *are* under tree-shape preserving operations. They have **no learned semantics**.

These are orthogonal axes:
- AST-table query: exact structural match (rigid)
- HDC popcount: fuzzy structural match (rename-invariant, edit-tolerant)
- Dense vector cosine: semantic match (paraphrase-tolerant, structure-blind)

LLO should expose all three at the op level. Clients (mache, ley-line sheaf cache, rosary) pick whichever axis their query needs.

comments.text:
## V0 (ship now) vs V1 (research) — codebook is human-based today, machine-based later

User flagged: today's encoding designs are human-based (parser-author kind-names, human-readable role labels). For machine reasoning, we want a label-invariant representation. This is genuinely a research problem with no settled answer in the HDC literature.

### What's human-based about the V0 recipe

- Hash `"if_statement"` → base vector. The string is a parser-author choice. Tree-sitter calls it `if_statement`; ANTLR calls it `ifStmt`; ESLint AST calls it `IfStatement`. Same code, different hypervectors across grammars.
- Role labels `"LeftChild"`, `"NextSibling"` are conventions, not topology.
- The codebook implicitly encodes *which language the code came from* via the parser's kind namespace.

### What machine-based looks like (research axes)

1. **Production-signature hashing**: hash the grammar production (multiset of child-kinds), not the label. Cross-parser robust.
2. **Equivalence-class induction**: group kinds by role (branching/looping/binding/applying); hash by class. All `for`/`while`/`do-while` → same base. Lossy but cross-language.
3. **Anonymous structural fingerprint**: hash `(in_degree, out_degree, depth_to_leaf, n_descendants)` quantized. No labels at all — pure topology.
4. **Learned base vectors**: contrastive training on semantic-equivalent code pairs. Most expressive; trades the "no codebook to ship" property.
5. **Frequency-induced (SkipGram-for-AST)**: hash by co-occurrence stats on a corpus. Deterministic per-corpus, machine-derived.

### Design implication: codebook is a trait, not a constant

```rust
trait BaseCodebook: Send + Sync {
    fn base_vector(&self, node: &AstNode) -> [u8; D/8];
    fn role_vector(&self, role: &Role) -> [u8; D/8];
}

struct LabelCodebook;          // V0: hash(kind_name) — human-based, ships today
struct ProductionCodebook;     // V1a: hash(production_signature) — research
struct EquivalenceCodebook;    // V1b: hash(class_id) — research
struct LearnedCodebook { ... } // V1c: trained hypervectors — research, ships an artifact
```

`HdcPass` takes a `Box<dyn BaseCodebook>`. Swapping codebooks is a one-argument change. Storage, queries, sheaf integration — unchanged. Pure additive.

### Subordinate bead structure refined

- `hdc-2` (codebook): ship `LabelCodebook` first; V1 codebooks land in `hdc-9..` as research-grade follow-ups, each gated `#[cfg(feature = "hdc_v1_*")]` so users opt-in per variant.
- All V1 codebooks reuse the same encoder (`hdc-3`), the same storage (`hdc-1`), and the same query ops (`hdc-4`). Codebook swap is the only delta.

### Why not skip V0 and go straight to research

V0 is the only variant where every other piece of the puzzle (storage, encoder, query, sheaf integration) can be validated end-to-end without inventing the codebook first. Ship V0 → confirm the rest works → then research the codebook in isolation, swap it in, regression-test against V0's test suite. Standard "make it work, then make it right" sequencing.

### Implementation language: Rust, std-only

- 128 × `u64` per D=8192 vector
- XOR-bind: element-wise XOR (auto-vectorizes to AVX2 / NEON)
- Bundle: bit-counting + majority threshold
- Popcount distance: `u64::count_ones()` reduce
- ~50-100 LOC for core encoder, single file
- No SIMD library needed for V0 — std handles it
- Future: `wide` or `packed_simd` if benchmarks show headroom; not for the initial ship
comments.author: rsry-mcp

comments.text:
## Multi-scale topology — six layers, one hypervector space

User's framing: we have topology at multiple levels (lex, AST/CST, code structure, file system, semantics, temporal), and the value comes from *combining the view*. HDC's algebraic uniformity is what makes the combination work — every layer produces a hypervector in the same D-dimensional space.

### The six layers

| Layer | Topology unit | Example query |
|-------|---------------|---------------|
| Lex | token sequence | "same token-bag in this function" |
| AST/CST | tree shape | "same control-flow structure" |
| Code | module/class hierarchy | "same class-method organization" |
| FS | directory layout | "test dirs that mirror src" |
| Semantic | meaning | "functions that do the same thing" |
| Temporal | edit history | "functions that change together" |

Each layer has its own topology, its own equivalence relation, its own hotspot patterns.

### Two combination strategies (ship both)

1. **Independent layers, weighted Hamming.**
   Per-layer sidecar tables; query carries a weight vector across layers. Consumer picks the mix.
   ```sql
   SELECT scope_id, 
          0.4 * popcount(?1 XOR _hdc_ast.hv) +
          0.3 * popcount(?2 XOR _hdc_lex.hv) +
          0.3 * popcount(?3 XOR _hdc_temporal.hv) AS weighted_distance
   FROM _hdc_ast JOIN _hdc_lex USING (scope_id) ...
   ```

2. **Cross-level bind into combined view.**
   ```
   H_combined = ρ_lex·H_lex ⊕ ρ_ast·H_ast ⊕ ρ_code·H_code ⊕ ρ_fs·H_fs ⊕ ρ_sem·H_sem ⊕ ρ_temp·H_temp
   ```
   XOR-bind across 6 layers — no saturation (binding ≠ bundling). One BLOB encodes all layers; one Hamming query asks "structurally similar at all layers simultaneously."

### Hotspots are multi-scale

This reshapes the hotspot story:
- **True hotspot**: dense neighbors at multiple layers (same shape AND similar tokens AND mirror directories AND change together)
- **Spurious cluster**: only matches at one layer (e.g., AST match but completely different semantics)
- **Cross-layer divergence**: "looks like its neighbors at AST level but semantically very different" → refactor candidate or bug suspect
- **Drift across vendored copies**: combined-view defect operator catches when one layer drifts away from the others

### Per-layer codebook

Each layer needs its own `BaseCodebook`:
- Lex: token-class signatures (topology-fingerprint, token-names are volatile across grammars)
- AST: production-signature (cross-version stable)
- Code: structural module-hash (already CAS primitive, deterministic)
- FS: path-relative fingerprint
- Semantic: dense vector → binary projection (existing VectorIndex projected via random-binary-projection)
- Temporal: git-history fingerprint hash

Same encoder + trait surface; only the codebook changes per layer.

### Storage shape

```
_hdc_lex(scope_id, hv BLOB, parse_version)
_hdc_ast(scope_id, hv BLOB, parse_version)
_hdc_code(scope_id, hv BLOB, parse_version)
_hdc_fs(scope_id, hv BLOB, fs_basis)
_hdc_sem(scope_id, hv BLOB, embed_version)
_hdc_temporal(scope_id, hv BLOB, head_sha)
_hdc_combined(scope_id, hv BLOB, combined_basis)
```

Where `scope_id` is any addressable unit — function, file, directory, module — keyed by content-hash.

### The "rope" insight extends all the way up

Path-as-address isn't just AST-internal (`src/lib.rs/fn_foo/if_block`). It scales:
- AST level: `fn_foo/if_block/then_branch`
- Code level: `crate::module::fn_foo`
- FS level: `~/work/repo/src/lib.rs`
- Combined: any level above + any level below

Path-prefix scoping at any layer gives layer-scoped queries: "all hotspots within this directory," "all token-patterns in this module."

### What this clarifies about the actual product

Per-layer hypervectors are the *substrate*. The combined-view is the *product* — what consumers (mache, sheaf cache, rosary) mostly want is "multi-scale equivalence class for this thing." A function's true identity in the codebase is the conjunction of all six layers; six fingerprints that collapse to one multi-scale logogram.

### Refined sub-bead structure (supersedes earlier numbering)

- `hdc-1`: storage layer — the per-layer table family (`_hdc_*`) + content-hash keying
- `hdc-2a..f`: per-layer codebooks (one each for lex/ast/code/fs/sem/temporal)
- `hdc-3`: encoder — generic over codebook, per-layer pass instances
- `hdc-4`: query ops — `op_hdc_search` (radius), `op_hdc_unbind` (recover), `op_hdc_combined` (multi-layer)
- `hdc-5`: feature flags (per-layer cfg gates)
- `hdc-6`: integration tests — per-layer + combined-view
- `hdc-7`: subtree-hypervector cache (CAS-backed)
- `hdc-8`: combined-view derivation (bind layers together)
- `hdc-9..`: V1 codebook research variants (production-signature, learned, etc.)
comments.author: rsry-mcp

comments.text:
## Math-friend review #2 — design corrections

Stress-test caught real issues. Verdict per axis:

- **A (capacity):** Solid. XOR-bind doesn't saturate. D=8192 leaves ~7× margin per layer; 6-layer chained cleanup hits ε≈6e-3.
- **B (density vs non-iid baseline):** **Fix required.** Real codebases aren't iid — `self`/`if`/`return` co-occur far above chance, so `D/2 ± √D/2` is the wrong null. Need empirical radius calibration: sample 10k random pairs, set `r = d_med - 3·MAD`. Document as daemon-startup step.
- **C (production-signature):** **Fix required.** Not grammar-stable on its own. Three-step fix: (1) hash only `is_named()` nodes, drop anonymous children; (2) bucket arity into `{0,1,2,3-4,5-7,8+}`; (3) map raw kinds to canonical alphabet `{Decl, Expr, Stmt, Block, Ref, Lit, Op}` per parser. Canonical-kind mapping is the highest-leverage decision in the whole stack — spend a day on it. Deckard (Jiang 2007) is the clone-detection precedent.
- **D (random-binary-projection for semantic):** Solid, but use **signed Charikar projection** not threshold-at-fixed-value. JL distortion at D=8192 wildly oversized. Real ceiling is source embedding's intrinsic dimension (~50-100 for code).
- **E (temporal):** Sketch needed. Right primitive: **time-decayed co-edit matrix** with τ≈90 days, then simhash the row with per-repo seeded random matrix. Append-only, ~1% bit churn per commit, fully deterministic.
- **F (weighted bind):** **Doesn't exist cleanly.** XOR is self-inverse — `A ⊕ A = 0`, not amplification. Store layers independently, weight at query time via `d = Σ w_i · d_i / Σ w_i`. Keep combined-view BLOB only as unweighted prefilter for top-k pruning before weighted rerank.
- **G (is this LSH-with-steps?):** **Justified only if unbind ships.** For indexing alone, Charikar simhash + multi-probe LSH (Lv 2007) gives same recall/throughput. What HDC adds is cluster explanation via unbind: "this hotspot shares callee X, loop pattern Y, error-handling Z." Hard test: **the hotspot UI must surface unbind output**, otherwise we ship simhash+LSH and delete the binding code.
- **H (layer redundancy):** **Ship 4, not 6.**
  - Lex × AST correlation ρ ≈ 0.6-0.8 — token-bag is downstream of tree shape. Drop Lex.
  - FS × Module correlation ρ ≈ 0.7+ in well-organized repos. Drop FS.
  - Keep AST, Semantic, Temporal, Module.
  - Schema enum keeps all 6 variants for cheap future optionality; populate 4 on day 1.

### Revised storage shape

```
_hdc(scope_id TEXT, layer_kind TEXT, hv BLOB(1024), basis INTEGER, PRIMARY KEY(scope_id, layer_kind))
-- layer_kind ∈ {ast, semantic, temporal, module, lex (reserved), fs (reserved)}
_hdc_combined(scope_id TEXT, hv BLOB(1024), basis INTEGER)
_hdc_baseline(layer_kind TEXT, median_distance INTEGER, mad INTEGER)  -- empirical r calibration
_hdc_subtree_cache(content_hash BLOB(32), hv BLOB(1024))  -- bidi recovery
```

### Final sub-bead numbering

- `hdc-1`: storage schema (4-layer enum extensible to 6)
- `hdc-2`: canonical-kind alphabet (`{Decl, Expr, Stmt, Block, Ref, Lit, Op}`) — single source of truth, per-parser mapping
- `hdc-3a`: AST codebook (named-only + arity-bucket + canonical-kind production-signature, Deckard-style leaf-erased Merkle)
- `hdc-3b`: Module codebook (structural module-hash, reuses CAS primitive)
- `hdc-3c`: Semantic codebook (Charikar signed-projection from dense embeddings)
- `hdc-3d`: Temporal codebook (time-decayed co-edit matrix + per-repo simhash)
- `hdc-4`: encoder — generic over `BaseCodebook` trait, content-hash subtree cache
- `hdc-5`: query ops — radius search, density count, unbind (hotspot explanation), combined-prefilter
- `hdc-6`: empirical radius calibration (10k random-pair sample at startup; per-layer r = d_med - 3·MAD)
- `hdc-7`: combined-view BLOB (unweighted XOR-bind prefilter only)
- `hdc-8`: cargo `hdc` feature flag, additive integration into ops registry
- `hdc-9`: integration tests — per-layer + combined + radius-calibration
- `hdc-10`: hotspot-explanation API surface (unbind → recover shared structural skeleton)

### Hard test we commit to

The hotspot UI must surface unbind output. If after `hdc-5`/`hdc-10` we can't render "this cluster shares structural skeleton X" from real unbind calls, we delete the binding code and ship simhash+LSH instead. This is the load-bearing test that justifies HDC over plain LSH.
comments.author: rsry-mcp

## Workspace placement correction — leyline-hdc is its own crate

User flagged: this is a Cargo workspace and HDC code should match the established pattern (one crate per capability). The workspace at `rs/Cargo.toml` auto-includes `ll-open/*`, and current crates are:

```
rs/ll-core/{core, schema}        — base primitives
rs/ll-open/{cli, cli-lib, fs, lsp, ts}
```

Each capability is a crate. `leyline-lsp` lives at `rs/ll-open/lsp/` and cli-lib uses it via:

```toml
leyline-lsp = { path = "../lsp", optional = true }
[features] lsp = ["dep:leyline-lsp"]
```

**HDC must mirror this.** Create `rs/ll-open/hdc/` as `leyline-hdc` crate. cli-lib pulls it in optionally under the `hdc` feature, just like LSP.

### Corrected file placement

The vast majority of HDC logic lives in the new crate:

```
rs/ll-open/hdc/                          (NEW CRATE: leyline-hdc)
├── Cargo.toml                           — blake3, deterministic-prng deps
└── src/
    ├── lib.rs                           — public surface
    ├── schema.rs                        — hdc-1 (CREATE TABLE _hdc, _hdc_combined, _hdc_baseline, _hdc_subtree_cache)
    ├── canonical.rs                     — hdc-2 (CanonicalKind enum + lookup trait)
    ├── canonical/
    │   ├── rust.rs, go.rs, python.rs, typescript.rs   — per-parser maps
    ├── codebook.rs                      — BaseCodebook trait
    ├── codebook/
    │   ├── ast.rs                       — hdc-3a (Deckard-style)
    │   ├── module.rs                    — hdc-3b (CAS-backed)
    │   ├── semantic.rs                  — hdc-3c (Charikar simhash)
    │   └── temporal.rs                  — hdc-3d (co-edit simhash)
    ├── encoder.rs                       — hdc-4 (HDC encoder, content-hash subtree cache)
    ├── query.rs                         — hdc-5 logic (radius/density/unbind/combined-prefilter)
    ├── popcount.rs                      — popcount UDF (registered into rusqlite::Connection by caller)
    ├── calibrate.rs                     — hdc-6 (radius baseline sampling)
    ├── combined.rs                      — hdc-7 (XOR-bind combined view)
    ├── explain.rs                       — hdc-10 (cluster centroid + skeleton recovery)
    └── util.rs                          — SplitMix64, blake3 helpers
```

The cli-lib daemon side gets the thin adapter only:

```
rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/daemon/
├── hdc_pass.rs                          — EnrichmentPass impl wrapping leyline_hdc::encoder
                                         — registers popcount UDF on Connection
                                         — ops handlers that delegate to leyline_hdc::query
```

### cli-lib changes (minimal, mirrors LSP pattern)

```toml
# rs/ll-open/cli-lib/Cargo.toml
[features]
hdc = ["dep:leyline-hdc"]

[dependencies]
leyline-hdc = { path = "../hdc", optional = true }
```

```rust
// rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/daemon/mod.rs
#[cfg(feature = "hdc")]
pub mod hdc_pass;
```

```rust
// rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/cmd_daemon.rs
#[cfg(feature = "hdc")]
{
    passes.extend(leyline_hdc::default_passes(...));
}
```

```rust
// rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/daemon/ops.rs
match op {
    #[cfg(feature = "hdc")]
    "hdc_search" => Some(crate::daemon::hdc_pass::op_hdc_search(ctx, req)),
    ...
}
```

### Workspace registration

`rs/Cargo.toml` workspace members glob `ll-open/*` already — adding `rs/ll-open/hdc/` directory is automatic.

### Why this matters

- `cli-lib` stays focused on the daemon (sockets, dispatch, lifecycle)
- `leyline-hdc` is independently testable, independently buildable
- Other consumers (e.g. ley-line private crate, future cloister gateway, mache integration) can depend on `leyline-hdc` directly without pulling in the daemon
- Mirrors the established LSP/FS/TS pattern — no new architectural precedent

### Sub-bead corrections

The 13 sub-beads currently list `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/daemon/hdc/...` paths. When implementing, **redirect to `rs/ll-open/hdc/src/...`** for everything except:
- `hdc-5` op-dispatch wiring → split: query logic in `leyline-hdc`, dispatch in `cli-lib/src/daemon/hdc_pass.rs`
- `hdc-8` cargo feature + integration → cli-lib only (just adds the optional dep + the pass registration)
- `hdc-9` integration tests → still in `cli-lib/tests/integration.rs` (they exercise the daemon)

I won't rewrite each sub-bead's `files` array as a separate edit — implementer (or future-me when scaffolding starts) reads this comment as the authoritative placement guide.

comments.text:
## IR layers (HIR / MIR / LLVM-IR) — the machine-native structural axes

User noted: HIR/IR layers belong in the topology stack. They're a strategic upgrade over AST for several reasons.

### Why IR layers leapfrog the codebook V0/V1 problem

The math friend flagged the canonical-kind alphabet (`hdc-2`) as the highest-leverage decision because raw parser kind-names aren't grammar-stable. **IR layers don't have this problem.** IRs are designed for the compiler, so their instruction sets ARE machine-defined canonical alphabets — picked by the compiler authors, deterministic per toolchain version, no human-readable label coupling.

| Layer | Catches equivalence after... | Source |
|-------|------------------------------|--------|
| AST | (syntactic) | tree-sitter |
| HIR | desugaring | rust-analyzer / gopls / tsc / mypy |
| MIR | CFG/data-flow simplification | rustc -Z dump-mir, go/ssa |
| LLVM-IR | optimization | rustc/clang LLVM backend |

Two functions written totally differently at source can be provably equivalent at MIR or LLVM-IR. That's *computational* equivalence, not the fuzzy dense-embedding "semantic" axis. Hotspot detection at MIR finds algorithmic dupes that AST and dense-semantic both miss.

### Cost tier matters

- **HIR is cheap** — rust-analyzer / gopls / tsc are already running for LSP enrichment. Sample their HIR walker output for fingerprinting; near-zero marginal cost.
- **MIR is expensive** — full rustc invocation per crate. Daemon-side enrichment opt-in.
- **LLVM-IR is very expensive** — full release-mode compile. Strictly research-grade.

### Layer stack with IR added

| Layer | Cost | Cross-language? | Layer kind enum |
|-------|------|-----------------|-----------------|
| AST | cheap | yes (via canonical alphabet) | ast |
| HIR | cheap | no (per-compiler) | hir |
| MIR | expensive | no | mir |
| LLVM-IR | very expensive | no | llvm |
| Module | cheap | yes | module |
| Semantic | cheap | yes (dense-embedded) | semantic |
| Temporal | cheap | yes | temporal |

Cross-language hotspot detection only works at AST + Module + Temporal layers. IR axes are intra-language but capture deeper structural truth. Both classes are valuable.

### Refined ship sequence (supersedes earlier "ship 4")

- **Ship 4 first** (math-friend verdict): AST + Module + Semantic + Temporal — the cross-language baseline.
- **Add HIR as fifth layer (hdc-3e)** — cheap, leapfrogs codebook problem, deeper structural truth per language. Feature-gated as `hdc_hir`.
- **MIR / LLVM-IR are deferred research** — file as `hdc-3f-research` and `hdc-3g-research` for later, behind `hdc_mir` / `hdc_llvm` flags.

### New sub-bead: hdc-3e (HIR codebook)

```rust
pub struct HirCodebook {
    lang: HirLang,  // Rust | Go | TypeScript | Python
}

impl BaseCodebook for HirCodebook {
    fn base_vector(&self, hir_node: &HirNode) -> [u8; D/8] {
        // Per-language: hash the HIR node's instruction kind + structural arity.
        // Rust: rust-analyzer's HIR walker produces enums like ExprKind::If, BlockKind, ...
        // Go: go/ssa produces typed instructions like *ssa.Call, *ssa.If, ...
        // No canonical alphabet mapping needed — the IR's enum IS the canonical alphabet.
        ...
    }
}
```

Storage: same `_hdc` table, `layer_kind = "hir"`. Same encoder, same query ops, no schema change.

### Why HIR over MIR for the cheap-tier addition

HIR preserves *source-level structure* in a desugared form. MIR is too low-level for hotspot detection (loop-unrolled, all control flow flattened to basic blocks — useful for "same algorithm" matching, but loses the "same function structure" signal). HIR is the sweet spot: deeper than AST, still recognizable as the source.

### Sub-bead numbering update

- `hdc-3e`: HIR codebook (per-language, opt-in via `hdc_hir` feature)
- `hdc-3f`: MIR codebook (deferred research, `hdc_mir` feature)
- `hdc-3g`: LLVM-IR codebook (deferred research, `hdc_llvm` feature)

Will file `hdc-3e` as a follow-up bead now that the design direction is captured.

title: leyline-ts/pyproject is declared but no shipping configuration enables it
description:
Found by the feature-reachability gate (ley-line-open-2607d2, instance 3).

`leyline-ts` declares:

    pyproject = ["dep:uv-pep508", "dep:uv-pep440", "dep:uv-normalize", "dep:toml"]

`cargo tree -f '{p} FEATURES={f}'` across all four shipping configurations (default, mount, all, full) shows it enabled by none. So the capability and its four dependencies are compiled out of every binary.

Unlike the other 25 leyline-ts features it is NOT a tree-sitter grammar — it is Python packaging-metadata parsing (PEP 508 dependency specifiers, PEP 440 versions). cli-lib's grammar list enumerates every other grammar explicitly, including the "Tier 1+2 bulk" added by ley-line-open-46ae48. `pyproject` is the single omission, which reads more like an oversight than a decision — but it could equally be deliberate, since it is a different kind of thing from the grammars around it.

Low severity: unlike ley-line-open-918a75 (splice), nothing appears to claim this capability works, and no test proves a behaviour the binary lacks. It is dead weight rather than a false promise. Filed so the not-shipping ledger entry has a real bead behind it instead of a bare suppression.

## Close condition

cargo build -p leyline-cli --no-default-features --features all, plus the reachability gate passing without the ledger line.

comments.text:
CORRECTION after reading the module — I filed this as a grammar-list omission and it is not that.

`rs/ll-open/ts/src/pyproject.rs` is 349 lines implementing a SECOND KIND OF PROJECTION, not a tree-sitter grammar. It parses pyproject.toml and projects Python package metadata into `nodes` as a mountable tree:

    /project/name              "gem"
    /project/requires-python   ">=3.11"
    /deps/accelerate           ">=1.10.0"
    /dev/pytest                ">=9.0.2"

That is the 'paths are queries' idea applied to a dependency graph rather than an AST — `ls /deps/` lists what a project depends on. Hence the uv-pep508/uv-pep440/uv-normalize deps: real PEP 508 specifier parsing.

TWO findings beyond the original one:

1. NOTHING CALLS IT. `project_pyproject` and `project_pyproject_into` have no callers anywhere outside their own module. So it is unwired AND compiled out — dead in two independent ways. That raises the question from 'add it to a feature list' to 'was this ever finished, and is the dependency projection still wanted?'

2. IT IS A FOURTH INTERPRETATION OF nodes.record. It calls leyline_schema::insert_node with version specifier strings. So that column holds: a JSON {data,properties} envelope (mache graph/sqlite.go:162), a raw AST leaf token (mache ast_walker_calls.go:341), raw file bytes (LLO graph.rs write_content), and now PEP 508 specifiers. Four, across two repos, with no discriminator.

Item 2 goes to ley-line-open-edec5b, which I had argued on three interpretations. Four is a stronger case, and the fourth arrived from a module nobody wired up — which is exactly how an undeclared contract accumulates meanings.

Revised close condition: decide whether the dependency projection is wanted. If yes it needs wiring AND a feature that ships AND a declared record contract for its rows. If no, remove the module and its four dependencies. Either way this stops being a one-line feature-list edit.
comments.author: rsry-cli

comments.text:
DECISION 2026-07-27: FINISH IT, do not remove.

Direction confirmed by jamestexas — a mountable dependency tree is wanted.

## The two deaths, and what finishing means for each

1. UNWIRED — nothing calls project_pyproject. Finishing means wiring it into a shipping path so the projection actually runs.
2. MIS-SCOPED — it is declared as a feature in the leyline-ts GRAMMAR lattice, but it is not a grammar. It is a 349-line pyproject.toml -> mountable /deps tree projection. Sitting in the grammar feature list is why it reads as 'just another language' in the reachability gate alongside rust/go/python.

Fixing (1) without (2) leaves it shipping under a misleading declaration. Give it a home that reflects what it is — a projection, not a parser.

## Completion condition

Same rule as 918a75: removing the ll-open/ts/pyproject line from the not-shipping ledger in tools/check_feature_reachability.sh, and having lint:feature-reachability still pass, IS the proof. The gate is the acceptance test.
comments.author: rsry-cli

acceptance_criteria: Either `pyproject` appears in cli-lib's leyline-ts feature list and a test exercises PEP 508/440 parsing through the shipped configuration, or the feature and its four dependencies are removed and the not-shipping ledger entry in tools/check_feature_reachability.sh goes with them. `sh tools/check_feature_reachability.sh .` passes either way, without the ledger line.

title: 5f7100-15: SQLite WAL adoption — file-backed live_db + connection pool (~600× p99 read win)
description:
Parent: 5f7100. Highest-leverage architectural move per empirical-validation-designer report at `docs/research/2026-05-08-workerd-wal-sqlite-experiment.md`.

## Why now

H1 measured (bench `wal_concurrent_readers.rs`): file-backed WAL @ N=10 readers + 1 writer hits **p99 reads of 290–375 µs** vs DELETE journal at **120–250 ms p99** — ~600× improvement. WAL@N=10 absolute throughput beats DELETE-solo by 3×. Daemon's current shape (`std::sync::Mutex<rusqlite::Connection>` over `:memory:`) cannot benefit because all readers serialize on the Mutex; reads collide with the snapshot writer.

H2 (workerd DO SQLite) and H3 (workerd V8 isolates sharing arena) both **fail** at the source level — workerd serializes everything per-DO via implicit txns and seals `sqlite3_deserialize` behind a `kj::Path`-only `Vfs`. Stay in-process Rust.

## Scope (two sub-beads)

### 5f7100-15a — file-backed live_db + WAL pragma
- `cmd_daemon.rs:410` — replace `Connection::open_in_memory()` with `Connection::open(live_db_path)` (path under arena dir, e.g. `${ctrl}.live.db`)
- Set `PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL`, `PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL`, `PRAGMA wal_autocheckpoint=1000` after open; verify journal_mode return value
- Warm-start path: skip arena→Cursor restore (file-backed is already persistent); Σ snapshot still flips arena
- Cold-start: `unlink` stale `.live.db` if Controller is FRESH
- Snapshot writer (`snapshot_to_arena` at cmd_daemon.rs:540) keeps using `serialize()` — output goes into mmap'd arena per Σ design

### 5f7100-15b — Mutex<Connection> → connection pool
- Introduce `LiveDbPool` (vec of `Connection` behind `parking_lot::Mutex<Vec<Connection>>` or `r2d2_sqlite`)
- Reader handlers (`with_live_db` in `daemon/ops.rs:221`) check out a connection, run query, return. ~30 call sites — most are reads.
- Writer handlers (op_reparse, op_load, op_flush, snapshot timer) keep exclusive lock semantics — single dedicated writer connection
- 30+ `live_db.lock()` / `with_live_db` call sites need conversion (see grep output for inventory)

## Followup risks
- Disk pressure: `:memory:` writes were free; WAL writes hit disk. Bench shows WAL@N=1 = 80K writes/sec which is fine, but cgroup-constrained envs may differ.
- Snapshot interaction: `serialize()` against a WAL'd db requires an exclusive write txn — confirm via small test before committing 15b.
- Test rig: `setup()` in tests/integration.rs creates many ephemeral daemons — ensure `.live.db` is rooted in TempDir, not leaked.

## Acceptance
- Bench `wal_concurrent_readers.rs` already exists; add a daemon-level integration variant that drives `op_get_node` from N=10 tasks while op_reparse runs and asserts p99 < 5ms.
- All existing integration tests pass.
- `task ci` green.

## Files cited (from agent report)
- `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/cmd_daemon.rs:200, 410, 535–584, 621–681`
- `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/daemon/ops.rs:81, 96, 630`
- `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/benches/wal_concurrent_readers.rs`
- `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/benches/wal_snapshot_experiment.rs`
- `docs/decades/2026-merkle-cas-substrate.md` §1.5 (arena ↔ Σ mapping)
- `docs/research/2026-05-08-workerd-wal-sqlite-experiment.md` (this report)

title: ghcr images are published unsigned — nothing attests they came from this workflow
description:
Found 2026-08-04 during a cross-repo supply-chain sweep from notme. Verified against this tree, not inferred.

FINDING: .github/workflows/release.yml publishes to ghcr.io/agentic-research/ley-line-open and there is NO cosign anywhere in the repo — `grep -rl cosign .github/workflows/ Taskfile.yml` returns zero files. So published images carry no signature and no attestation.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN "we should sign things": the registry push credential is not a trust anchor and cannot be made into one. Anyone who obtains it can push an image. What normally bounds that is a keyless signature — an attacker with only a push token has no OIDC identity, so they cannot produce one, and a consumer who verifies rejects their image. With no signature at all, there is nothing for a consumer to verify against and the push credential IS the whole of the security model.

The workflow already grants `id-token: write` (1 occurrence), so the OIDC identity keyless signing needs is present. The gap is the signing itself.

REFERENCE IMPLEMENTATION, worth copying rather than reinventing — notme's Taskfile `image:publish:*`:

1. Sign the DIGEST, never the tag. A tag is mutable; a re-push moves it and strands the signature on something else.
2. If using apko, take the digest from `--image-refs` and use the LAST line — apko writes per-arch manifests first and the multi-arch INDEX last, and the tag resolves to the index. Signing the first line signs a child manifest, so `cosign verify <image>:<tag>` finds no signature and the signing is silently useless.
3. `cosign attest --type spdxjson` for the SBOM against the same digest.
4. VERIFY IMMEDIATELY AFTER SIGNING, in the same job, against `https://github.com/${GITHUB_WORKFLOW_REF}` as an EXACT identity (not a regex). Without this, a signature nothing checks is indistinguishable from one that silently did not happen — notme shipped three npm releases whose `--provenance` flag was a no-op for exactly that reason (notme-77ead7).
5. When documenting the consumer verify command, pin the identity to the release WORKFLOW, not just the repo. notme's published command was `^https://github.com/agentic-research/notme/` with no terminator, which matched any workflow in the repo — so any workflow with `id-token: write` could produce a signature that passed it.

See notme docs/design/016-signing-surfaces.md and notme PR #65.

NOT filed as a shared GitHub Action deliberately. A verify step supplied by another repo means a mistake or compromise there silently neuters the check in every consumer — and the check exists to catch exactly that class of event. Twenty lines of independent shell is the right amount of duplication here.

comments.text: Signet blocker resolved: agentic-research/signet#145 merged as `8af4e08fe4408a9b6a4e71bf2b92abe0068eee41`. The reusable, language-neutral file-artifact Action is `agentic-research/signet/.github/actions/sign-artifact@8af4e08fe4408a9b6a4e71bf2b92abe0068eee41`; it supports a Cloister-hosted Notme authority by setting the authority URL to the cluster's `/identity` route. Filed `ley-line-open-a28476` for signing GitHub Release/Rust file assets. Keep `ley-line-open-9abefd` focused on OCI image digest signing plus SBOM attestation.
comments.author: rsry-mcp

acceptance_criteria: Published ghcr images carry a cosign keyless signature over the image DIGEST plus an SBOM attestation, verified in the same job against the exact GITHUB_WORKFLOW_REF identity, with the release failing if verification does not pass. Consumer-facing verify command pins the release workflow, not just the repository.

title: Readiness signal: daemon notifies mache when initial parse + arena load is complete
description:
mache starts before daemon finishes parsing → gets empty graph. Need a signal.

Options:
1. UDS op: `{"op": "status"}` → `{"state": "ready", "generation": 3, "files_parsed": 190}`
2. Control block field: `ready` flag alongside generation
3. Arena convention: generation 0 = not ready, generation > 0 = has data

mache's HotSwapGraph poller already detects generation bumps. The simplest fix: daemon doesn't bump generation until first parse is complete. mache waits (already has 30s timeout in buildControlGraph). But mache should surface "still loading" to MCP clients instead of returning empty results.

title: Progressive/streaming parse: incremental arena flips as files are parsed
description:
Instead of parsing all files → single arena flip, flip incrementally:
parse batch of N files → load partial .db → arena flip → mache hot-swaps → continue

mache's graph grows progressively. MCP tools return partial results immediately. Users don't wait 10s for the first response.

Design:
- Batch size: 10-20 files per flip (balance latency vs overhead)
- Each flip is a complete valid .db (just with fewer files)
- Sheaf topology can inform batch order (high-fan-in files first)
- node_refs/node_defs populated incrementally as files are parsed

comments.text: Subsumed by decade ley-line-open-eb0252 (living daemon). Progressive parse is step 4 of the daemon lifecycle.

title: Priority queue: user MCP request promotes files to front of parse queue
description:
When mache receives find_callers("NormalizeID") during initial parse, it should tell the daemon "parse graph/graph.go next" so the user gets results faster.

Flow:
1. MCP tool request → mache can't resolve → missing file
2. mache sends {"op": "prioritize", "files": ["graph/graph.go"]} over UDS
3. daemon moves those files to front of parse queue
4. parse → flip → mache hot-swaps → retries the tool request

Requires: daemon parse queue (not just sequential walk), UDS prioritize op, mache retry-after-swap logic.

comments.text: Subsumed by decade ley-line-open-eb0252 (living daemon). Priority queue depends on the file watcher + reparse loop.

title: Git-aware incremental reparse: use git status/diff to determine what changed
description:
The daemon should use git to determine what needs reparsing:

1. On startup: `git status --porcelain` → untracked + modified files → parse those first
2. On file change: `git diff --name-only HEAD` → only reparse changed files
3. On branch switch: `git diff --name-only HEAD@{1}..HEAD` → bulk reparse the delta
4. Store last-parsed commit SHA in the .db metadata → skip files unchanged since then

Categories:
- new (untracked): parse from scratch, add to .db
- modified: reparse, update _ast + node_refs + node_defs for that file
- deleted: remove from .db
- unchanged: skip

The git SHA becomes the cache key. If the .db was built at commit abc123 and HEAD is now abc456, only files in the diff need reparsing. This makes subsequent daemon starts near-instant for clean repos.

comments.text: Subsumed by decade ley-line-open-eb0252 (living daemon). Git-aware reparse is step 3 of the daemon lifecycle.

title: Make release publication one fail-closed Taskfile operation
description: The v0.10.3 recovery exposed a split release contract: payload assets can publish without the public SHA256SUMS asset, and the root release tag can exist without the nested clients/go/leyline-schema tag. Add one Taskfile-owned release publication entrypoint that validates a clean exact source commit and aligned versions, creates or verifies immutable root and nested Go-module tags at that commit, delegates multi-platform builds to the existing workflow, verifies all staged payloads before publication, publishes an aggregate SHA256SUMS that never lists itself, and performs public postflight checks including go list -m for the nested module. Publication must be structurally gated so upload cannot execute after verification fails.

comments.text: Design decision approved 2026-07-26: artifact versions are independent. PR #272 changes AGPL storage/CDC implementation but not the Apache-2.0 public schema contract, so the next binary release is v0.10.4 while clients/go/leyline-schema remains v0.10.3. release:publish must read and verify SCHEMA_VERSION, require public resolution of the compatible nested schema tag, and create a new nested tag only when the Apache-licensed schema version actually advances. Empirical packaging proof: the source submodule and downloaded v0.10.3 Go module each contain clients/go/leyline-schema/LICENSE with Apache-2.0; the nested license prevents Go module packaging from inheriting the repository-root AGPL LICENSE.
comments.author: rsry-cli

title: δ⁰-driven reaper: daemon op returns reclaimable regions, payload-blind
description:
## Premise

Today `sheaf_invalidate` answers "which regions are invalid right now?" — useful but not operationalized into eviction. mache (and any future consumer) needs to know "which cache keys can I free?" without LLO inspecting their payload. This is the GC piece of the sheaf-as-cache-coherence story.

## What this op does

New daemon op `sheaf_reap` (UDS + MCP). Given the current `CellComplex` state, returns a structured list of region IDs whose stalks fail the δ⁰ projection check AND whose downstream BFS neighbours also fail. The consumer evicts those keys without LLO knowing what their cached payload was.

This is structurally identical to file-system inotify-driven cache eviction — the trigger is structural (boundary failed), the payload is opaque.

## Wire shape

```capnp
struct ReapRequest {
  # Empty for now; future: scope to a subgraph.
}
struct ReapResponse {
  reclaimable @0 :List(Text);  # region IDs the consumer should evict
  generation @1 :UInt64;       # sheaf generation when this snapshot was computed
  reaped_at_defect @2 :Float32;  # current Σ‖δ⁰‖² at compute time, for diagnostics
}
```

## Algorithm sketch

1. Walk all regions in the complex.
2. For each, run `RestrictionMap::project` on its stalk.
3. Compare against baseline (`refresh_baseline`'s snapshot).
4. Any region where `‖δ⁰‖² > DELTA0_EPS_SQUARED` joins the seed set.
5. BFS outward from seeds through the restriction graph.
6. Return the union as `reclaimable`.

## Falsifiability gates

1. Reaper output is a superset of the regions that have changed stalks (no false negatives).
2. Reaper output is empty when nothing has changed (no false positives on noise).
3. Payload-blind: same test with two different `Stalk` impls (f32 vector vs alternative numeric type) yields identical reclaim set.
4. Black-box UDS test: real daemon, no in-process `cache().put()` cheats.

## Files

- `rs/ll-core/public-schema/capnp/daemon.capnp` — add ReapRequest/ReapResponse
- `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/daemon/sheaf_ops.rs` — handler
- `rs/ll-open/sheaf/src/cache.rs` — `SheafCache::reap()` method that walks the complex and returns reclaim set
- `rs/ll-open/sheaf/tests/falsifiability_gates.rs` — gates 1-3
- `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/tests/sheaf_uds_blackbox_test.rs` — gate 4

## Relationship to other beads

- Depends on conceptual model from [[ley-line-open-d03e7d]] (cascade contract)
- Pairs with [[ley-line-open-9ccbc7-followup-prior-gen]] (task #84) — the reap response includes the generation so consumers can correlate
- Depends on `sheaf_update_topology` (task #82) being in place so the test can demonstrate "topology shifts → reap returns the affected subgraph, not the whole world"

title: Cold-parse insert phase: BufWriter capnp dual-write + defer indexes
description:
## Empirical baseline

Just-measured on `~/github/art/mache` (mixed-language repo, 764 files):

```
leyline parse: 5.32s wall / 745 MB peak RSS
  - parse  90.2ms  (rayon-parallel tree-sitter)
  - insert 4.10s   (single-conn serial SQLite insert + capnp dual-write)
```

The insert phase is **45× slower than tree-sitter**. Root cause: not the SQL layer (which is well-formed: `BEGIN ... COMMIT` + `prepare_cached` + `synchronous=OFF`) — it's the capnp dual-write inside the same transaction loop.

## Audit findings (Agent A, read-only)

| # | Finding | Location | Cost on baseline |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | capnp `write_ast_node_record` issues one `write(2)` per AST node into an unbuffered `File`. ~380K syscalls for a typical Go repo. | `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/cmd_parse.rs:460-464` | **1.5-2.5s** |
| 2 | CREATE INDEX runs at DDL time, so every INSERT pays B-tree maintenance per-row instead of one O(N log N) sort after load. | `rs/ll-open/ts/src/schema.rs:37-38, 104-114` + `rs/ll-core/schema/src/lib.rs:41` | **0.8-1.5s** |
| 3 | `ensure_dirs` uses unprepared `conn.execute` per novel dir component. | `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/cmd_parse.rs:1049-1053` | ~15ms |
| 4 | Missing `PRAGMA mmap_size` + `PRAGMA temp_store=MEMORY` for bulk-load workload. | `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/cmd_parse.rs:102-111` | ~100ms |

## Scope

Two surgical changes (items 1 + 2) that close 2.3-4.0s of the 4.1s budget. Items 3 + 4 are hygiene; include if cheap.

1. **Wrap the capnp output `File` in `BufWriter<File>`** (4 MB buffer) before the insert loop opens. Flush on `COMMIT`. Collapses ~380K unbuffered `write(2)` calls into dozens of buffered ones.
2. **Defer `CREATE INDEX` until after the insert loop.** Move every `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS ...` out of the DDL strings in `ts/src/schema.rs` and `ll-core/schema/src/lib.rs` into a new `create_indexes_post_load(conn)` function. Call it in `parse_into_conn` after `COMMIT`.
3. **Hoist `ensure_dirs` to `prepare_cached`.** Pass the prepared statement into the function as a parameter.
4. **Add the two missing pragmas** to `cmd_parse::cmd_parse` after the existing block.

Do NOT touch `parse_into_conn`'s outer shape or the `to_parse` ordering — that's owned by the topology pre-pass bead (parallel sibling).

## Falsifiability gates

Gate 1 (wall-clock primary):
```
time leyline parse ~/github/art/mache -o /tmp/bench.db
```
- ✅ pass: total wall < **1.0s** (was 5.32s, target ~0.5-1.0s)
- ❌ fail if total wall ≥ 2.0s — didn't move the needle enough; revisit before merging

Gate 2 (correctness):
- Existing `cli-lib/tests/integration.rs` suite all green
- Row counts in `nodes`, `_ast`, `node_refs`, `node_defs`, `_imports`, `_file_index` **byte-identical** to a baseline run before the change. Generate the baseline once on main, store as a fixture.

Gate 3 (no regression in incremental):
- `time leyline parse ~/github/art/mache -o /tmp/bench.db` (warm — `_file_index` populated, 0 dirty files)
- Must be **faster than** the cold case post-fix. Incremental should hit the "0 to_parse" early-exit and finish in <100ms.

## Non-goals

- Topology-aware ordering (separate bead).
- Schema redesign of `_ast` table.
- Changing capnp serialization shape (just the I/O wrapper).

## Why parallel-safe

Files: `cmd_parse.rs`, `ts/src/schema.rs`, `ll-core/schema/src/lib.rs`. Does NOT touch `topology_pass.rs` (new file, owned by parallel bead). Does NOT touch any ADR or docs. Dispatchable in parallel with the topology + lazy-access beads.

comments.text:
## Gate results

Branch: `fix/ley-line-open-9ccbc7` (worktree at `/Users/jamesgardner/.rsry/worktrees/ley-line-open/ley-line-open-9ccbc7`)
Commits (unpushed — gate #1 failed):
- `d23ad4e` perf(cmd_parse): defer index creation until after COMMIT
- `1b73a7d` perf(cmd_parse): wrap capnp dual-write in BufWriter

### Gate 1: wall-clock < 1.0s — ✗ FAIL

Both audit-cited changes applied successfully, but on this machine the wall clock did not collapse to <1s. The two changes still account for a ~35% reduction:

Apples-to-apples runs against current mache (765 files, freshly stat-cached):

| Run | Baseline (main) | Patched |
|-----|-----------------|---------|
| 1   | 7.32s (insert 5.6s) | 6.18s (insert 3.9s) |
| 2   | 7.70s (insert 6.4s) | 4.46s (insert 3.4s) |
| 3   | 8.48s (insert 7.1s) | 5.04s (insert 3.4s) |
| **Median wall** | **7.70s** | **5.04s** |
| **Median insert** | **6.4s** | **3.4s** |
| **Median parse** | 143ms | 200ms |

The audit's predicted "5.32s → <1s" assumed the insert phase was ~100% of the gap. Empirically the insert phase compresses ~47% (6.4s → 3.4s) — that's the indexes-deferred + BufWriter wins, both real and measurable — but the residual non-insert work isn't bounded by either change. Profiling on an instrumented build attributes:

- `write_head_after_parse` (Σ root hash): ~400–550ms per run, dominated by re-reading and `canonicalize()`ing the 163 MB ast.capnp segment from disk.
- `sweep_orphaned_dirs` + meta writes + connection close: ~500ms.
- Insert phase floor: 2.4–3.4s even with deferred indexes (still ~534k single-row INSERTs through prepared statements with B-tree maintenance on the primary keys).

To hit <1s, additional work outside this bead's scope is needed (e.g. batching INSERT statements, deferring/short-circuiting `write_head_after_parse` to a lazy pass, or eliminating the cold-cache `canonicalize()` re-read in Σ root).

### Gate 2: integration tests — ✓ PASS

```
cargo test -p leyline-cli-lib --test integration --release
test result: ok. 44 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out
```

Full unit suite across the touched crates (leyline-schema, leyline-ts, leyline-cli-lib) also clean: 277 tests passing.

### Gate 3: row count parity — ✓ PASS

Byte-identical across all 7 tables on the mache fixture (765 files):

| Table | Baseline | Patched |
|-------|----------|---------|
| nodes | 534630 | 534630 |
| _ast | 534553 | 534553 |
| node_refs | 39534 | 39534 |
| node_defs | 2634 | 2634 |
| _imports | 1593 | 1593 |
| _file_index | 765 | 765 |
| _source | 765 | 765 |

### Honest surprises

- **The audit's baseline was 5.32s wall / 4.10s insert; on this machine today, baseline measured 7.70s / 6.4s.** Same fileset (mache @ 95ad816 + the 4 untracked subdirs that drove the count to 765), same binary build flags (release LTO=thin, codegen=1). Likely transient — laptop thermal state, FS cache hit rates, etc. The relative win is what matters.
- **The "1 file delta" was real.** Initial baseline I captured (against the snapshot the audit measured against) used 764 files; mid-run a `git status` showed `?? cmd/pack.go` plus 3 untracked dirs in mache. Re-ran both baseline and patched against the 765-file state for the comparison above.
- **BufWriter flush ordering is load-bearing.** `write_head_after_parse` re-reads the capnp segments from disk; without an explicit `flush()` before that pass, the buffered tail would be invisible to the Σ root and the chain hash would disagree with the on-disk bytes once the writer dropped. Caught this by reading `write_head_after_parse` carefully — no test would have failed loudly (the head-write is best-effort and logs on error) but the chain invariant would silently break. Added explicit flush+drop before COMMIT.
- **The schema-split keeps the unified path intact for non-bulk callers.** `create_schema` / `create_ast_schema` / `create_refs_schema` still create indexes; only `parse_into_conn` uses the new `create_*_tables` + `create_post_load_indexes` variants. This was required because `leyline-lsp`, `leyline-fs`, daemon ops, `ts/project.rs`, `ts/pyproject.rs`, `fs/graph.rs`, and the test helpers all depend on the unified path producing indexed connections.

### Decision

Per the bead's instruction ("push when done — or leave unpushed if the gates don't pass — surface the failure honestly"), the commits are local-only. The work is real and the row-count contract is preserved; the wall-clock gate as written is not achievable with just these two changes.

title: sheaf_update_topology: incremental delta op (foundation for sheaf-as-GC)
description:
## Premise

Today `sheaf_set_topology` replaces the entire `CellComplex` atomically. Every region rebuild — even a 2-region delta in a 1000-region graph — invalidates the full cache. This makes the sheaf functionally bulk-replace, which is unusable for a streaming GC consumer.

We need an incremental op that applies a delta and preserves cached entries for untouched regions.

## What this op does

New daemon op `sheaf_update_topology` (UDS + MCP). Takes a delta payload describing added regions, removed regions, edge additions/removals, and stalk updates. Applies it to the in-memory `CellComplex`, re-runs `refresh_baseline` ONLY for the regions in the delta's footprint + their direct BFS neighbours (radius 1), and returns the generation counter so consumers can correlate.

## Wire shape

```capnp
struct TopologyDelta {
  addedRegions @0 :List(RegionInput);
  removedRegions @1 :List(Text);
  addedEdges @2 :List(EdgeInput);
  removedEdges @3 :List(EdgeRef);
  updatedStalks @4 :List(StalkUpdate);
}

struct UpdateTopologyRequest {
  delta @0 :TopologyDelta;
  nodeStalkDim @1 :UInt32;
}

struct UpdateTopologyResponse {
  generation @0 :UInt64;
  affectedRegions @1 :List(Text);  # for consumer awareness
  defectAfter @2 :Float32;          # post-update Σ‖δ⁰‖² for diagnostics
}
```

## Algorithm sketch

1. Lock the cache.
2. For each removedEdge → remove from restriction graph.
3. For each removedRegion → drop region + all edges touching it.
4. For each addedRegion → insert into complex with its stalk + agreement_dim.
5. For each addedEdge → wire restriction map.
6. For each updatedStalk → replace stalk bytes for that region.
7. Compute the affected-region set: union of touched regions + their radius-1 BFS neighbours.
8. Re-run `refresh_baseline` over this subgraph only (not the whole complex).
9. Increment generation, return affected set + post-update defect.

## Falsifiability gates

1. Apply a single-region edit to a 100-region complex → the cache entries for the 99 untouched regions survive verbatim.
2. Apply removeEdge → affected_regions includes both endpoints exactly once.
3. Apply addRegion → the new region's baseline matches `set_topology`-from-scratch.
4. Concurrency: two threads calling update_topology serialise correctly (CellComplex behind Mutex).
5. Black-box UDS: real daemon, no in-process back-doors.

## Files

- `rs/ll-core/public-schema/capnp/daemon.capnp` — add the 5 messages above
- `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/daemon/sheaf_ops.rs` — `op_sheaf_update_topology` handler
- `rs/ll-open/sheaf/src/complex.rs` — `CellComplex::apply_delta(delta) -> AffectedRegions`
- `rs/ll-open/sheaf/src/cache.rs` — partial `refresh_baseline_subset(regions)` method
- `rs/ll-open/sheaf/tests/falsifiability_gates.rs` — gates 1-4
- `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/tests/sheaf_uds_blackbox_test.rs` — gate 5

## Relationship to other beads

- Prereq for [[ley-line-open-9c867f]] (reaper) — without incremental updates, the reaper just sees full-graph churn
- Pairs with task #84's prior_generation work — the response carries the generation counter

## Out of scope

- Network-level streaming protocol (HTTP/2 server-sent events for sheaf events). The op returns a single response per call; long-poll comes later.
- Versioned schema migrations. We assume schema is pinned per LLO version.

Decade-level architectural primitive: a content-addressed, Merkle-structured, CAS-advanced state substrate Σ = (𝓥, 𝓒, ρ, σ, R, S) is necessary to satisfy the platform's R1–R7 requirements (concurrent writes, cross-host distribution, integrity, crash consistency, time-travel, registry-scale partial updates, compositionality with workerd/signet/mache/rosary).

The current arena protocol (Controller, ArenaHeader, HotSwapGraph) is a degenerate case of Σ — sequence-named instead of hash-named. ADR-A (Sheaf Cache, Čech cohomology) and ADR-B (Merkle Sheaf Sync) are upper layers built on Σ.

This decade decomposes into 7 threads:
- T1: Mathematical foundations (substrate + necessity proof + falsifiability)
- T2: Controller migration (current_root replaces generation)
- T3: Content-addressed blob store (git-shaped objects/)
- T4: Subtree Merkle structure (per-file/per-table)
- T5: Composition seams (signet/workerd/rosary/mache integration)
- T6: Concurrent-write protocol (optimistic CCC + rebase)

title: Topology pre-pass module: walk + manifest + regex import sweep (no integration)
description:
## Premise

LLO's ingest is topologically blind: `collect_files` produces a flat `Vec<PathBuf>`, `par_iter` parses each independently, no community awareness, no parse ordering. The filesystem already carries structure (sizes, manifests, naming conventions, import-shape regex) we don't exploit.

This bead builds the **standalone topology pre-pass module** — Phases A-C of the full design — without integrating into `cmd_parse.rs`. Integration is a sibling bead that depends on this + the insert-fix bead landing first.

Design source: Agent B's blueprint (~600 lines, attached as comment).

## Scope

New module at `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/topology_pass.rs`:

```rust
pub fn run(files: &[PathBuf], source: &Path) -> Result<TopologyOutput>;

pub struct TopologyOutput {
    pub parse_order: Vec<usize>,
    pub file_regions: Vec<FileRegion>,
    pub edge_estimates: Vec<EdgeEstimate>,
    pub region_edges: Vec<(RegionId, RegionId, f32)>,
    pub stats: TopologyStats,
}
```

Sub-phases (run sequentially inside `run`):

- **P1 walk + stat** — reuse `collect_files` + `is_bloat_dir` predicates from `cmd_parse.rs` (just import them; do not modify). Capture `FileMeta { size, mtime, extension, depth }` from `DirEntry::metadata()` — zero extra syscalls vs the current walk.
- **P2 manifest scan** — detect `Cargo.toml`, `go.mod`, `package.json`, `pyproject.toml`, `setup.cfg`, `BUILD`, `BUILD.bazel`, `WORKSPACE`, `requirements.txt`, `Pipfile`. Each manifest anchors a region; files beneath inherit (union-find by directory ancestry).
- **P3 regex import sweep** — for each file in the parseable subset, read first 4KB, apply language-keyed patterns:
  - Go: `^import\s+` (single + block)
  - Rust: `^use\s+`
  - Python: `^(?:from\s+\S+\s+)?import\s+`
  - TS/JS: `^import\s+` and `^const\s+\S+\s*=\s*require\(`
  - C/C++: `^#include\s*[<"]`
  Resolve specifiers against the known file list by suffix-match + manifest-relative path.

Module surface only — `run` returns `TopologyOutput`; no daemon ops, no `parse_into_conn` changes, no SQL.

## Falsifiability gates

**Gate 1 (cost ceiling).** On a 1000-file synthetic fixture (commit it under `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/tests/fixtures/topology/`):
- ✅ pass: `run(files, source)` returns in **<150ms** wall (criterion bench)
- ❌ fail if >200ms — either the regex sweep is too slow or the manifest scan is doing too much

**Gate 2 (recall).** Unit test with hand-crafted fixture files:
- Go file with `import "github.com/foo/bar"` + Rust file `use crate::baz::qux;` + Python `from foo.bar import baz` + TS `import { x } from './util';`
- ✅ pass: regex sweep recovers **≥4 of the 4** imports as `EdgeEstimate` entries

|---|------|--------|---------|
| 1 | Cost ceiling <150ms on 1000 files | PASS | debug **48.31ms**, release **17.80ms** on 1005 files; 5 regions, 3770 edges |
| 2 | ≥4/4 language imports detected, confidence > 0 | PASS | Go `main.go → bar.go` (1.000), Python `main.py → bar.py` (1.000), Rust `lib.rs → baz.rs` (0.900), TS `main.ts → util.ts` (1.000) |

### Design notes
- Resolver is **language-preferred**: a Go import's `last` component first tries `.go`, only then falls back to other extensions. Without this, `import "github.com/foo/bar"` was resolving to `bar.py` because the basename `bar.py` exists in the fixture (Gate 2 caught this on first run).

- `TopologyStats` carries `elapsed_us` (non-deterministic) plus `for_determinism()` which projects it out — used by Gate 4 to compare runs.
