title: T3: V1 — bigram binding extension (conditional on T2 pass)
description:
Thread under decade ley-line-open-a660ab. **Hard gated on T2 passing both τ_dense and τ_sym.** If V0 falsifies, T3 does not run.

V0 explicitly forfeits sentence-level word order (Dog bites man ≡ Man bites dog at sentence level). V1 reclaims local order by layering shift-invariant bigram binding at the sentence level:

```
sentence level:   HV(sentence) = Σ_i ( HV(word_i) ⊗ HV(word_{i+1}) )
```

## Beads

- T3.1: add bigram binding layer at sentence level (extend encoder.rs)
- T3.2: re-run STS-B with bigram extension; verify τ_dense still passes (risk: bigram halves overlap, may dip below threshold)
- T3.3: add new symbolic claim — word-bigram-partner recovery; commit threshold ex-ante before measurement
- T3.4: decide V2 (parser-aware role-filler binding) or stop

## Why P2

Lower priority than V0 because:
- V0 must pass first (gating)
- V1's incremental value is order-sensitivity, useful but not the load-bearing claim
- The decade's headline result is V0's existence; V1 is refinement

title: T1.1: hdc-translate crate scaffold + BLAKE3-seeded BPE codebook
description:
Bead 1.1 of T1 under decade ley-line-open-a660ab. Foundation crate.

## Deliverables

- `rs/ll-open/hdc-translate/Cargo.toml` — depends on `leyline-hdc`, `tokenizers` (HuggingFace tokenizers Rust crate), `blake3` (already in workspace)
- `rs/ll-open/hdc-translate/src/lib.rs` — module re-exports
- `rs/ll-open/hdc-translate/src/codebook.rs` — `BlakeCodebook` struct: BPE token → bipolar HV via BLAKE3 seed expansion. Deterministic, no learned parameters, codebook seed locked at 0.
- `rs/ll-open/hdc-translate/src/tokenizer.rs` — GPT-2 BPE wrapper (50,257 token vocab; pulls the canonical merges/vocab).

## Codebook contract (locked per ADR / decade write-up)

```rust
fn token_hv(bpe_id: u32) -> [i8; D] {
    // 1. seed = blake3::hash(bpe_id.to_le_bytes() || token_text.as_bytes())
    // 2. expand seed to 10000 bytes via BLAKE3 XOF
    // 3. for each byte, take low bit; map 0 → -1, 1 → +1
    // returns Vec<i8> of length 10000
}
```

D = 10000. Bipolar `{-1, +1}`. Reproducibility: bit-exact across machines, build configs, rust versions.

## Tests

- `codebook_is_deterministic` — same BPE id → same HV across two builds
- `codebook_distinct_tokens_are_near_orthogonal` — pairwise cosine on a sample of 1000 tokens has mean |cosine| < 0.05 (high-D random vectors are near-orthogonal)
- `codebook_bipolar_invariant` — every element in {-1, +1}; no zeros, no other values

## Acceptance

`cargo test -p leyline-hdc-translate codebook` green. Crate compiles in workspace. No clippy warnings.

title: T1.2: V0 encoder (sub-word permutation + sentence/document BoW)
description:
Bead 1.2 of T1. The V0 encoder. **Locked architecture per decade §2.3** — no design choices made here, only implementation.

## Encoder (locked)

```text
sub-word level:   HV(word)     = Σ_j Π^j ( codebook(bpe_j) )
sentence level:   HV(sentence) = Σ_i HV(word_i)              ← BoW; no Π
document level:   HV(doc)      = Σ_k HV(sentence_k)          ← BoW
```

Where Σ is bundle (element-wise sum + sign-thresholding for bipolar majority vote), Π is cyclic shift by integer offset.

## Deliverables

- `rs/ll-open/hdc-translate/src/encoder.rs` — `V0Encoder` struct with methods:
  - `encode_word(&self, word: &str) -> Hypervector` — BPE-tokenize the word, apply sub-word level
  - `encode_sentence(&self, sentence: &str) -> Hypervector` — split into words, apply sentence level
  - `encode_document(&self, doc: &str) -> Hypervector` — split into sentences (simple `.`/`?`/`!` split), apply document level

## Tests

- `anagram_test` — `encode_word("cat") ≠ encode_word("act")`. Cosine should be far from 1 (positional permutation differentiates).
- `morphological_overlap` — `encode_word("happy")` and `encode_word("happiness")` share BPE tokens, cosine should be > 0.3 (well above orthogonal)
- `bow_shift_invariance` — `encode_sentence("dog cat fish")` ≡ `encode_sentence("fish dog cat")` (BoW; this is the explicit V0 forfeit, pin so V1 can break it intentionally)
- `same_bytes_invariant` — encoder produces a single `Hypervector` per input; both readouts (T1.3, T1.4) consume that same vector. Not a unit test in this bead per se, but document the contract.

## Acceptance

`cargo test -p leyline-hdc-translate encoder` green. Hypervectors round-trip through bipolar `{-1, +1}` (no float/int mixing).

title: T1.3: dense readout — JL projection + STS-B harness + Spearman
description:
Bead 1.3 of T1. The dense readout — projects D=10000 HDC vectors down to d=384 (matching MiniLM output) via Johnson-Lindenstrauss, then computes Spearman ρ on STS-B test split.

## JL projection (locked)

- Random matrix `R ∈ ℝ^{10000 × 384}` with entries `~ N(0, 1/D)`
- Seed locked at 0 (reproducibility — codebook seed and projection seed are both 0; orthogonal RNGs to prevent collision)
- **Never trained, never updated**. Lock the bytes once and they're permanent.
- Save to `rs/ll-open/hdc-translate/src/projection.bin` so the projection is bit-exact across machines (or generate from seed at build time — pick whichever gives the cleanest reproducibility story)

## Deliverables

- `rs/ll-open/hdc-translate/src/readout_dense.rs`:
  - `JLProjection` struct holding the fixed matrix
  - `project(hv: &Hypervector) -> Vec<f32>` — `R^T @ hv` (or equivalent fast variant)
  - `cosine(a: &[f32], b: &[f32]) -> f32`
  - STS-B fixture loader (test split, 1379 sentence pairs, gold scores 0.0–5.0 normalized to 0–1)
  - `eval_sts_b(encoder: &V0Encoder, projection: &JLProjection) -> f64` — returns Spearman ρ

## STS-B fixture

- Public benchmark; download once, commit under `rs/ll-open/hdc-translate/tests/fixtures/sts_b_test.tsv`
- Format: each line = `(score_normalized, sentence_a, sentence_b)`
- Source: official STS-B test split, no curation

## Tests

- `jl_projection_preserves_pairwise_distances` — sample 100 random hypervectors, compute pairwise cosine in HDC space and projected space, assert correlation > 0.9 (JL property)
- `sts_b_fixture_loads` — assert 1379 rows, all scores in [0,1]
- `eval_sts_b_runs_to_completion` — smoke test, doesn't assert ρ value (T2.1 measures it)

## Acceptance

`cargo test -p leyline-hdc-translate readout_dense` green. The Spearman computation is correct (sanity-check against `scipy.stats.spearmanr` on a tiny fixture; commit the comparison output).

title: T1.4: symbolic readout — depth-3 BPE recovery harness against CC-100 sample
description:
Bead 1.4 of T1. The symbolic readout — given an encoded word HV, recover the BPE token at sub-word position j via inverse-permutation + nearest-neighbor in the codebook.

## Recovery procedure (locked)

```text
Given: HV(word) = Σ_j Π^j(codebook(bpe_j))
Want: bpe_k for some k ∈ [0, len(word_bpe))

Step 1: candidate = Π^{-k}(HV(word))
Step 2: for each token in codebook: similarity = cosine(candidate, codebook(token))
Step 3: predicted_bpe_k = argmax_token similarity
```

This is approximate unbinding via inverse permutation + codebook nearest-neighbor cleanup. Plate's HRR cleanup pattern.

## Held-out composition fixture

- Sample 1000 depth-3 words from CC-100 English (words whose BPE tokenization yields exactly 3 BPE tokens)
- Sampling seed locked at 0
- Held-out from any process touching the codebook (codebook is hash-based so this is automatic)
- Commit under `rs/ll-open/hdc-translate/tests/fixtures/cc100_depth3_words.txt`

## Deliverables

- `rs/ll-open/hdc-translate/src/readout_symbolic.rs`:
  - `recover_bpe_at(word_hv: &Hypervector, position: usize, codebook: &BlakeCodebook) -> u32` — returns predicted BPE token id
  - `eval_recovery(encoder: &V0Encoder, codebook: &BlakeCodebook, fixture: &[String]) -> f64` — top-1 accuracy across the 1000 held-out words × 3 positions per word

## Tests

- `recovery_smoke_test` — encode "happiness" (depth-3: ["happi", "ness"]... or similar), recover position 0 and position 1, assert non-trivial accuracy
- `recovery_above_chance` — on a 50-word fixture, recovery should be > 50% (chance ≈ 0.00002, so any non-broken implementation crushes this)
- `eval_recovery_runs` — smoke test, doesn't assert τ_sym value (T2.2 measures it)

## Acceptance

`cargo test -p leyline-hdc-translate readout_symbolic` green. Recovery is bit-exact reproducible.

title: T1.5: falsify binary — single binary, both readouts, threshold-checked exits
description:
Bead 1.5 of T1. Tying it together — one binary, one HDC encoding pass per input, both readouts, exit-non-zero on threshold miss. This binary IS the experiment.

## Deliverables

- `rs/ll-open/hdc-translate/src/bin/falsify.rs`:

```text
1. Load codebook (T1.1)
2. Load V0 encoder (T1.2)  
3. Load STS-B fixture (T1.3)
4. Load depth-3 fixture (T1.4)
5. Encode each STS-B sentence ONCE → HV(sentence). Both readouts share this.
6. Encode each depth-3 word ONCE → HV(word). Both readouts share this.
7. Dense readout on STS-B → ρ (T1.3 logic)
8. Symbolic readout on depth-3 → acc (T1.4 logic)
9. Same-bytes invariant verification: assert each input encoded exactly once; both readouts pulled from cached encoding
10. Print results JSON to stdout: {ρ, acc, effective_rank, same_bytes_ok}
11. Exit non-zero if ρ < 0.553 OR acc < 0.70 OR same_bytes_ok != true
```

## Same-bytes invariant verification

The encoder is called once per input. Both readouts read from the encoder's output cache. Wrap the encoder in a thin counter-instrumented wrapper for the duration of `falsify`'s run; assert encoder call count == input count. Bit-exact: each input maps to exactly one HDC byte sequence; both readouts hash the same bytes.

## CI integration

- `cargo test -p leyline-hdc-translate --test falsify` invokes the binary
- Test passes if binary exits 0; fails if non-zero
- Output JSON committed to `rs/ll-open/hdc-translate/tests/last_run.json` for inspection (gitignored after V0)
- After T2 publishes, the JSON of the actual falsification run is committed permanently

## Note on dispatch ordering

T1.5 depends on T1.1, T1.2, T1.3, T1.4 all being available. Dispatch last among T1.x.

## Acceptance

`cargo test --test falsify` runs end-to-end. Exit code reflects threshold pass/fail. Output JSON parsed by T2 for the writeup.

title: T1.6: effective-rank invariant test (mode-collapse regression pin)
description:
Bead 1.6 of T1. Mode-collapse pin against the failure mode the math-friend flagged on the L-shape baseline.

## Why

The L-shape baseline shows 60% compression with "preserved relationships," but the manifesto JSON reports `lshape_selectivity = -0.0017` and the per-relationship cosine table shows DISSIMILAR going 0.19 → 0.96 — that's mode collapse, not preservation. Any encoder can score "high cosine" if it collapses everything to the same point. We need to pin against that failure mode.

## Test

- Encode N=500 diverse STS-B sentences via V0 encoder
- Stack into matrix `M ∈ ℝ^{500 × 10000}`
- Compute effective rank: `effective_rank(M) = exp(H(σ_normalized))` where H is the Shannon entropy of the singular value distribution
- Assert `effective_rank ≥ 2048` (≥ 20% of D)

This is independent of τ_dense and τ_sym — it pins that the encoded space is *not collapsed*. A degenerate encoder that maps everything to the same HV would have effective rank ≈ 1 and pass cosine-based tests trivially while teaching nothing.

## Deliverables

- `rs/ll-open/hdc-translate/tests/effective_rank.rs` — single test, ~30 LoC

## Acceptance

`cargo test --test effective_rank` green. Asserts `effective_rank ≥ 2048` on the actual STS-B fixture. If V0 fails this test, the encoder is degenerate and the experiment is invalid before τ_dense/τ_sym are even meaningful.

title: hdc-1: storage schema — _hdc, _hdc_combined, _hdc_baseline, _hdc_subtree_cache
description:
## Scope

Land the SQLite schema for the HDC sidecar tables. Pure schema work — no encoder, no codebooks, no ops yet. Establishes the contract that downstream beads write to.

## Tables

```sql
CREATE TABLE _hdc (
  scope_id   TEXT NOT NULL,
  layer_kind TEXT NOT NULL,         -- {ast, semantic, temporal, module, lex(reserved), fs(reserved)}
  hv         BLOB NOT NULL,         -- D/8 bytes (default D=8192 → 1024 bytes)
  basis      INTEGER NOT NULL,      -- per-layer freshness key (parse_version, embed_version, head_sha hash, etc.)
  PRIMARY KEY (scope_id, layer_kind)
);

CREATE INDEX _hdc_layer_basis_idx ON _hdc(layer_kind, basis);

CREATE TABLE _hdc_combined (
  scope_id  TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  hv        BLOB NOT NULL,           -- XOR-bind of per-layer HVs
  basis     INTEGER NOT NULL         -- max(per-layer basis)
);

CREATE TABLE _hdc_baseline (
  layer_kind        TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  median_distance   INTEGER NOT NULL,  -- popcount over corpus sample
  mad               INTEGER NOT NULL,  -- median absolute deviation
  sample_size       INTEGER NOT NULL,
  computed_at_ms    INTEGER NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE _hdc_subtree_cache (
  content_hash BLOB(32) PRIMARY KEY,  -- BLAKE3 of subtree canonical form
  hv           BLOB NOT NULL,
  ref_count    INTEGER DEFAULT 1
);
```

## Why this shape

- `_hdc` keyed on `(scope_id, layer_kind)` so any one row is independently queryable per layer.
- `layer_kind` is TEXT not enum so it's extensible at the data layer without migrations.
- Schema reserves `lex` and `fs` variants for future addition without schema change.
- `_hdc_combined` is the unweighted XOR-bind prefilter (math friend's review F).
- `_hdc_baseline` stores the empirical radius calibration (math friend's review B). Computed at daemon startup.
- `_hdc_subtree_cache` is the content-hash-keyed cache that makes bidi unbind tractable (avoids re-encoding subtrees on every query).

title: hdc-2: canonical-kind alphabet — single source of truth, per-parser mapping
description:
## Scope

The single highest-leverage decision in the whole HDC stack (per math friend's review C). Define a canonical alphabet of structural kinds that every parser-specific node-kind maps into. Without this, AST equivalence classes are unstable across language frontends; with it, cross-language hotspot detection becomes possible.

## The alphabet

```rust
pub enum CanonicalKind {
    Decl,    // function, class, struct, enum, type, variable declarations
    Expr,    // expressions, calls, member accesses, indexing
    Stmt,    // statements (assignment, return, throw, expression-statement)
    Block,   // compound statements, blocks, scopes
    Ref,     // identifier references, qualified names
    Lit,     // literals (number, string, bool, nil)
    Op,      // operators, control-flow keywords (if/else/loop tags)
}
```

7 variants, fits in 3 bits. Maps to the alphabet Deckard (Jiang 2007) uses for clone detection. Other clone-detection literature uses similar small canonical alphabets — converged on this scale.

## Per-parser mapping

For each tree-sitter grammar in scope, ship a `Vec<(&str, CanonicalKind)>` table mapping the grammar's node-kinds to the canonical kind. Tables live in `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/daemon/hdc/canonical/<lang>.rs`.

Initial languages:
- Rust (~150 named node-kinds)
- Go (~120)
- Python (~100)
- TypeScript (~180)

Anything not mapped defaults to `Block` (the most-neutral structural carrier — picks up boilerplate without polluting other classes).

## Why this matters

The math-friend review caught that production-signature hashing alone isn't grammar-stable: tree-sitter inlines what ANTLR keeps named, so child-kind multisets genuinely differ across parsers. Mapping every parser-kind into a 7-element canonical alphabet collapses parser-specific noise. Two functions with the same control-flow shape — written in Rust vs Go — produce the same canonical-kind sequence, even if their parser-kind names diverge.

## Cross-version stability test

Run two consecutive tree-sitter versions side-by-side; confirm that the canonical-kind sequence for a given file is identical even when individual node-kind names changed (tree-sitter has changed e.g. `if_statement` → `if_clause` between minor versions; canonical mapping survives that).

## Files

- `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/daemon/hdc/canonical.rs` (NEW — `CanonicalKind` enum + lookup trait)
- `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/daemon/hdc/canonical/rust.rs` (NEW)
- `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/daemon/hdc/canonical/go.rs` (NEW)
- `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/daemon/hdc/canonical/python.rs` (NEW)
- `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/daemon/hdc/canonical/typescript.rs` (NEW)

## Tests

- `canonical_kind_mapping_stable_across_grammar_versions` — mapping output unchanged when tree-sitter dependency bumps.
- `cross_language_canonical_invariance` — fixture: same control-flow shape in Rust + Go + Python yields the same canonical sequence.

The four initial-language tables are complete (every named tree-sitter kind in those grammars has a mapping). The cross-language invariance test passes on a hand-written `if-then-return` fixture in all four languages.

description:
## Scope

Module-layer `BaseCodebook` for code-organization topology. Reuses the CAS primitive ley-line already has (content-addressed module hashes).

## Recipe

For each module/class/file scope, compute hypervector encoding the structural skeleton at that level:

```
H_module(scope) =
    base[scope_kind: module|class|file]
    ⊕ ρ_for_each_child · H_child_canonical_skeleton
    ⊕ ρ_dependencies · H_set_of_dependency_module_ids
```

Where:
- `child_canonical_skeleton` is a hash of the canonical-kind sequence at the child's signature level (function: parameter kinds + return kind; class: method canonical-kind set)
- `dependency_module_ids` is the set of imported/depended-on module IDs (using ley-line's existing CAS hashes for stable cross-instance addressing)

## Why this is cheap

The CAS layer already gives us deterministic module hashes. We just *bind them as roles* into a hypervector instead of using them as Merkle leaves. The XOR-bind elevates equality-only Merkle to continuous Hamming similarity at the module level.

## Tests

- `module_codebook_method_reorder_invariant` — same class with methods in different order → same HV (use sorted multiset)
- `module_codebook_dependency_isomorphism` — two classes that depend on isomorphic dependency sets produce nearby HVs

title: hdc-3d: Temporal codebook — time-decayed co-edit matrix → simhash
description:
## Scope

Temporal-layer `BaseCodebook` from git history. Per math-friend review E, the right primitive is a **time-decayed co-edit matrix** simhashed per row.

## Recipe

```
1. For each pair (i, j) of scopes (functions, files), accumulate weight:
   w_ij = Σ_{commits c containing both i and j} exp(-(t_now - t_c)/τ)
   τ ≈ 90 days

2. The temporal vector for scope i is the row W[i, :] (real-valued).

3. Hash via Charikar simhash (same as semantic layer):
   H_temporal(i) = sign(W[i, :] · R)
   where R is a per-repo seeded random matrix.
```

## Why this works (per review)

- **Append-only updates**: a new commit nudges weights for the affected pairs; ~1% bit churn per new commit (per Charikar's stability properties)
- **Fully deterministic** given seed: any daemon with the same git history + same seed produces identical temporal HVs
- **τ knob**: default 90 days. Older commits decay exponentially. Effectively makes the temporal HV a "recent edit pattern" fingerprint.

## Implementation considerations

- The co-edit matrix W can be large (N × N where N is scope count). Most entries are zero — store sparsely.
- Recompute incrementally on each new commit: only weights involving newly-touched scopes change.
- `head_sha` is the basis for `_hdc_baseline.basis` for this layer — when HEAD advances, the temporal HVs may need refresh.

```rust
pub struct TemporalCodebook {
    coedit: SparseMatrix,           // scope × scope, time-decayed
    hyperplanes: Box<[[f32; ?]; D]>, // simhash projection
    tau_seconds: u64,                // 90 days default
}

impl TemporalCodebook {
    pub fn refresh_from_git_log(&mut self, source_dir: &Path) -> Result<()> { ... }
    pub fn project(&self, scope_id: &str) -> [u8; D/8] { ... }
}
```

## Tests

- `temporal_codebook_decays_old_commits` — synthetic git log; verify weights at t=10·τ are ~exp(-10) of fresh weights
- `temporal_codebook_simhash_charikar` — same Charikar collision-probability test as semantic codebook
- `temporal_codebook_incremental_stability` — adding one commit causes <2% bit changes for unaffected scopes

## Files

- `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/daemon/hdc/codebook/temporal.rs` (NEW)

## Definition of done

3 unit tests pass. Temporal HVs incrementally stable under realistic commit cadence.

description:
## Scope

Wire HDC ops into the daemon's `handle_base_op` dispatch + MCP `tool_registry`. Four ops total, each opt-in via `#[cfg(feature = "hdc")]`.

## Ops

### `op_hdc_search` — radius query

```json
{"op":"hdc_search", "query": "<base64 hv or scope_id>", "layer": "ast", "r": 512, "limit": 50}
```

`SELECT scope_id, popcount(hv XOR ?1) AS d FROM _hdc WHERE layer_kind=?2 AND d <= ?3 ORDER BY d LIMIT ?4`

Returns ranked list of similar scopes within Hamming radius `r`.

### `op_hdc_density` — equivalence-class membership test

```json
{"op":"hdc_density", "query": "...", "layer": "ast", "r": 512}
```

`SELECT count(*) FROM _hdc WHERE layer_kind=?1 AND popcount(hv XOR ?2) <= ?3`

Returns the count of scopes within radius. >1 means the query is in a cluster (hotspot membership).

### `op_hdc_unbind` — cluster explanation

```json
{"op":"hdc_unbind", "scope_id": "...", "layer": "ast", "role": "child_0"}
```

Take the function-level hypervector for `scope_id`, unbind via role permutation, run cleanup-memory against the lazily-materialized codebook of known kinds, return the recovered kind. Recursive variant takes `path: ["child_0", "child_1", ...]` to walk arbitrary depth.

This is the load-bearing op per the math-friend review G — without it, the binding algebra doesn't pay rent and we ship simhash+LSH instead.

### `op_hdc_combined_prefilter` — multi-layer top-k pruning

```json
{"op":"hdc_combined_prefilter", "query": "...", "limit": 1000}
```

Query against `_hdc_combined` for fast top-k pruning. Caller then issues weighted per-layer reranks via SQL JOIN on `_hdc`.

## SQL UDF for popcount

Register a custom SQLite function `popcount(blob)` that uses `std::simd` or platform popcount. Without this, popcount distance is a slow byte-by-byte loop.

## Dispatch wiring (additive, per the design discipline)

```rust
// daemon/ops.rs
match op {
    ...
    #[cfg(feature = "hdc")]
    "hdc_search" => Some(op_hdc_search(ctx, req)),
    #[cfg(feature = "hdc")]
    "hdc_density" => Some(op_hdc_density(ctx, req)),
    #[cfg(feature = "hdc")]
    "hdc_unbind" => Some(op_hdc_unbind(ctx, req)),
    #[cfg(feature = "hdc")]
    "hdc_combined_prefilter" => Some(op_hdc_combined_prefilter(ctx, req)),
    ...
}

// base_op_names()
#[cfg(feature = "hdc")] v.extend_from_slice(&["hdc_search", "hdc_density", "hdc_unbind", "hdc_combined_prefilter"]);

// daemon/mcp.rs tool_registry — same #[cfg] gate, four McpTool entries
```

## Tests

- `op_hdc_search_radius_filter` — populate _hdc, query at varied r, assert correct count returned
- `op_hdc_density_counts_cluster_size` — populate cluster, query density of cluster centroid
- `op_hdc_unbind_recovers_known_kind` — encode a known fixture, unbind first child role, assert canonical kind matches
- `op_hdc_combined_prefilter_correctness` — populate combined view, prefilter against query, assert top-k contains all true matches
- `popcount_udf_correctness` — register UDF, run on known BLOBs, verify count matches `count_ones()` reference
- `hdc_ops_present_in_canonical_op_names` — drift guard on `base_op_names()`

title: hdc-6: empirical radius calibration — daemon-startup baseline sampling
description:
## Scope

The fix for math-friend review B. Real codebases aren't iid — `self`/`if`/`return` co-occur far above chance, so the theoretical D/2 ± √D/2 prediction is the wrong null. Need empirical calibration of the radius threshold per layer.

## Algorithm

```
on_daemon_start():
    for each layer in {ast, semantic, temporal, module}:
        sample 10000 random pairs (a, b) of scopes from _hdc WHERE layer_kind = layer
        compute d_a_b = popcount(a.hv XOR b.hv) for each pair
        d_med = median(d_a_b values)
        mad = median(|d_a_b - d_med|)
        recommended_r = d_med - 3 * mad
        write to _hdc_baseline(layer_kind, median_distance, mad, sample_size, computed_at_ms)
```

The query ops in `hdc-5` use `_hdc_baseline.median_distance - 3 * mad` as their default `r` if the caller doesn't override.

## Why this matters

Without this calibration, every density/radius query is uncalibrated noise. With it:
- Radius queries produce *meaningful* equivalence-class membership tests
- Hotspot detection has principled thresholds
- Per-codebase tuning is automatic (a Python-monorepo and a Rust-microservice cluster will get different baselines, both correct for their domain)

## Recompute trigger

The baseline is invalidated when:
- Schema changes (rare)
- The corpus grows by >10% (`_hdc.scope_id` count increases significantly)
- Manual recalibration ops call

Otherwise sticky — baseline computed once, reused.

## Implementation

```rust
pub fn calibrate_radius(conn: &Connection, layer: LayerKind, sample_size: usize) -> Result<RadiusBaseline> {
    let pairs: Vec<(Vec<u8>, Vec<u8>)> = sample_random_pairs(conn, layer, sample_size)?;
    let distances: Vec<i64> = pairs.iter().map(|(a, b)| popcount_xor(a, b) as i64).collect();
    let median = quickselect_median(&distances);
    let mad = quickselect_median(&distances.iter().map(|d| (d - median).abs()).collect::<Vec<_>>());
    Ok(RadiusBaseline { median, mad, sample_size, computed_at_ms: now_ms() })
}
```

## Tests

- `calibrate_radius_uniform_baseline` — populate _hdc with i.i.d. random vectors, verify median ≈ D/2 and mad ≈ √D/4
- `calibrate_radius_skewed_baseline` — populate with vectors that share boilerplate prefix, verify median < D/2 (the "self/if/return" effect)
- `calibrate_radius_persists_in_baseline_table` — call calibrate, query _hdc_baseline, assert row present

## Files

- `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/daemon/hdc/calibrate.rs` (NEW)
- `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/cmd_daemon.rs` — call calibrate_radius for each layer at end of run_daemon init

## Definition of done

3 unit tests pass. Daemon startup runs calibration for each populated layer, records baseline, and `op_hdc_search` defaults to using calibrated r when client omits it.

title: CDC boundary mask is 11 bits, not 16 — measured mean chunk 10 KiB against the documented 64 KiB xet target
description:
External review (relayed by James 2026-07-29), verified empirically before filing: BOUNDARY_MASK 0x0000_5890_5303_0000 (cdc/src/lib.rs:41) has count_ones()==11, and 64 MiB of deterministic random data chunks to mean=10,194 B / median=9,572 B / max=23,576 B / zero chunks at MAX — the doc comment claims '16 bits ⇒ ~64 KiB average, xet's target'. The comment even says 'we do not assert it, we falsify it' via chunk_sizes_respect_the_xet_bounds — but that test only checks [8,128] KiB bounds and chunk-count floors, which a 10 KiB mean passes comfortably. The falsifier was too weak to falsify.

Consequences: ~6x manifest rows/chunk hashes/blob lookups vs intended; per-chunk BLAKE3 overhead; and the ADR's CDC throughput/premium numbers (1,547 MiB/s, ~12%) were measured on a materially different distribution than claimed — re-benchmark after fixing.

Fix: choose the real target deliberately (xet 64Ki ⇒ 16 set bits; or keep ~10 KiB and fix the docs), assert BOUNDARY_MASK.count_ones() == 16 as a compile-adjacent test, AND add the distribution test the reviewer specified: chunk thousands of chunks of random data, assert mean within [48,80] KiB. Note GearHash entropy is not uniform across bit positions (h = (h<<1)+gear[b] concentrates mixing high), so mask bit PLACEMENT matters — validate empirically after any change, and prefer high-bit masks per upstream convention. Distribution shape is a property test: this is exactly where proptest/hypothesis-style testing pays (James's point) — rechunk==chunk equivalence under random edits is the sibling property already unit-tested at fixed cases.

comments.text:
Independent confirmation + extensions from the type-driven-correctness agent (blind review, no knowledge of this bead; full report in _agent_log/2026-07-29-types-friend-cdc-report.md):
- Independently MEASURED via examples/throughput.rs over 256 MiB: boundary spacing 2,043 B (predicted 2,048), mean chunk 10,229 B. Two independent measurements now agree.
- The smoking gun was already in the code: rechunk_work_is_sublinear's own comment says '14 chunks over ~138 KB' = 9.9 KB mean — measured, written down, explained away as 'the window fills with near-minimum chunks'.
- CONSEQUENCE MISSED EARLIER: the xet-interop claim dies — identical BLAKE3 over differently-placed boundaries = disjoint chunk sets, no cross-system dedup. Whatever this mask is, it does not yield xet's target.

title: hdc-10: hotspot-explanation API — load-bearing test that justifies HDC over LSH
description:
## Scope

The load-bearing test that justifies HDC over plain LSH. Per math-friend review G: **if the hotspot UI doesn't surface unbind output, we delete the binding code and ship simhash+LSH instead.**

This bead implements the surface that proves HDC pulls its weight.

## The API

```json
{"op":"hdc_explain_cluster", "centroid_scope_id": "...", "layer": "ast", "radius": 512}
```

Returns:
```json
{
    "ok": true,
    "centroid": "...",
    "members": ["scope_a", "scope_b", "scope_c"],
    "shared_skeleton": {
        "root_kind": "Block",
        "child_0": "Op",        // recovered via unbind
        "child_1": "Stmt",
        "child_2": "Stmt"
    },
    "diverging_positions": ["child_3"]  // positions where members disagree
}
```

## Algorithm

```
1. Find members within radius of centroid via op_hdc_search.
2. Compute the cluster centroid as the bit-wise majority of all member HVs.
3. For each role position [child_0, child_1, ..., child_max_arity]:
   a. unbind(centroid, role_position)
   b. Run cleanup-memory: nearest neighbor in codebook
   c. If confident (margin > threshold) → record the canonical-kind for that role
   d. Else → mark as "diverging"
4. Return the recovered shared skeleton + the diverging positions
```

## Why this is the load-bearing test

LSH gives you "these N items are similar." It cannot tell you *why* — what they share, what they don't. HDC's bind algebra gives you both the cluster AND the structural recipe. If we can answer "this hotspot shares: `Block` root, `Op` child_0, `Stmt` children at child_1+2" — we're delivering something LSH can't.

If we can't surface this output reliably (cleanup memory keeps returning ambiguous results, recovery success rate <80%), HDC isn't pulling its weight. We delete the binding code and ship simhash+LSH.

## Tests

### `hotspot_explanation_recovers_shared_skeleton`

Plant 10 functions that all have the same skeleton `if x { return y; }` but different variables. Encode. Query `op_hdc_explain_cluster` against one. Assert:
- `shared_skeleton.root_kind == "Block"` (the function body)
- `shared_skeleton.child_0 == "Op"` (the if statement)
- `shared_skeleton.child_1 == "Stmt"` (the return)
- `diverging_positions` is empty

### `hotspot_explanation_marks_diverging_positions`

Plant 5 functions with the same skeleton + 5 with a slight variation (one has an extra statement). Query the cluster centroid. Assert the extra-statement position appears in `diverging_positions`.

### `hotspot_explanation_recovery_success_rate`

Run on real codebase fixture (not synthetic). Measure: for the 10 largest clusters, does explanation return non-empty `shared_skeleton`? **Pass threshold: ≥80% recovery success rate.** Below that, HDC has lost its case against LSH.

## Files

- `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/daemon/hdc/explain.rs` (NEW)
- `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/daemon/hdc/ops.rs` — wire `op_hdc_explain_cluster`
- `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/tests/integration.rs` — 3 integration tests

## Definition of done

3 integration tests pass. Real-codebase test demonstrates ≥80% recovery success on found hotspots. **If recovery rate is below that threshold, this bead's outcome is "delete binding code, ship simhash+LSH" — file the alternative bead for that.**

## Parent

ley-line-open-96b1a9

title: mount ships via install:full+mount with zero tests — no FUSE/NFS test exists at any level
description:
Found by the feature-coverage half of the reachability gate (ley-line-open-2607d2).

## The gap

README documents three install paths, so all three reach users:

    task install              # default: lsp, validate, hdc, cdc
    task install:full         # --features all: + vec, text-search
    task install:full+mount   # --features full: + FUSE/NFS

`mount` has ZERO test files gated on it — not one, at any level:

- rs/ll-open/cli-lib/tests: 0 files reference `cfg(feature = "mount")`
- rs/ll-open/fs: fuse.rs / nfs.rs have no test module exercising a mount

Contrast `vec` (27 inline cfg sections) and `text-search` (16), both of which had real coverage that simply never ran — those are now wired via `test:vec` and `test:text-search`. `mount` cannot be fixed the same way because there is nothing to turn on.

## What exists instead

Two BUILD checks: `cargo build -p leyline-cli --features mount` (Taskfile:298) and `build:fs-nfs-isolated`, added after ley-line-open-95cd90 — which the Taskfile describes as "an nfs-only libc bug that the default build masked". So this exact class already bit once, and the response was a compile check rather than a test.

A build check proves it links. It says nothing about whether a mount serves correct bytes.

## Why it matters more than the raw severity suggests

`flush_node` is a silent no-op in every shipped build (ley-line-open-918a75), so mount WRITES never reproject. Nothing would have caught that either, because nothing tests the mount. The two defects share a cause: the mount path is shipped, documented, and unexercised.

## Minimum viable coverage

A round-trip: mount a projection, read a file through the mount, assert the bytes equal what `read_content` returns for the same node and range. That single test would have caught 95cd90's libc bug, and would catch a regression in the chunked read path reaching the mount.

Needs libfuse-t (macOS) / libfuse (Linux) at test time, which is why it was likely skipped. Options: gate it behind a `mount-e2e` target that CI runs on a runner with the dep installed, or use the NFS backend, which needs no kernel module.

## Interim

`cli-lib/mount` is recorded in the coverage ledger in tools/check_feature_reachability.sh pointing at this bead. Remove that line when a test lands.

## Close condition

The mount round-trip in acceptance_criteria, running in the ci chain.
acceptance_criteria: A test target enabling `mount` runs in the ci chain and exercises at least one mount round-trip: mount a projection, read a file through the mount, verify the bytes match `read_content`. `sh tools/check_feature_reachability.sh .` passes without a coverage-ledger entry for `cli-lib/mount`.

title: PartitionSpec::address drops framing + entry order — content-address collision (found by cloister at v0.11.3)
description:
Filed from cloister; mirrors cloister-944766. Found bumping cloister's LLO pins from five mixed revs to 39e1e9b4 (v0.11.3). File paths are a best guess from the v0.11.3 tree layout — adjust if the fold lives elsewhere.

`cargo check --workspace --all-targets` passes. `cargo test -p cloister-cas` fails:

```
assertion `left != right` failed: framing must be committed to, not ignored
```

**Characterized with a temporary probe.** At rev 39e1e9b4, `PartitionSpec::address` commits to a MULTISET OF ENTRY ADDRESSES AND NOTHING ELSE:

| varied | address changes? |
|---|---|
| `Entry.a`/`b` swapped `(0,1)`→`(1,0)` | NO |
| `b` changed outright `(0,1)`→`(0,2)` | NO |
| `(5,7)`→`(7,5)` | NO |
| **entry order** `[X,Y]`→`[Y,X]` | NO |
| entry count | yes |
| entry `addr` | yes |

The `a`/`b` framing fields are not hashed at all, and the fold is order-insensitive. Two materially different decompositions share one address. Length-prefixed framing exists precisely to prevent this.

**Separable question:** order-insensitivity may be deliberate (a set-like commitment over entries) while the `a`/`b` omission is the actual bug. A multiset commitment can still be framing-committed. Worth deciding explicitly rather than fixing both by accident.

---

**Three additions to the stated plan (partition fix → generator publishing + ServerMeta multi-package → release):**

**1. Does the fix bump `canon_version`?** `PartitionSpec` already carries that field. If the fold changes without bumping it, the same `canon_version` denotes two different algorithms, and an address computed before the fix silently disagrees with one computed after — under an identical version tag. That is strictly worse than the original bug, because the version field is exactly what a consumer would check to detect this. If there is a reason not to bump (e.g. the buggy fold shipped in no release any consumer could reach), recording that reasoning is worth more than leaving it implicit.

Related: anything already persisted under the buggy fold — build-cache/v1 blob identity, arena roots — is keyed on addresses the fix changes. Cloister does not appear to persist them (it exposes `cloister_partition_address` as FFI and computes on demand), so cloister is likely unaffected; other consumers may not be.

**2. The regression test should live upstream.** This was caught by a test in cloister's tree asserting an ADR-0032 D2 property about LLO's code. The invariant currently has exactly one detector, in a downstream repo, and it only fired because cloister happened to bump. A property test in LLO — vary `a`/`b`, vary order, assert the address moves — catches it at the source. Also worth asking how it regressed undetected: if no upstream test covered the fold's framing commitment, the gap is broader than this one bug.

**3. Publishing the generator solves tools, not libraries.** Cloister git-pins five LLO crates (`leyline-core`, `leyline-cas-ffi`, `leyline-fs`, `leyline-sign`, `leyline-schema-bridge`). They had drifted to five distinct revs, with `leyline-core` resolving THREE times simultaneously (0.4.5 / 0.8.0 / 0.10.4) — `cargo update -p leyline-core` refuses as ambiguous. Publishing generator binaries fixes build-tool delivery, but consumers still SHA-pin the libraries and can still end up with mixed revs of a shared type substrate. Whether the libraries go to crates.io is a separate decision from publishing the binaries, and the "released ≠ deliverable" argument applies to both.

On the 5-binaries-doubles-the-build note: shipping all five and measuring is the right call. Cloister consumes `capnpc-schema-bridge-zod` only.

comments.text:
Confirmed fixed from cloister's side at `74db5a97`. Repinned in cloister PR #215; `cargo test -p cloister-cas` 11/11 including `address_matches_upstream_fold_for_a_known_spec`.

Re-ran the characterization probe against the new rev — both stated behaviours verified rather than taken on trust:

```
FRAMING (0,1) vs (1,0) differs: true    ← was false
FRAMING (0,1) vs (0,2) differs: true    ← was false
ORDER   [X,Y] vs [Y,X] differs: false   ← unchanged, deliberate
determinism (same twice equal): true
```

The `canon_version` answer is the right one, and more usefully it was established rather than assumed — `git tag --contains` empty is exactly the check that makes "stays v1" a fact instead of a judgement call. Recording it in the code is what makes it auditable later.

---

**One thing worth knowing before v0.12.0 release notes, not a bug.**

Regenerating `cluster.zod.ts` against 8c00c6 broke a cloister test, and the cause is inherent to the fix rather than wrong:

capnp has no required fields — `Text` defaults to `""` — so emitting `.default("")` per scalar is faithful capnp semantics. It also means the generated zod schema can no longer distinguish "field absent" from "field present and empty". A `cluster.toml` with no `metadata.name` now validates clean and builds an unnamed cluster; previously it failed with a schema error citing the field path.

For decoding a wire message that is exactly right. For validating a hand-authored operator surface it silently drops a check. Cloister's fix was to move required-ness into its own "semantic checks the schema can't express" pass, which seems like the correct division: the schema models capnp, the consumer models its own surface.

Flagging it because any other zod consumer of schema-bridge loses required-field rejection the same way, silently, on upgrade — and a release note is much cheaper than each of them discovering it via a failing test. No action wanted on your side unless you think the generator should distinguish the two cases.
comments.author: rsry-mcp

comments.text:
Fixed in **PR #290** (`74db5a97`), released in **v0.12.0**.

## Root cause — the bead's own fix caused it

`ad272d3`, titled *"[ley-line-open-b67a73] fix(core): make set-domain addresses
a function of the set"*, landed 24h before this was filed. It canonicalized set
folds by sorting entry addresses AND dropping `Entry.a/b`, on the premise that
framing "carries no defined meaning" in set domains. `Entry` documents those
fields as scheme-defined, and cloister's `glob-closure/v1` defines them — so
every framing variant of one address multiset collided.

The original fold (`eca1b99`) committed framing for all domains. So b67a73's own
fix introduced the collision it existed to prevent.

## Resolution

The two halves of `ad272d3` were independent and only one was wrong:

- **Enumeration-order erasure KEPT** — a set has no order; folding it in is a
  malleability slot.
- **Framing erasure REVERTED** — framing is content of the DECLARED
  decomposition. The fold cannot know which fields a scheme uses, so it commits
  all of them; a scheme assigning framing no meaning must canonicalize it, and a
  garnished sender is caught by re-derivation, not by erasure.

Set domains now sort whole entries by `(addr, a, b)` and fold `addr‖a‖b`.

## Verified, both directions

TDD: three collision tests written first, RED on actual address equality. The
full cloister probe table was reproduced at HEAD first, confirming all four "NO"
rows collided. Mutation: fix neutered back to the sorted-address fold → exactly
the 3 new tests fail; restored → 15/15 partition, 89/89 leyline-core.

`ByteStream` is bit-identical, pinned by `byte_stream_address_pin` with a
known-answer vector computed at the pre-fix revision, so `cmd_parse`'s segment
root does not move and `_meta.ir_schema_version` does not bump.

## Two follow-ups this surfaced

- `ley-line-open-c3916b` — the reason it regressed undetected. An upstream test
  `framing_is_committed_to_the_address` predated the regression and tests
  `Domain::ByteStream` ONLY. A universal-sounding name over a one-domain body,
  so erasing framing for set domains failed nothing upstream. The single
  detector was in cloister's tree.
- `PARTITION_CONTEXT` deliberately stays `v1`; the reasoning is recorded in the
  code, including that a future fold change shipping in a tag MUST bump. The
  buggy fold reached no tag (`git tag --contains ad272d3` is empty), which is
  the only thing making an in-place algorithm change acceptable here.
comments.author: rsry-mcp

comments.text: CLOSING as already-fixed (verified against the tree 2026-07-30, pre-v0.14 sweep): PartitionSpec::address at rs/ll-core/core/src/partition.rs:164 now (a) length-frames every variable field (scheme, params, entry count — the framing half), (b) canonicalizes unordered domains by sorting entries wholesale by (addr, a, b) so the address is a function of the entry MULTISET not enumeration order (the ordering half), and (c) domain-separates via blake3 derive_key(PARTITION_CONTEXT) with a falsifier (address_is_domain_separated_from_plain_blake3). partition.rs sits in the cargo-mutants allowlist (mutants:partition, 5 mutants, green on every recent run), so the encoding is mutation-guarded. The collision class cloister found at v0.11.3 is unrepresentable in the current encoding.

title: op_query structural skip — design call: reconcile rows shape vs schema's positional List(QueryRow)
description:
Filed 2026-05-12 after A-3 (`b69606`) landed. Follow-up on the one structural skip in the cross-runtime fixture gate. P2 design; "we'll fix this later" candidates harden if left undated.

## The mismatch

`daemon.capnp` declares:
```
struct QueryRow {
  values @0 :List(Text);
}
struct QueryResponse {
  ok @0 :Bool;
  columns @1 :List(Text);
  rows @2 :List(QueryRow);
}
```

Handler in `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/daemon/ops.rs` emits:
```json
{"ok":true,"columns":["col_a","col_b"],"rows":[{"col_a":"v1","col_b":"v2"}]}
```

i.e. column-keyed maps rather than positional `values: [v1, v2]`. The fixture `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/tests/fixtures/daemon-protocol.json` carries this as the one `go_drift_skip` entry (with the reason quoted in-line).

## Why it's structural, not additive

ADR-0014 §2 forbids removing/renaming ordinals. Three real options:

1. **Change handler to match schema** — emit `rows: [{values: [v1,v2,...]}, ...]`. Cleanest from a schema-discipline view, but breaks every existing debug consumer that does `row[colName]` — including the typed-Go fixture decoder and probably mache's own SQL-projection consumers. Wire-shape break.
2. **Add a parallel field at next ordinal** — e.g. `rowsMap @3 :List(Text)` carrying the JSON-encoded column-keyed shape. Additive, doesn't break consumers. Costs: schema now carries both shapes; "which one is canonical" becomes a documentation problem; consumer code has to pick a side.
3. **Document the carve-out** — keep handler + schema as-is, accept `query` lives outside the typed-mirror contract. This is what we're doing today, expanded on in the post-A-3 docs (PR #10). Lowest-effort but the gap calcifies.

## What I'd recommend (but it's a design call)

Option 1 if and only if we can do a coordinated debug-consumer flip (cloister's MCP query proxy + mache's SQL projection). Otherwise Option 3 stays the right answer for now, gated on the forcing function: the next consumer that wants typed query rows. File the bead, let it sit, reopen when triggered.

## Scope

- Decision artifact: short ADR addendum or a dated note in `docs/TABLE_CONTRACT.md`'s daemon-protocol section.
- If Option 1 picked: handler rewrite + fixture update + Go decoder switch + mache notify + cloister notify (if affected).
- If Option 2: schema bump + handler emits both + fixture covers both + Go decoder picks one + deprecation note for the column-keyed shape.
- If Option 3: nothing in code; doc-only commit clarifying the carve-out is durable.

## Files

- `rs/ll-core/public-schema/capnp/daemon.capnp` (QueryResponse / QueryRow ordinals)
- `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/daemon/ops.rs` (`op_query` handler)
- `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/daemon/wire.rs` (no QueryResponse struct today — Option 1/2 would add one)
- `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/tests/fixtures/daemon-protocol.json` (the `query.go_drift_skip` reason)
- `clients/go/leyline-schema/daemon/daemon_protocol_test.go` (the Skip path)

## Forcing functions to watch for

- Cloister or another consumer files a "we need typed query rows" bead.
- A real bug surfaces where the column-keyed shape causes a decode error in production (e.g. column name with a slash, JSON-unsafe character).
- We start using `query` for non-debug paths (today it's nominally a debug escape hatch).

Decade: `daemon-typed-wire`. Thread: `daemon-json-type-lockdown` (closes out one of the two known carve-outs from A-3).

title: wire.rs codegen: emit typed serde structs from daemon.capnp at build time (A.1a path from `a373ba`)
description:
Filed 2026-05-12 after A-3 (`b69606`) landed. The original tracking bead `a373ba` had two implementation paths:

- **A.1a (preferred):** `build.rs` codegen — `rs/ll-core/public-schema/build.rs` emits serde-Serialize/Deserialize structs from `daemon.capnp` alongside the Cap'n Proto Rust bindings.
- **A.1b (fallback):** hand-written serde mirror in `daemon/wire.rs` + cross-runtime fixture gate.

A-3 shipped A.1b. This bead is the follow-up that takes us from A.1b to A.1a, closing the "wire.rs is hand-written; schema↔wire parity is enforced at test/CI time, not compile time" gap that PR #10's Copilot review surfaced.

## Why this matters

- **Compile-time enforcement.** Adding a field to `daemon.capnp` would either auto-flow into the serde structs (schema-driven codegen) or fail the build (handler doesn't match the new shape). Today the same change requires a manual `wire.rs` edit; if missed, the fixture gate catches it at test/CI time but `cargo check` is happy.
- **Eliminates one source of doc drift.** The current ADR-0014 interim-status paragraph + Go-module README + top-level README all carry caveats about wire.rs being hand-written. Codegen removes the caveats.
- **Scales as the typed surface grows.** 17 of 23 base ops are typed today. Each new op is a wire.rs PR. With codegen, each new op is a daemon.capnp PR + auto-generated wire.rs.

## What needs investigating

1. **Toolchain.** Options surveyed in `a373ba`:
   - `capnp-conv` / `capnp-derive` — third-party crates that derive serde for capnp-generated types. Maturity unknown; license fit unknown; need to read the source before pinning.
   - Custom build.rs that parses `daemon.capnp` via the `capnp` Rust API and emits serde structs directly. Maximum control, maximum maintenance burden.
   - Two-stage: capnpc-rust emits the Cap'n Proto Rust bindings; a thin wrapper layer derives serde via `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]` on a manually-attribute-mapped facade. Splits the difference.

2. **JSON-as-carrier customizations.** wire.rs today has hand-applied attributes the codegen needs to handle:
   - `#[serde(rename = "snake_case")]` for camelCase→snake_case (capnp uses camelCase; JSON wire uses snake_case).
   - `#[serde(skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")]` on `Node.record`, `StatusResponse.lastReparseAtMs`, etc.
   - `serde_json::Value` for open-ended payloads (`StatusResponse.enrichment`, `EnrichResponse.passes`).
   - The `BaseRequest` tagged enum (`#[serde(tag = "op", rename_all = "snake_case")]`) — this is the request-side discriminator that has no capnp equivalent.

   Decision: which of these are codegen'd from schema annotations and which stay as a thin hand-written adapter layer?

3. **Carve-outs from typed surface.** Per `b07a79` and the LSP/vec_search untyped ops: codegen needs to either skip these or let hand-written mirrors coexist. wire.rs today is hand-written so coexistence is trivial; under codegen, the boundary needs to be explicit.

4. **The `Cap'n Proto schema is Rust-side`** boundary. Cloister, mache, and downstream Go consumers don't ingest Rust source — they consume `daemon.capnp` directly. So whatever codegen path we pick stays an LLO-internal compile-time concern.

## Out of scope (deliberately)

- Cross-runtime codegen unification (TS, Swift). The schema is already cross-runtime; the question here is only the *Rust serde mirror*.
- Code-level changes to handlers in `ops.rs`. Handlers consume the typed structs; if codegen produces structurally identical types, handler code is untouched.
- Solving `op_query`'s structural skip (`b07a79`). Codegen + the structural skip are independent.

## Acceptance

- `daemon.capnp` is the single source of truth for the typed surface; `wire.rs` either disappears or shrinks to a thin adapter that only encodes the JSON-carrier conventions (rename rules, skip-serializing).
- `task ci` green; the cross-runtime fixture gate stays as a defense-in-depth check but is no longer load-bearing.
- A handler trying to construct a typed struct with a field that doesn't exist in `daemon.capnp` is a compile error.
- README + ADR-0014 + Go module README can drop the "hand-written / fixture gate is load-bearing" caveats.

## Files

- `rs/ll-core/public-schema/build.rs` (codegen entry point)
- `rs/ll-core/public-schema/Cargo.toml` (build-deps: capnp-conv or chosen toolchain)
- `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/daemon/wire.rs` (shrinks or disappears)
- `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/Cargo.toml` (consume codegen output)
- `docs/adr/0014-capnp-as-protocol.md` (drop the interim-status caveat)
- `README.md` + `clients/go/leyline-schema/README.md` (drop hand-written caveat)

Decade: `daemon-typed-wire`. Thread: `daemon-json-type-lockdown` (the codegen closeout). Related: `a373ba` (parent — closed when A.1b shipped; this is the deferred A.1a path).

title: Mutation gate is blind to three feature-gated modules — 23 root_signer tests never evaluated
description:
`tools/mutants_diff.sh`'s generic slice runs with default features. cargo-mutants
mutates source whether or not a `#[cfg(feature = ...)]` gate is on, so a mutant in
a module compiled OUT survives having tested nothing. It reports as MISSED, which
reads as "you are missing a test" when the truth is "the gate could not see this
module at all."

The script already knows this failure mode. It passes `--features hcl` for
`refs.rs`, and its own comment says: "If another crate ever hides covered code
behind non-default features, it needs the same routing — a default-features run
structurally cannot test it."

PR #363 hit it on `leyline-ts`'s `pyproject` feature and fixed that one instance
(`--features hcl,pyproject`). Found while investigating: **three more modules in
generic-slice packages are still invisible.**

| module | feature | crate default | `#[test]` fns invisible |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ll-open/sign/src/root_signer.rs` | `root-signer` | `["ffi"]` | **23** |
| `ll-open/text-search/src/witchcraft.rs` | `engine-witchcraft` | `[]` | 5 |
| `ll-core/core/src/interrupt.rs` | `interrupt` | `[]` | 3 |

`ll-open/sign/src/ffi.rs` is fine — `ffi` IS in that crate's default set.

`root_signer.rs` is the one that matters: 23 tests over trust-root signing code
that the mutation gate has never actually evaluated. Any PR touching it gets a
green mutants check that proves nothing, or a wall of false survivors.

Packages the generic slice EXCLUDES (`ll-open/fs`, `ll-open/runtime`,
`ll-open/cli-lib`, `ll-open/cli`, `ll-open/schema-bridge`) are not affected —
they have package-specific slices carrying their own feature sets, which is
exactly the routing this bead asks to extend.

## Why not folded into #363

Enabling `root-signer` and `engine-witchcraft` in the generic slice changes what
the baseline compiles and runs. If either has environment-dependent tests or a
slower build, it destabilizes the gate for every PR — and it would do so from
inside a PR about a schema column, where a failure would be misattributed. It
needs its own verification cycle: confirm the baseline stays green, confirm the
added build time is acceptable, confirm the previously-invisible mutants are
actually caught rather than merely enumerated.

## Suggested shape

Same one-line routing as `hcl` and `pyproject`:
`run_slice lib --features hcl,pyproject,root-signer,engine-witchcraft,interrupt`

Then verify per module with:
`cargo mutants --features <set> -C --lib --file <path> --package <pkg> --test-workspace=false`
and confirm it reports caught rather than missed — the check PR #363 used to
prove the `pyproject` fix (1 missed -> 4 caught, 1 unviable, 0 missed).

Worth also adding a guard so the next feature-gated module cannot silently join
this list: enumerate `#[cfg(feature = "x")] pub mod` declarations in
generic-slice packages and fail if `x` is neither in the crate's default set nor
in the slice's `--features` list.

comments.text:
Worked this on `perf/parent-id-generated` (PR #363). Three of the four claims in
the original description held; the investigation turned up two things the
description did not anticipate, one of them a live bug in the shipping gate.

## Measured, before/after enabling each feature

| module | gate as it stood | with its feature |
|---|---|---|
| `ll-open/sign/src/root_signer.rs` | 24 tested, **24 MISSED** | 2 missed, 18 caught, 4 unviable |
| `ll-core/core/src/interrupt.rs` | 25 tested, **25 MISSED** | 7 missed, 18 caught |
| `ll-open/text-search/src/witchcraft.rs` | 28 tested, **28 MISSED** | 17 missed, 8 caught, 3 unviable |

`root_signer`'s 23 tests are strong — 18 of its 20 viable mutants caught. The
gate had simply never run them.

## 1. `witchcraft.rs` did not compile, and had not since 2026-07-14

Not a coverage gap — a build failure. PR #210 (`std::sync::{Mutex,RwLock}` ->
parking_lot) rewrote the mutex type and left six `.map_err()` calls on a guard
that no longer returns a `Result`. Six `error[E0599]`. The module is 444 lines
with five tests; those tests passed on the first run they have ever had.

Five weeks invisible, because every gate skipped it: no CI job builds a
not-shipping feature, and the mutation gate mutates gated source whether or not
the gate is on, so its 28 mutants reported MISSED while testing nothing.

Fixed in PR #363.

## 2. A live bug in `mutants_diff.sh`, pre-dating all of this

`--features hcl` was a STATIC list. cargo-mutants selects only the packages the
diff touches, and cargo rejects a `--features` name that none of the selected
packages declares. So any diff not touching `leyline-ts` failed the generic
slice with:

    error: the package 'leyline-text-search' does not contain this feature: hcl

Reproduced directly. That is a BASELINE BROKEN whose message says nothing about
the code under test — the gate reporting its own misconfiguration as a failure
of the change. The feature list is now derived from the packages actually in the
diff.

## 3. `witchcraft` is excluded from mutation, not given its feature

Its whole `TextSearchEngine` impl needs a live `Embedder`, and `Embedder::new`
needs a T5 model directory (tokenizer + safetensors). CI has none — that is the
same reason the feature is on the not-shipping ledger. Enabling it makes the
gate honest and then permanently red: 7 whole-method stubs no CI-runnable test
can kill.

So it is excluded WITH the reason written at the exclusion site. Without the
feature the same 7 would still be enumerated and reported MISSED, so this trades
a false survivor for a stated carve-out. Remove it when the DB layer is
separable from the `Embedder`, or when CI carries the assets. **That is the
remaining work on this bead.**

## 4. The structural fix: Claim 3 in `check_feature_reachability.sh`

The root hole was that the not-shipping ledger declared intent and nothing
enforced it. "Not shipping" silently became "never compiled."

Claim 3 now requires every ledger entry to compile WITH its test targets
(`--lib --no-run` catches `#[cfg(test)]`-only breaks). All nine entries pass;
~11s warm. Verified in both directions — reintroducing one `.map_err()` site
makes it fail with a reproduce command.

## Still open

- 2 genuine survivors in `root_signer.rs` (`verify_head`: `==`/`!=` at 159:67,
  `||`/`&&` at 161:16 — both in the same function, worth one test).
- 7 genuine survivors in `interrupt.rs` (match-arm deletions in `bit_name`,
  `&`/`|`/`^` in `iter_set_bits`).
- The witchcraft exclusion above.

These only fire on a diff touching those lines, so they are not blocking
anything today — but they are now visible instead of laundered.

acceptance_criteria: The generic slice enables root-signer, engine-witchcraft and interrupt; each module verified to report caught (not missed) via a targeted cargo mutants run; baseline stays green and added build time recorded; a guard fails CI if a generic-slice package declares a #[cfg(feature)] module whose feature is neither default nor in the slice's --features list.

title: Research: hierarchy wants hyperbolic coordinates, not higher-D Euclidean — and the AST is already 1-D laminar intervals
description:
From a design conversation (2026-07-29). Two halves, one recorded fact and one research question.

FACT (costs nothing, guides indexing decisions): a parse tree's spans form a laminar family on the byte axis — any two node intervals are disjoint or nested, never partially overlapping — so the tree IS the nesting and 1-D interval indexing (e.g. SQLite's R*Tree module) is sufficient for containment/overlap queries over _ast spans. No N-D structure is ever needed for 'what encloses offset X'. Only act on this if a profile shows a hot range scan (same evaluate-first discipline as 0ee88a/hotpath).

RESEARCH QUESTION (ties to the coordinate-based embedding work): when flattening hierarchy (AST, directory tree, mache communities) into coordinates, the natural geometry is hyperbolic — trees embed with low distortion in negative curvature because volume grows exponentially with radius, matching node count growing exponentially with depth. Euclidean N-D is the wrong geometry for hierarchy at ANY N. Worth a small experiment: compare distortion of mache community / AST-shape embeddings in 2-D hyperbolic (Poincaré disk) vs 2-D/10-D Euclidean, using existing semantic_search vectors as the baseline. Related product-structure note: the repo-wide fact space factors as (path-tree) × (byte offset) × (history) — node_hash is the coordinate invariant along the last two axes.
acceptance_criteria: a written finding (bead comment or doc) with measured distortion numbers for hyperbolic vs Euclidean embedding of at least one real hierarchy from this repo, and a keep/drop recommendation

title: Lazy AST materialisation: 97% of ingested rows are an AST projection nothing queries eagerly
description:
Measured 2026-08-18, kibana v9.5.1 TypeScript slices, release builds, M-series. Follow-up to ley-line-open-e9f829 (chunked pipeline, PR #357), which bounded Rust-side memory but left ingest at 6 min for 32k files — user verdict: 'still unacceptable, lazy loading seems the way'. ## The gap

`_cfg.node_hash` IS reflow-invariant (ADR-0027 merkle-AST content address; whitespace-invariant by construction). But `_cfg.entry_offset` / `_cfg.exit_offset` are body-*source*-relative — they measure position in the raw text of the body, which includes interior whitespace. Reflow shifts them.

The F1 gate had to be narrowed from "byte-identical row content" to "byte-identical row COUNT + node_hash + block_kinds", with offsets deliberately excluded from the invariant. That works for T3's differential-dataflow `arrange` (which keys on node_hash + block_id) but it means consumers reading offsets after dedup get **first-writer's source-relative positions**, which are only valid for that specific parse of that specific file.

## The right fix: staging layer

Offsets should be positions INTO A CANONICAL STAGED FORM of the body, not into raw source. Two candidates, both already in the substrate:

1. **Pre-serialized capnp `AstNodeList` blob** (ADR-0026 Phase 1 today, per-file). Phase 2 (`ley-line-open-ddfc1c`) explicitly names per-semantic-unit refinement — that's this staging layer. `_ast_pointer.offset_in_blob` is already exactly this shape for AST nodes.
2. **The linearized fold buffer** the merkle hash consumes (κ kind + tokens + child hashes) — content-addressed by construction, portable.

If `_cfg.entry_offset` / `_cfg.exit_offset` were offsets into a per-body staged blob (option 1) instead of body-source-relative, reflow would be fully byte-identical — offsets included — AND sub-file parsing fits by direct extension (staging IS the sub-file unit).

## Impact on already-shipped work

- T1.b2's schema doesn't need to change *shape* — `entry_offset INTEGER, exit_offset INTEGER` still works. Only the *semantics* flip. No migration needed; rows already merged in v0.7.x carry source-relative offsets and can be respected as "legacy source-relative" while new rows carry blob-relative.
- T1.b3's cfg.rs and F1 gate DON'T change — they're offset-agnostic under the narrowed invariant.
- T1.b4 (cyclomatic complexity, `ley-line-open-471195`) is offset-agnostic — safe to land unchanged.
- T2 (dfg-ssa) is offset-agnostic — safe to land unchanged.

## When to decide

**Before T3.b3 (Bootstrap-mode taint, `ley-line-open-485113`).** T3's differential-dataflow arrangement compounds on content-addressed keys; if downstream consumers start depending on the offset semantics before we lock them, migration cost climbs.

## Scope

1. Add a decade-doc section naming the staging layer explicitly (docs/decades/analysis-substrate.md §2 or §5).
2. Decide: canonical staged form = ADR-0026 pointer blob (per-body variant) OR fold buffer OR something else. Coordinate with `ley-line-open-ddfc1c` (ADR-0026 Phase 2) so we don't fork the pointer-store discipline.
3. Migrate cfg.rs to emit blob-relative offsets. Rewrite F1 to assert byte-identical row CONTENT (including offsets) under reflow.
4. Companion change in T2's `_dfg` and T3's `_taint` when they land.

## Close condition

`cargo test -p leyline-cli-lib --test f1_cfg_reflow_stable` passes with STRENGTHENED invariant (row bytes byte-identical, offsets included) under reflow. Task ci green.

## Priority

Invariant: existing snapshot + `sqlite3_serialize` still works under WAL.

### Pointer store 3e87ad (`ley-line-open-3e87ad`)

Invariant: dual-write is transactional — both schemas advance together or not at all.

- **[Transaction atomicity]** — inject a failure between the `_ast` INSERT and the `_ast_pointer` INSERT. Assert both rollback (neither table has the file's rows) — no split-brain schemas.

- **[Large-blob handling]** — parse a source file whose canonical `List(AstNode)` blob exceeds the 8 KiB first-segment default that panicked v0.5.7 (bead 661727). Reuse the `write_canonical_message` helper. Assert no panic.

### Fine-grained region diff e40566 (`ley-line-open-e40566`)

Invariant: `region_ids` is precisely the regions touched by `changed_files`.

- **[Multi-region file]** — a file that provides observations to 3+ regions. Payload's `region_ids` must contain all 3, not just the first.
- **[Zero-region file]** — a file that provides no observations to any region (e.g., a config file matched by CDC but with no code). Payload behavior must be documented + tested — probably skip the emit or emit with empty `region_ids` + `scope: "no-touched-regions"`.
- **[Stale file→region map]** — modify a file such that some regions it USED to touch are gone (function deleted) and some regions it now touches are new. Payload should include BOTH sets (or explicit design decision documented).
- **[Fallback to coarse]** — force the file→region map into an "unknown" state (e.g., pre-first-topology-set). Payload must fall back to `scope: "all-known"` cleanly.

## Why lazy is SAFE here

 already stores every file's exact bytes (byte-verbatim, F1s pins
the round-trip), and the AST fold is a pure function of those bytes — bead
ley-line-open-20988a establishes node_hash is a fold over source BYTES only.
Therefore the AST tables are a derived CACHE, not a source of truth: any file's
AST layer can be rebuilt deterministically at any time. Caches may be lazy.

The invalidation primitive also already exists: the extraction-epoch machinery
(ley-line-open-20988a, shipped) forces re-derivation when extraction rules
change.

## Constraint discovered while measuring

node_refs.node_hash and node_defs.node_hash carry an FK into
node_content.node_hash — the symbol layer points INTO the content-addressed
layer. Skipping node_content fails the transaction with 'FOREIGN KEY constraint
failed' (error 787). So node_content must stay eager, or the FK must go. It is
the deduped layer (1.16M of 14.0M rows), so keeping it eager is cheap.

Lazy set is therefore: nodes (AST rows), _ast, node_child, _ast_pointer,
capnp_blobs + the ast.capnp snapshot.

## Measured ceiling (experiment: skip AST-layer WRITES only)

8 000 files:   wall 53 672 -> 7 403 ms  (-86%, 7.2x)
                 sql_flush 32 847 -> 3 580 ms  (-89%)
                 index_build 15 442 -> 1 142 ms  (-93%)
                 db 9 029 -> 1 904 MB  (-79%)

32 000 files:  wall 358 303 -> 78 385 ms  (-78%)
                 parse 7 647 ms (UNCHANGED)
                 peak RSS 8.3 -> 21.4 GB (WORSE)

## The finding that decides the design

Skipping the writes does not skip the WORK.  still builds the
complete AST for every file — the BLAKE3 fold over every subtree, node_contents,
node_children, ast_entries, ast_capnp_bytes, pointer_blob_bytes — and the
experiment then discards it. That is why parse time is unchanged and peak RSS
gets WORSE (the structures are still constructed; fewer flushes means the
allocator holds more at once).

So a real implementation must push laziness INTO parse_file_pure: a mode that
produces only the symbol layer and does not run the fold or the capnp
serialisation. That makes the win larger than measured above, not smaller, and
is what fixes the memory rather than moving it.

With memory bounded (no swap) the projected 32k figure is roughly
7.6s parse + ~5s buffer + 28s sql_flush + 6.5s index_build ~= 45-50s, i.e. ~7-8x
versus today's 358s.

## Suggested staging

1. Make the ADR-0026 pointer dual-write opt-in (default off) until Phase 2
   actually flips consumers. Pure redundancy today; -22.5% rows on its own.
2. Split parse_file_pure into a symbol pass and an AST-fold pass; ingest runs
   the symbol pass only.
3. On-demand materialisation: given a file id, re-read its source_blobs bytes,
   run the fold, insert the AST layer for that file. Key the cache on
   (blob_hash, extraction_epoch) so it is self-invalidating.
4. Decide whether the eager AST layer survives at all as an opt-in
   (--project-ast) for consumers that want a fully warm arena.

Harness: scratchpad/bench/run_ingest_bench.sh; corpora manifest in
scratchpad/corpora/MANIFEST.md. Experiment gate LEYLINE_EXPERIMENT_SYMBOLS_ONLY
lives on branch fix/krun-spawn-timeout (measurement only, not for shipping).

comments.text:
CORRECTION — the description written at create time was damaged: it was passed
through a double-quoted shell argument, so every backticked identifier was
command-substituted and dropped (four "command not found" errors on
_ast_pointer, _ast, source_blobs, parse_file_pure). Sentences containing them
lost the identifier, and the FK paragraph vanished entirely. This comment is the
authoritative version.

## Where the work goes (8000 files, LEYLINE_PROFILE=1)

    parse                1 220 ms   2.3%
    buffer+capnp_write   2 904 ms   5.4%
    sql_flush           32 847 ms  61.2%
    index_build         15 442 ms  28.8%
    commit                  33 ms
    wall                53 672 ms

## What is written (8000 files: 14.0M rows, 9.0 GB db for 46 MB of source, 196x)

    3 411 305  node_child       AST layer
    3 150 850  nodes            13.6M rows = 97.3%
    3 150 849  _ast
    3 150 849  _ast_pointer
    1 156 416  node_content
      316 777  node_refs        symbol layer
       39 139  _imports         377k rows = 2.7%
       20 911  node_defs

Two distinct problems:

1. The table _ast_pointer is an exact 1:1 mirror of _ast (3.15M rows, 22.5% of
   all volume). Written on every ingest, read by NOTHING in production: grepping
   the workspace for _ast_pointer outside .beads and CHANGELOG returns only the
   cmd_parse.rs writes plus pointer_store_dual_write_test.rs. This is ADR-0026
   Phase 1 dual-write whose Phase 2 (flip consumers to the pointer store) never
   landed, so both representations are paid for indefinitely.

2. The AST layer as a whole is materialised eagerly for every file whether or not
   anything reads it. What mache queries -- find_definition, find_callers,
   imports -- is the 2.7% symbol layer.

## Why lazy is SAFE

The source_blobs table already stores every file's exact bytes (byte-verbatim;
F1s pins the round-trip), and the AST fold is a pure function of those bytes --
bead ley-line-open-20988a establishes that node_hash is a fold over source BYTES
only. The AST tables are therefore a derived CACHE, not a source of truth: any
file's AST layer can be rebuilt deterministically at any time. Caches may be
lazy. The invalidation primitive also already exists: the extraction-epoch
machinery from that same bead forces re-derivation when extraction rules change.

## Constraint discovered while measuring (this paragraph was lost)

node_refs.node_hash and node_defs.node_hash carry a FOREIGN KEY into
node_content.node_hash -- the symbol layer points INTO the content-addressed
layer. Skipping node_content aborts the transaction with "FOREIGN KEY constraint
failed" (SQLite error 787). So node_content must stay eager, or that FK must go.
It is the deduped layer (1.16M of 14.0M rows), so keeping it eager is cheap.

The lazy set is therefore: nodes (AST rows), _ast, node_child, _ast_pointer,
capnp_blobs, and the ast.capnp snapshot.

## Measured ceiling (experiment: skip AST-layer WRITES only)

    8 000 files    wall        53 672 ->  7 403 ms   (-86%, 7.2x)
                   sql_flush   32 847 ->  3 580 ms   (-89%)
                   index_build 15 442 ->  1 142 ms   (-93%)
                   db size      9 029 ->  1 904 MB   (-79%)

    32 000 files   wall       358 303 -> 78 385 ms   (-78%)
                   parse        7 647 ms  UNCHANGED
                   peak RSS       8.3 -> 21.4 GB     WORSE

## The finding that decides the design

Skipping the writes does not skip the WORK. The function parse_file_pure still
builds the complete AST for every file -- the BLAKE3 fold over every subtree,
node_contents, node_children, ast_entries, ast_capnp_bytes, pointer_blob_bytes --
and the experiment then discards it. That is why parse time is unchanged and peak
RSS gets WORSE (structures are still constructed; fewer flushes means the
allocator holds more at once).

A real implementation must push laziness INTO parse_file_pure: a mode producing
only the symbol layer, running neither the fold nor the capnp serialisation. That
makes the win larger than measured above, not smaller, and fixes the memory
rather than relocating it.

With memory bounded (no swap) the projected 32k figure is roughly 7.6s parse +
~5s buffer + 28s sql_flush + 6.5s index_build = ~45-50s, i.e. ~7-8x versus
today's 358s.

## Suggested staging

1. Make the ADR-0026 pointer dual-write opt-in (default off) until Phase 2
   actually flips consumers. Pure redundancy today; -22.5% rows on its own.
2. Split parse_file_pure into a symbol pass and an AST-fold pass; ingest runs the
   symbol pass only.
3. On-demand materialisation: given a file id, re-read its source_blobs bytes,
   run the fold, insert that file's AST layer. Key the cache on
   (blob_hash, extraction_epoch) so it self-invalidates.
4. Decide whether the eager AST layer survives at all as an opt-in
   (--project-ast) for consumers wanting a fully warm arena.

Harness: scratchpad/bench/run_ingest_bench.sh; corpora in
scratchpad/corpora/MANIFEST.md. The measurement gate
LEYLINE_EXPERIMENT_SYMBOLS_ONLY is measurement-only and must not ship.

    node_content   1 156 416   ZERO SELECTs, but it is the FK target of
                               node_refs.node_hash / node_defs.node_hash, which
                               is why omitting it aborts with SQLite 787.
    capnp_blobs        8 000   ZERO

So the defensible figure is 7 726 570 of 14 003 090 rows = 55% with no
production reader, NOT 97%.

Consequence for the measured ceiling: the LEYLINE_EXPERIMENT_SYMBOLS_ONLY run
(8k files, 53.7s -> 7.4s) dropped _ast and nodes as well, so it measures a mode
that cannot answer find_definition-with-position or tree navigation. It is an
upper bound on a lazier design, not the value of dropping unread tables.

Dropping ONLY the zero-reader tables, keeping the node_content FK target:
node_child + _ast_pointer + capnp_blobs = 6 570 154 rows = 47%. With sql_flush +
index_build at ~90% of wall and roughly row-proportional, expect ~45-50% off
wall: 32k files ~358s -> ~180s. Real, but not an order of magnitude.

## The finding that actually matters

Every zero-reader table exists for a planned-but-unlanded phase:

- _ast_pointer + capnp_blobs: ADR-0026 Phase 1 dual-write. Phase 2 (dual-read ->
  measure -> flip) landed nothing since 2026-07-08 per ADR §9.1. ADR §9.2.5 and
  §7 define an explicit kill path, gated on F2 read-side measurement.
- node_child + node_content: ADR-0027 Merkle IR content layer.

So ~half of every ingest writes substrate for migrations that have not landed.
That is a roadmap decision, not an optimisation, and ADR-0026 specifies its own
process for making it. Not actionable unilaterally.

## What IS unilaterally safe

Nothing here. Each candidate table is ADR-mandated substrate. The lazy design in
the description remains correct in shape -- the AST layer is a derived cache
rebuildable from source_blobs -- but which tables become lazy is a call for the
ADR owners, and _ast/nodes going lazy requires an on-demand materialisation path
first (staging item 3) or find_definition regresses.
