title: Daemon-side topic filtering on Subscribe (currently emits ALL events to every subscriber)
description:
## Surfaced by

Mache PR #384 + the evolve-coverage-trunk campaign (2026-05-18). Observed empirically via `tools/sheaf-subscribe-probe/main.go`:

> "the daemon's Subscribe op publishes ALL events, regardless of which topics the client passed. (Confirmed empirically: a `daemon.files.changed` from the git-watcher poll comes through even when we subscribed to sheaf.invalidate only.)"

Mache's `internal/leyline/sheaf_subscriber.go::dispatch` confirms this with a client-side filter:

```go
topic, _ := ev["topic"].(string)
if topic != "sheaf.invalidate" {
    // Only sheaf.invalidate is subscribed; silently ignore the
    // impossible case rather than emit log noise per event.
    return
}
```

Comment says "impossible case" but in fact the daemon DOES push other-topic events; the filter is load-bearing.

## What's wrong with the current behavior

1. **Wasted UDS bandwidth.** Every subscriber on the bus receives every published event, even those it doesn't care about. With `daemon.snapshot` firing every ~5s during normal operation, a subscriber interested only in `sheaf.invalidate` pays the JSON serialize + UDS write + JSON deserialize + topic-check cost on every irrelevant event.

2. **Every consumer reimplements the filter.** Mache filters in `dispatch`. Future consumers (cloister, third-party agents) will all do the same. One filter belongs upstream, not N filters scattered downstream.

3. **Subscribe op contract is misleading.** The op accepts `topics []string` — a typed surface that promises filtering. Today that promise is broken; the topics array is effectively documentation-only.

4. **Glob-pattern semantics implied.** `internal/leyline/socket.go::Subscribe` docs:
   > Topics use dot-separated hierarchical matching:
   >   - "daemon.snapshot" — exact match
   >   - "daemon.*" — one segment wildcard
   >   - "daemon.**" — any segments wildcard
   
   The wildcard semantics suggest a topic-pattern matcher was intended at the daemon. The implementation never landed.

## Fix shape

Daemon-side: in `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/daemon/socket.rs` (the `handle_subscribe` path that PR #390 of LLO recently fixed for `ley-line-open-5caa59`), record the per-subscriber topic list, and BEFORE publishing each event to that subscriber's `mpsc::Sender`, match the event's topic against the subscriber's list. Drop non-matching events at the publish site, not on the wire.

Glob semantics:
- `topic` exact match
- `topic.*` matches `topic.foo` but not `topic.foo.bar`
- `topic.**` matches `topic.foo`, `topic.foo.bar`, etc.
- empty list = subscribe to everything (current effective behavior; preserve as a fallback for debugging — e.g. the probe's `**` use case)

## Regression guards

Tests in `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/tests/event_push_blackbox_test.rs` (the file PR #390 added for ley-line-open-5caa59):

1. `subscribe_exact_topic_filters_other_topics` — subscribe to `["sheaf.invalidate"]`, emit `daemon.snapshot` and `sheaf.invalidate`, assert subscriber sees ONLY the latter.
2. `subscribe_glob_one_segment` — `["daemon.*"]` matches `daemon.snapshot` but not `daemon.files.changed.deep` (or similar — depending on `*` semantics).
3. `subscribe_glob_recursive` — `["daemon.**"]` matches everything under `daemon.*`.
4. `subscribe_empty_topics_receives_all` — preserve the current "no filter" behavior for the probe / debugging.

## Mache-side impact

Once the daemon filter lands, mache can:
- Drop the `if topic != "sheaf.invalidate"` filter in `dispatch` (becomes truly impossible from the daemon side).
- Stop subscribing to `**` in `tools/sheaf-subscribe-probe/main.go` (no longer needs the workaround).
- Reduce subscriber CPU / GC by ~Nx where N is the daemon's other-topic emit rate.

Paired mache bead: filed separately after this lands. Title sketch: `chore(leyline): drop client-side topic filter once daemon implements topic-aware Subscribe`.

## References

- `tools/sheaf-subscribe-probe/main.go` (mache) — the observable
- `internal/leyline/sheaf_subscriber.go::dispatch` (mache) — the current client-side filter
- `internal/leyline/socket.go::Subscribe` (mache) — the docstring promising glob semantics
- `ley-line-open-5caa59` (LLO) — the recent v0.4.3 fix that re-established event delivery; this bead is the natural next step
- `ley-line-open-503971` (LLO) — paired typed payload structs; both improve subscriber ergonomics

title: ring-io/v1 reference impl: host drain loop + descriptor types in rs/ll-open/ring/ (LLO ships the substrate; cloister consumes as CSI-shape capability)
description:
## Framing (user, 2026-05-21)

> "LLO prob handle the uring stuff? Not cloister. Cloister consumes it like a CSI?"

Apply the cred-iso/v1 pattern: cloister defines the capability interface (`cloister-spec/ring-io/v1/`, see cloister-baac45 reframed); LLO ships the reference implementation. cloister consumes the impl when hosting units, the same way it consumes the vault-DO impl for cred-iso/v1.

## Why this lives in LLO

- LLO already owns the substrate I/O surface (arena, BlobStore, ContentAddressed trait — see ley-line-open-082202).
- The "schema/scope check" in §3.1 of the Ring Seam spec — host validating writes against the content-addressed store — is *literally* an LLO BlobStore operation.
- Cross-arena (cluster-spanning) units consume the same impl regardless of which cloister bundle hosts them. Substrate logic ≠ composition logic.

## Scope (for this bead)

1. **Crate** at `rs/ll-open/ring/` — `Cargo.toml`, public API in `lib.rs`.
2. **Descriptor types** — capnp schema for `Submission { op, handle, buf_ptr, buf_len, offset, user_data, flags }` and `Completion { user_data, res, flags }`. Lives under `rs/ll-core/public-schema/capnp/ring.capnp` so it's reusable like daemon.capnp (cloister can `use ring/v1` from Go bindings the same way it uses leyline-schema/daemon).
3. **Host drain loop** — async Rust task: read submission → capability check → schema/scope check (for writes) against the BlobStore substrate → dispatch to op handler → post completion.
4. **Op dispatch table** — v1 surface: `read`, `write`, `open-at`, `readdir`, `stat`. Each op handler is a small Rust function with a uniform signature; substrate ops go through the BlobStore trait so any LLO-resident store can back the ring.
5. **Test harness** — Rust test that pretends to be a WASI guest (Vec-as-SQ, Vec-as-CQ), validates capability bounds, POSIX `res` codes for denied ops.

## What this bead does NOT do

- Doesn't wire the crate into workerd / wasmtime. That's the cloister-side adapter (separate bead, filed later in cloister).
- Doesn't implement zero-copy via `MemoryCreator`. Defer to v1.1.
- Doesn't define the Unit Format manifest (which handles get dispensed at instantiation) — that's a cloister responsibility (cloister-c26528, capability matchmaker layer per ADR-0027).
- Doesn't define the capability interface spec. That's the cloister-side bead (cloister-baac45 reframed).

## Files

- `rs/ll-open/ring/Cargo.toml`
- `rs/ll-open/ring/src/lib.rs`
- `rs/ll-open/ring/src/descriptor.rs`
- `rs/ll-open/ring/src/drain.rs`
- `rs/ll-open/ring/src/ops/` — per-op handlers
- `rs/ll-open/ring/tests/host_integration.rs`
- `rs/ll-core/public-schema/capnp/ring.capnp`

## Dependencies

- Depends on `cloister-baac45` (capability interface declaration — being reframed to `cloister-spec/ring-io/v1/`)
- Adjacent to ley-line-open-783d72 (BlobStore crate + SqliteBlobStore default) — the ring's writes flow through BlobStore; if that bead's trait shape changes, ring's op handlers track it
- Adjacent to ley-line-open-dffb77 (me-repo) — me-bundle as a live arena reads/writes through this ring

comments.text: DESIGN CONSOLIDATED as ADR-0035 (docs/adr/0035-ring-io-v1.md, on branch design/ring-io, rides the 0.15 landing). Three corrections to this bead's premises, verified against both trees 2026-07-30: (1) cloister-baac45 DOES NOT EXIST in cloister's store at any status and cloister-spec/ was never created — the interface bead must be re-filed on their side (asked via cloister bead, four items); the capability-spec-dir pattern has since migrated into LLO's rs/ll-core/schema-spec/ (confinement/v1 precedent), so ring-io/v1's spec dir lives THERE per the leyline-net regime (digest-pinned vectors, cross-runtime pinnable independent of SCHEMA_VERSION — the ADR's D3). (2) BlobStore is not the single backing trait: this bead's own v1 op set (open-at/readdir/stat) needs a namespace, which rings back onto leyline_fs::Graph (cloister's only live LLO consumption today); blob-shaped ops ride BlobStore — the bead predates Graph's maturation. (3) io_uring is the wire SHAPE, not the v1 syscall backend — portable async drain loop first, Linux io_uring fast-path later behind the same descriptors; zero io_uring code exists anywhere today and the ADR says so. Implementation remains this bead's scope, sequenced as an 0.15 opener, spec-first.

User clarification (2026-07-31): treat this bead as the FS-capability seam between LLO and cloister, with V8/workerd as a runtime consumer—not as the FS authority.

title: Add bulk-export ops: get_refs_map + get_defs_map (full token→[node_id] dumps)
description:
Filed 2026-05-11. T2 of decade `daemon-typed-wire`, thread `missing-ops`. Parallel to `a47d7d` (find_callees) — different files mostly, no dep between them.

## Context

Mache's `SQLiteGraph` exposes `DefsMap()` and `RefsMap()` — bulk snapshots of the entire `token → [node_id]` index. Multiple serve handlers consume these for graph-wide analysis:

- `serve_diagram.go` — Louvain community detection over the full refs graph
- `serve_handlers.go` — `find_definition` (defs map), `get_communities` (refs map)
- `serve_impact.go` — BFS seed enumeration from defs
- `serve_architecture.go` — both maps for module-level dependency analysis

`udsGraph` doesn't implement these methods because LLO has no daemon op that returns the full map in one call. The only existing token-lookup ops are `find_callers` and `find_defs`, which take ONE token and return its node refs. Iterating those across all tokens would be N daemon round-trips and isn't tractable.

## What's blocked today

In `--control` (read-only) mount, mache silently degrades:
- `get_diagram` returns no community grouping
- `get_communities` returns nothing
- `get_architecture` fails
- `get_impact` runs but with no seed candidates from defs

These regressions don't error out — type assertions for `refsMapProvider` / `defsMapProvider` just return `nil`, callers degrade. So this looks like "the daemon works fine" until you try one of these features.

## Why bulk-export, not raw SQL via `query` op

`op_query` exists and takes arbitrary SQL — mache COULD call `SELECT token, node_id FROM node_refs` to extract the map. But:

1. Per `docs/TABLE_CONTRACT.md`: *"Post-T8 (2026-05-08)... the cross-process contract moved to canonical-encoded capnp segment files at `${db}.{bindings,...}.capnp`. SQL column names are NOT the contract."*
2. Using raw SQL re-couples mache to LLO's internal table schema — exactly what T8.10 / ADR-0014 forbids.
3. Typed bulk-export ops are the right abstraction. Same modal-evidence frame as `find_callers` (Derived-from-the-living-db), just bulk.

## Work

### Schema (`daemon.capnp`)

Add two messages:

```capnp
struct TokenMapEntry {
  token   @0 :Text;
  nodeIds @1 :List(Text);
}

struct GetRefsMapRequest {}

struct GetRefsMapResponse {
  ok      @0 :Bool;
  entries @1 :List(TokenMapEntry);
}

struct GetDefsMapRequest {}

struct GetDefsMapResponse {
  ok      @0 :Bool;
  entries @1 :List(TokenMapEntry);
}
```

`TokenMapEntry` is reusable between refs and defs since their shape is identical (one token → many node_ids).

### Daemon handlers (`ops.rs`)

```rust
"get_refs_map" => Some(op_get_token_map(ctx, "node_refs", "refs")),
"get_defs_map" => Some(op_get_token_map(ctx, "node_defs", "defs")),
```

`op_get_token_map(ctx, table, json_key)` queries `SELECT token, node_id FROM <table>` once, groups in-memory by token, emits the typed response. Read-only (not in STATE_CHANGING_OPS).

### Tests + fixtures

- Integration test that parses a fixture, populates `node_refs` / `node_defs`, calls each new op, asserts the returned map shape
- Add `get_refs_map.json` / `get_defs_map.json` entries to `tests/fixtures/daemon-protocol.json` (the A-1 drift gate fixtures)

### Regen Go bindings

- `clients/go/leyline-schema/regen.sh` picks up the new schema types automatically
- The `leyline-schema-go` CI workflow's `git diff --exit-code` gate enforces regen-on-commit

## Acceptance

- `get_refs_map` and `get_defs_map` daemon ops in `base_op_names`
- `daemon.capnp` updated additively (per ADR-0014 §2 schema evolution rules)
- Go bindings regenerate cleanly
- A-1 drift gate (bead `b5a77b`) extends to cover the two new ops (with appropriate `go_drift_skip` set to null since the schema is being designed fresh — no drift possible)
- Integration test green
- `task ci` and `task image:smoke` green

## Downstream

title: Versioned wire-format handshake on connect (replace empirical drift detection)
description:
## Surfaced by

Mache PR #384 + PR #388 audits (2026-05-18). The campaign hit version-drift seams multiple times:

1. **v0.4.2 daemon silently dropped sheaf.invalidate events** (`ley-line-open-5caa59`). Mache had no way to detect this from the client side — the subscribe op succeeded, just no events ever arrived. Diagnosed by writing `tools/sheaf-subscribe-probe/main.go` and waiting for a timeout.

2. **Auto-download URL drift** (`mache-9051f0`). Mache's `downloadLeyline` fetched `/releases/latest/` against a private repo. PR #388 pinned to `v0.4.1` mirroring `leyline-schema v0.4.1` in `go.mod`. But `leyline-schema` versions and daemon-binary versions are separate streams — the schema-client at `v0.4.2` and daemon binary at `v0.4.3` can drift apart silently.

3. **`parseUint64` silent coercion** (`mache-5159a2`). Mache parses generation field from the daemon's JSON wire. If LLO ever emits a different numeric encoding (hex string, capnp-quoted int, raw uint64 vs string), mache silently coerces to 0 — the generation reads as "fresh daemon, never advanced" forever.

The common pattern: **the client cannot tell at connect/subscribe time whether it's talking to a wire-format-compatible daemon.** All three issues above would have been a single loud error if a handshake existed.

## What to ship

A `leyline_version` (or `hello` / `handshake`) op that:

- Accepts the client's reported version (mache passes its `leylineBinaryVersion` const, or its embedded schema-client version)
- Returns the daemon's binary version + the capnp schema version + the JSON wire-format major
- Includes a `compat` field: `{compatible: bool, since: "v0.4.1", note: "..."}`
- Clients call this immediately after `DialSocket`, BEFORE any `SendOp` or `Subscribe`
- Mismatch = clear error: "mache built against schema v0.4.1; daemon is v0.4.3 — upgrade mache or downgrade daemon; see <docs URL>"

Could be a Subscribe-time check too (every Subscribe op replies with the wire-version) so subscribers don't get stale-shape events.

## Why this beats the alternatives

- **Beats "guess and pray"**: today's `parseUint64` returns 0 on malformed input; consumers see a value but not the version skew.
- **Beats "pin everywhere"**: PR #388 pins one URL to one version. The pin will rot the next time LLO releases. A handshake lets the daemon advertise compatibility live; clients don't need hardcoded pins.
- **Beats "log and hope"**: a log line doesn't stop processing. A handshake-mismatch error fails fast.

## Paired with

- `ley-line-open-503971` — typed JSON payload structs. The handshake's `wire-format major` is exactly the right gate for those types: "schema-client v0.4.3 requires daemon wire-format major X."
- `mache-8kif` — mache-side startup leyline-version check. Already filed on mache; the handshake's daemon-side response is what mache-8kif consumes.

## Fix shape

- Daemon side: `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/daemon/socket.rs` — add `op: "leyline_version"` handler that returns:
  ```json
  {
    "ok": true,
    "binary_version": "0.4.3",
    "schema_version": "0.4.3",
    "wire_format_major": 1,
    "compat_min": "0.4.1",
    "build_date": "2026-05-18"
  }
  ```
- Client side (mache, future): `internal/leyline/socket.go::DiscoverOrStart` or `DialSocket` calls `leyline_version` and either logs (warning) or errors (incompatible) on mismatch.
- Wire-format major bumps EVERY time the JSON shape on the wire changes incompatibly. Capnp schema version bumps independently for capnp-only consumers.

## Test plan (LLO side)

`rs/ll-open/cli-lib/tests/version_handshake_blackbox_test.rs`:

1. `version_op_returns_known_shape` — call `leyline_version`, assert all fields present + types correct.
2. `version_op_is_idempotent` — call twice, get identical responses.
3. `version_op_works_before_subscribe` — call before any other op, no daemon initialization required.

## References

- `ley-line-open-5caa59` (closed) — the bug that motivated this; would have been caught by a handshake
- `ley-line-open-503971` — typed payloads (mache uses these once published); paired with this
- `mache-8kif` — mache-side consumer
- `mache-9051f0` (closed) — version-pinned URL that this handshake makes redundant
- `mache-5159a2` — parseUint64 silent coercion; handshake catches wire-format drift before it hits parseUint64

## Out of scope

- Cross-version migration (auto-upgrade daemon binary) — separate problem, separate bead.
- Capnp RPC interface — `ley-line-open-a4e860` covers the JSON → capnp migration arc; this handshake works equally well in either framing.

title: Cold-parse falsifiability gate: wall < 1.5s on mache repo (extends 9ccbc7)
description:
## Premise

Bead [[ley-line-open-9ccbc7]] (insert-phase fix) landed two real improvements: BufWriter on capnp dual-write (-1.5s on the syscall path) and deferred indexes (-1.4s on per-row B-tree maintenance). Net 47% reduction on insert phase, 35% on wall. But the **falsifiability gate (wall < 1.0s) FAILED at 5.04s**. The work is not done.

The 9ccbc7 bead deliberately scoped itself to three files and refused to extend. This bead removes that constraint: drill into every phase that sits on the wall budget until the gate goes green.

## Baseline (post-9ccbc7, mache repo, 765 files)

Median of 3 runs in release mode:

| Phase | ms | % of wall | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| parse | 200 | 4% | green |
| insert | 3400 | 67% | red — biggest single line item |
| head_write_after_parse | 500 | 10% | red — re-reads 163 MB ast.capnp from disk |
| sweep_orphaned_dirs + meta + close | 500 | 10% | red |
| **wall** | 5040 | 100% | **red, gate fails** |

## Falsifiability gate (binary, no ratchet)

```
time leyline parse ~/github/art/mache -o /tmp/bench.db
```

- ✅ PASS: median wall < **1500ms** across 3 runs, release build
- ❌ FAIL: anything above. No partial credit. No "we made progress."

Composite gate is fine for now — once we land this we add per-phase gates as a separate hardening bead so future regressions surface phase-locally.

## Attack plan (drill in priority order — keep going until gate passes)

### Attack 1 — batched VALUES INSERTs (target: insert 3400ms → <1000ms)

Today: 534K single-row INSERTs through `prepare_cached` against the prepared statement, one execute per row. Even with all the right pragmas, that's 534K PK B-tree insertions in serial.

Fix: rewrite the insert loop to use multi-row `VALUES(?,?,...),(?,?,...),...` batches. SQLite handles up to 32K bound parameters per statement — at ~5 params per row that's 6.5K rows per execute. Should reduce insert phase to ~500-800ms (10x fewer transaction edges, 10x fewer B-tree page splits per execute).

Caveat: `prepare_cached` doesn't help when the SQL string changes per batch. Need to bucket rows by batch size (e.g. always-batch-of-N + a final smaller batch) so the per-batch-size SQL string is reusable.

Files: `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/cmd_parse.rs` (insert loop), possibly helpers in `rs/ll-open/ts/src/schema.rs`.

### Attack 2 — head-write phase (target: 500ms → <100ms)

`write_head_after_parse` re-reads the 163 MB ast.capnp segment from disk to compute the chain hash. The bytes were just written by the BufWriter — we held them in memory until flush. Don't re-read; compute the hash incrementally while writing, OR compute via mmap of the already-on-disk file (kernel page cache is hot from the flush, mmap is essentially free).

Files: `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/cmd_parse.rs::write_head_after_parse`, possibly `rs/ll-core/core/src/` (Controller / head chain).

### Attack 3 — sweep_orphaned_dirs + meta + close (target: 500ms → <100ms)

The sweep walks `nodes` to find directory rows with no children. For 534K rows that's a real query cost. Either:
- Add an index that makes it O(log n) instead of O(n)
- Make it incremental (only sweep dirs we actually touched this parse)
- Defer it to a background task post-COMMIT

Meta writes + connection close: should be ~ms. If they're taking 100s of ms, investigate.

Files: `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/cmd_parse.rs` (sweep + meta), `rs/ll-open/ts/src/schema.rs`.

### Stop condition

Wall < 1500ms median of 3 runs in release mode. Don't stop at "close enough." Don't reframe the gate.

## Non-goals

- Don't add new functionality. Pure perf work.
- Don't change wire shapes, daemon ops, or any consumer-visible API.
- Don't touch the daemon path (`op_reparse`); this is the CLI cold-parse path only. Daemon's incremental path is separate.

## Why this is its own bead, not a 9ccbc7 reopen

9ccbc7 is a clean record of two specific surgical changes that work and ship value (47% insert reduction, 35% wall reduction, gates 2+3 green). This bead is the bigger drill that wasn't in 9ccbc7's scope. Keeping them separate means the audit history of "what worked, what didn't, what's left" is legible.

9ccbc7's commits stay in its worktree as the starting point for this bead's worktree.

### Per-phase final breakdown (median of 3 runs)

comments.text:
**[IMPORTANT] sweep-skip on cold parse is correct but untested; the condition is subtly different from what the comment describes**

File: `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/src/cmd_parse.rs`, line 925:
```rust
if scope.is_none() && deleted > 0 {
    let swept = sweep_orphaned_dirs(conn)?;
```

The comment (lines 919–923) claims the optimization is sound because "when no files were deleted this run, no dir node can be orphaned." This claim is technically correct, but the reasoning only holds under a specific assumption: that `ensure_dirs` (now called `collect_dirs` in this PR) only inserts dirs for files being parsed in the current run. If any future refactor inserts a dir node without a corresponding file insertion — e.g. a pre-seeded hierarchy, or a new code path that calls `collect_dirs` for an empty directory — the `deleted == 0` short-circuit would silently leave orphaned dirs in the `nodes` table.

**More critically: there is no test that exercises the scenario `scope=None, deleted > 0` with actual orphaned dirs to verify that sweep DOES fire correctly in that case.** The sweep is only exercised at all if deleted > 0 and scope is None — the "skip" path (deleted == 0) is tested implicitly on every cold parse, but the "run" path is never explicitly asserted.

**Concrete reproducer for the missing test:**
```
1. Parse repo with dir foo/ containing foo/a.go and foo/b.go.
2. Delete both files from disk.
3. Reparse (scope=None). deleted == 2, sweep runs. foo/ dir node should be removed.
4. Assert nodes table does NOT contain 'foo'.
```

This scenario is not covered by any test in `cmd_parse.rs` or `integration.rs`.

**Fix:** Add a unit test under the `#[cfg(test)]` block in `cmd_parse.rs` named `sweep_removes_orphaned_dirs_after_all_children_deleted` that exercises the above scenario end to end against a `:memory:` connection with a file-backed db.

**[NIT] row-count parity check is necessary but the integration test for parse does not verify record CONTENT**

File: `rs/ll-open/cli-lib/tests/integration.rs`, `test_parse_creates_db` (line 209).

The existing test verifies `COUNT(*) >= 3` for nodes and `COUNT(*) == 2` for `_source`. It does not verify that the actual row contents are correct. Specifically: the cbbedf commits changed the insert path (batched multi-row VALUES, pre-serialized capnp, parallel parse). If the batching produced a reordering bug — e.g. params being misaligned across a batch boundary — rows could have valid count but wrong field values.

**Concrete scenario where the test passes but is broken:**
If `flush_in_batches` misaligned params at a chunk boundary (e.g. using `chunk.len() * cols` but providing fewer params), `rusqlite` would either return an error (caught) or bind wrong values. The test catches the error case but not the "different values" case.

```rust
let node_id: String = conn.query_row(
    "SELECT id FROM _source WHERE path LIKE '%main.go'",
    [], |r| r.get(0)
).expect("main.go should have a source row");
assert_eq!(node_id, "main.go", "source id should be the relative path");
```
Or equivalently, verify one specific `nodes.record` field is non-empty for a known file node, or that `_ast.node_kind` for a known row is the expected tree-sitter kind string. This is the minimum spot-check that would catch a params-misalignment bug at the batch boundary.

This is a test quality issue, not a correctness issue — no evidence of actual misalignment in the code. But the gate is "row-count parity" and the review brief correctly identifies this as insufficient.

title: projection-v4 release coordination: bump the version on integration (the pin is currently blind), and cut an RC mache can test against
description:
# mache → LLO: one blocking hazard, one request, four questions

Context: `mache-bc6ca3`. mache's forward-compatible half is in review (mache #633) — it writes and probes both the stored and generated `parent_id` shapes today. The remaining half is the DDL re-pin, which is blocked on a release.

## 1. BLOCKING HAZARD — the version did not move, so mache's pin is blind

`rs/ll-open/cli/Cargo.toml` on **`origin/integration`** still reads:

```toml
name = "leyline-cli"
version = "0.18.2"
```

Identical to `origin/main`. But `origin/integration` declares:

```rust
pub const PROJECTION_SCHEMA_VERSION: &str = "projection-v4";
```

mache gates on `<binary> --version` and requires an **exact** match to its pin (`internal/leyline/binary_pin.go:leylineVersionMatchesPin`). A leyline built from `integration` reports `leyline 0.18.2 (open)`, so mache **accepts it as the pinned release** and then runs a v4-schema producer against a v2-pinned consumer.

That is precisely the failure `mache-608a3c` created the exact-version pin to prevent — v0.7.4/v0.7.5 changed the `_ast` schema in *patch* releases, a floating pin let a wrong-version binary through, and the smell gate silently zeroed rules locally while CI saw them. The exact pin closes that **only while the version string moves with the schema**. Here it did not, so the pin cannot see the largest schema change since.

This is live right now: a `cargo install` from `integration` lands a binary that mache will happily adopt as "the pinned v0.18.2".

**Ask: bump `leyline-cli`'s version on the branch before merge.** A schema change that leaves the version untouched is undetectable downstream by construction.

## 2. REQUEST — a prerelease tag, so mache can test before either of us ships

We want to validate mache against v4 *before* release rather than discover drift after. Today mache **cannot**: `internal/lltest.PinnedBinaryOrSkip` resolves only `~/.mache/bin/leyline-<pin>`, verifies `--version` against the pin, and otherwise **skips**. No override, never downloads. So the cross-repo conformance gate can only run against an already-released, already-pinned binary.

We are fixing our side (an override so the gates can point at an arbitrary binary, and gating on the artifact's declared `projection_schema_version` rather than only the producer's version). What we need from you is **a prerelease tag with platform assets and digests**, so `TestLeylineSchema_MatchesPinnedBinary` can re-derive `schema_leyline.go` from a real published artifact and we can hand you a green/red answer before you cut the final.

## 3. QUESTIONS

**a. Is `projection-v4` final?** Verified on `origin/integration`. Confirming it will not become v5 before release, since our gate text will name it.

**b. Does #362 give us new columns to read, and what are they called?** "The range lives on the occurrence, not behind a join" is directly relevant: mache's `graph.RefRangeOf` (shipped in mache #627) does exactly the join you removed —

```sql
SELECT source_id, start_byte, end_byte, start_row, start_col, end_row, end_col
  FROM _ast WHERE node_id = ?
```

If `node_defs`/`node_refs` now carry their own span and grammar kind, we should read them there. Please confirm the column names, and confirm **`_ast` retains its span columns** so the existing path stays valid as a fallback for pre-v4 arenas.

**c. Are integer nids / `parent_nid` in this release or a later one?** That decides whether mache does one migration or two. Related: `ley-line-open-17c271`, where the standing ask is to materialise depth-1 containment because it is **not** derivable from byte spans (a parent sharing its only child's span is indistinguishable by `>=`/`<=`), and to carry a parent field on `emit_ast`'s `ASTRow`.

**d. Anything removed?** You said reads are unaffected and we have no evidence otherwise. Asking explicitly because our fallback paths assume `_ast`, `_source`, `node_content` and `_imports` keep their current shapes.

## 4. FYI — a blind spot in your migration guard, not a bug

Your migration "refuses rather than migrates if any row's stored parent disagrees with the derivation". That is **sound for value preservation**: a row with a non-empty stored parent whose name is longer than its id derives `''`, disagrees, and is correctly caught.

It does pass one degenerate class: `id='a'`, `name='aaa'`, stored parent `''`. `length(id) > length(name)` is false, the CASE falls to `ELSE ''`, and `'' == ''` agrees — so it migrates. Harmless (the value round-trips), but the row is structurally incoherent. mache rejects that class on write; noting it only so you know the guard is a value check, not a structural one.

## 1. STILL BLOCKING: the version does not move — now confirmed by running it, not by reading

`cargo build --release -p leyline-cli` from `origin/integration` produces a binary that reports:

```
leyline 0.18.2 (open)
```

…while emitting `_meta.projection_schema_version = projection-v4` and a generated `nodes.parent_id` (`pragma_table_xinfo` hidden=2). Byte-identical version string to the release whose schema it changes.

mache's `leylineVersionMatchesPin` accepts that binary as the pinned v0.18.2. This is the exact failure `mache-608a3c` created the exact-version pin to prevent, and **the pin cannot see it**, because it keys on a string that stood still.

Please bump `rs/ll-open/cli/Cargo.toml` before tagging 0.19.0. Anyone who `cargo install`s from the branch today gets a binary mache will silently adopt as the pin.

## 2. mache is no longer the gate on the parent_id change

`mache-bc6ca3` merged (mache #633). It writes both shapes: it probes `pragma_table_xinfo` once per transaction and omits `parent_id` from the column list when it is generated.

Verified against **your actual binary**, not a fixture:

```
producer 0.18.2: projection=projection-v4, parent_id hidden=2
--- PASS: TestMaterializeVirtuals_AgainstRealProducerArena
```

The same test on pre-#633 main fails with `cannot INSERT into generated column "parent_id"`, so it is genuinely discriminating. And the generated expression your binary emits is **byte-identical** to the one mache implements.

What still gates a *pin bump* on mache's side is only re-deriving the DDL mirror, which needs a tag — see item 4.

## 3. Question (b) answered — I read it off the binary

The occurrence columns from #362 are:

```
node_defs  + node_kind, start_byte, end_byte, start_row, start_col, end_row, end_col
node_refs  + the same seven
```

**Same names as `_ast`**, which makes this a drop-in for mache: `graph.RefRangeOf` currently does `SELECT … FROM _ast WHERE node_id = ?` and can read the span straight off `node_refs` instead. That is the 3.15M-row join your PR description says you removed — mache was still paying it. No reply needed; filing our own follow-up.

Also answered (d): **nothing removed.** `_ast` keeps every span column and gains `blob_ord INTEGER`, so our fallbacks stay valid. Full measured worklist:

| table | change |
|---|---|
| `_ast` | `+ blob_ord INTEGER` |
| `nodes` | `parent_id TEXT` → `GENERATED ALWAYS AS (…) VIRTUAL` |
| `node_defs` / `node_refs` | `+` the seven above |

Still open: **(a)** is `projection-v4` final, and **(c)** are integer nids / `parent_nid` in this release or a later one (one migration or two — relates to `ley-line-open-17c271`).

## 4. What we still need, and it is small

A **tag** — prerelease is fine. mache's `TestLeylineSchema_MatchesPinnedBinary` re-derives `schema_leyline.go` by *running the pinned binary*, so the mirror cannot be hand-edited; that is the point of the gate. With a tag we flip the pin, re-derive, and CI answers green/red before you cut final.

mache #634 (in review) makes the gated tests honour `MACHE_LEYLINE_BINARY`, the override production already respected, so we can point every gate at an RC. That is how the results above were produced.

## 5. One note on your `_meta` channel

`PROJECTION_SCHEMA_VERSION` is **unreleased** — absent from v0.18.0/v0.18.1/v0.18.2, present on main and integration. So the v4 release will be the first arena that declares its shape at all. mache now reads it (#634) and treats absence as normal rather than as an error, which it has to, since every released leyline produces an undeclared arena.

Worth knowing that your `version.rs` comment cites mache's DDL pin as the motivation for adding that channel — and mache had never read it. That is fixed now. Thanks for building it; it was the right call and we were the ones not holding up our end.

# mache: yes to the prerelease, and your "two migrations" call validates a design choice here

Both answers received and they close (a) and (c). Taking the RC offer.

## Yes, please cut the prerelease

That is the whole remaining gate on our side, and you are right that it costs a CI cycle rather than a decision. `TestLeylineSchema_MatchesPinnedBinary` re-derives `schema_leyline.go` by *running* the pinned binary and asserts `pin == leylineSchemaVersion` first, so the mirror cannot be hand-edited ahead of a tag — that is the point of the gate, and it is also why we cannot simply pre-land the re-pin against a branch build.

With a tag we flip the pin, re-derive, drop `parent_id` from the ~152 fixture inserts the re-derived mirror will start rejecting, and CI answers green or red before you cut final. Any tag works; it does not need to be the release.

## "Deliberately two migrations" is the right call, and it happens to vindicate how we implemented v4

This is worth stating because it could easily have gone the other way here.

mache does **not** key the write path on the projection version. `nodeTx` probes `pragma_table_xinfo('nodes')` once per transaction and omits `parent_id` from the column list only when `hidden` is 2 or 3:

```go
return hidden == 2 || hidden == 3
```

So when 17c271 lands and the generated column is deleted in favour of a stored integer FK, `derivedParent` simply goes false again and the INSERT names the column — no mache change for the write *mechanics*, at either tag. An implementation that had said "if projection-v4 then omit parent_id" would have been correct for exactly one release and then silently wrong at the next, which is precisely the shape of bug the version pin exists to catch and would not have caught.

We will still be gated on 17c271, but on the **id scheme**, not the column: `materializeVirtuals` constructs ids as `dirID + "/callers"` and writes string path-ids. Integer nids change what an id *is*, and that is real work on our side rather than a probe. Good to know it is a separate tag with its own break.

## The corollary we are recording on our side

Your line that the derivation "only means something while id is path-shaped" is the useful part. mache added `checkParentDerivable`, which refuses any row where `id != parent + "/" + name`, on **both** shapes — it exists because a wrong parent under a derived column surfaces as an empty directory rather than an error.

That check has a **known expiry**: under integer nids it would reject every write. It fails loudly rather than silently, which is the right failure mode, but we are annotating it now rather than discovering it during the 17c271 migration. Filed against `mache-bc6ca3`.

## Confirmations on our side

- **projection-v3 never exists as a shipped artifact.** "v3 and v4 in the same tag, cumulative" means no released arena declares v3. mache's `knownProjections` deliberately omits it, with a test asserting the omission, so that we cannot start recognising a shape that was never produced.
- **(b)/(d) corroborated.** We had already read the column names off your branch binary and confirmed nothing was removed; good to have that be deliberate rather than incidental. `RefRangeOf` dropping the `_ast` join is now a straight follow-up for us.

## One thing still worth fixing before you tag

The version. `rs/ll-open/cli/Cargo.toml` on `origin/integration` still reads `version = "0.18.2"`, and a binary built from it reports `leyline 0.18.2 (open)` while emitting projection-v4 — so mache's exact-version pin accepts it as the pinned release. If the prerelease carries a bumped version this resolves itself; flagging only because "cumulative, same tag" makes it easy for the bump to be the step that gets skipped.

comments.text:
# Correction: I overstated the #362 win for mache. There is none on our access pattern.

v0.19.0 is pinned and adopted (mache #635, `085952e`) — that part is done and green. This is a retraction of a claim I made twice, in this bead and in mache's PR bodies.

## What I claimed

> The occurrence columns carry the same names as `_ast`, so `graph.RefRangeOf` can read the span off `node_refs` instead of joining the 3.15M-row `_ast` table.

Phrased as a win we were leaving on the table.

## What I measured

A v0.19.0 arena of mache's own tree (971,533 `_ast` rows, 134,246 `node_refs`), 300 real node_ids, same query shape:

| source | plan | cost |
|---|---|---|
| `_ast WHERE node_id=?` | `SEARCH _ast USING INDEX sqlite_autoindex__ast_1` | **8.2 µs** |
| `node_refs WHERE node_id=?` | `SEARCH node_refs USING INDEX idx_refs_node` | **8.3 µs** |

**1.0×.** Both are index seeks. `_ast.node_id` is a PRIMARY KEY and you ship `idx_refs_node`, so mache was never scanning — the row count difference does not enter into it. Switching would also **lose 7% of spans**: 124,819 of 134,246 `node_refs` rows have a non-NULL `start_byte`.

I checked mache's other `_ast` readers too. The one that looks like a bulk join — `nodes_table_reader.go`'s `LEFT JOIN _ast a ON a.node_id = n.id` — is on a `WHERE n.id = ?` single-node query, deliberately, so Origin rides along instead of costing a second round-trip.

## Why the claim was wrong

Your #362 win is real; I mapped it onto the wrong access pattern. `find_definition` doing a bulk join against 3.15M rows for a 337k-row answer is a genuine scan-shaped problem. mache resolves spans **one node_id at a time**, which was already a seek. I reasoned from your row counts to mache's cost without checking that mache's query had the shape those counts matter for.

**Nothing changes on your side.** The columns are still right, and being able to read a span without the join is still the better contract for anyone doing bulk work. This only corrects mache's side of the ledger: we are not carrying a perf debt here, so please do not treat "mache still joins `_ast`" as an outstanding item.

## Unrelated, and genuinely ours

While auditing for perf I did find real inaccurate behaviour in mache: `find_smells` capped results at 200 by default and reported the truncated count as `total`, so on mache's own repo `cyclomatic_complexity` reported 200 when it has 3,980. Our ratchet gate passes `--limit 100000` so the baseline was never affected — the exposed surface was the agent-facing MCP tool. Fixed in `mache-2b1ea7`; mentioning it only because it is the sort of thing that would have quietly skewed any cross-repo smell comparison we did.

title: Release version coupling: daemon binary, schema-client, capnp wire — define the matrix
description:
## Surfaced by

PR #388 audit on mache (2026-05-18). LLO ships three independently-tagged versioned artifacts that consumers must keep in sync:

1. **Daemon binary** (`leyline`) — released via `agentic-research/ley-line-open` GitHub Releases. Latest: `v0.4.3` (as of 2026-05-18 evening).
2. **Schema-client Go module** (`clients/go/leyline-schema`) — released via tags `clients/go/leyline-schema/vX.Y.Z`. Latest: `v0.4.2`.
3. **Capnp schema** — embedded in the schema-client module; bumps when the wire format changes.

The audit confirmed:
> "In parallel work (commit b1ba5ec, 3 hours ago, on a different branch), mache's `go.mod` was updated to `leyline-schema v0.4.2`. This is not yet on the base branch, so the PR is not *immediately* stale. However, v0.4.2 exists on the LLO releases page and includes additional sheaf GC features (per release notes)."

So in the same week:
- Daemon binary is at v0.4.3
- Schema-client Go module is at v0.4.2
- Some mache branches pin v0.4.1, others v0.4.2

This isn't necessarily broken — semver allows compatible versions to talk — but the discipline is **undocumented**. There's no single source of truth saying "daemon v0.4.3 is compatible with schema-client v0.4.x for x >= ?".

## What to define

A `compatibility.md` in `rs/ll-open/` (or top-level) that, for each released version of each artifact, specifies:

| Daemon binary | Compatible schema-client | Wire-format major | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| v0.4.0 | v0.3.x, v0.4.0 | 1 | sheaf ops introduced |
| v0.4.1 | v0.4.0+ | 1 | δ⁰ inputs |
| v0.4.2 | v0.4.0+ | 1 | (had the sheaf.invalidate event-push bug per `ley-line-open-5caa59`) |
| v0.4.3 | v0.4.0+ | 1 | fixed event push; pre-publishes typed payloads (after `ley-line-open-503971` lands) |

The wire-format major bumps when the JSON event/op envelope shape changes incompatibly (e.g., the `data: {...}` nesting we hit in `ley-line-open-5caa59`). Inside the same major, additions are non-breaking; removals or renames bump.

## Implementation choices

1. **Static doc**: hand-maintained `compatibility.md`. Cheap, drifts under pressure.
2. **CI-enforced**: each LLO release tags a `compatibility.json` artifact alongside the binary. Consumers can `curl` it at install/build time. Slightly more infra.
3. **Daemon-reported**: the handshake op (`ley-line-open-{handshake-bead-id}`) returns this matrix at runtime. Combines with (2) — the daemon serves the same matrix it ships with.

Recommendation: start with (1), graduate to (3) once the handshake bead lands.

## Mache-side coupling

`mache-9051f0` (closed) pins the daemon auto-download URL to a hardcoded `leylineBinaryVersion` const. That const mirrors `go.mod`'s schema-client pin. Today the discipline is "they should match, more or less"; with a compatibility matrix this becomes "the daemon-binary version must satisfy the schema-client's `compat_min` requirement," which is a hard contract.

## Test plan

`compatibility.md` itself doesn't need tests, but:

- A CI job that parses `compatibility.json` (if option 2/3) and verifies the matrix is self-consistent (no version listed as compatible with a non-existent counterpart).
- The handshake op tests (`ley-line-open-{handshake-bead-id}`) automatically validate the runtime version against the documented matrix.

## References

- `ley-line-open-503971` — typed payloads; defines the JSON wire shape that the matrix's "wire-format major" refers to
- `ley-line-open-a4e860` — future capnp migration; this matrix gets a new column for "capnp protocol version" once that lands
- `mache-9051f0` — the pin-to-version-or-rot symptom this bead addresses
- `mache-8kif` — mache-side startup version check, consumes the matrix
- This bead's sibling — handshake op — surfaces the matrix at runtime

## Why P3 (not P2)

The drift hasn't bitten anyone yet (compatibility happens to hold across recent versions). The handshake bead (sibling) and typed-payloads bead (`ley-line-open-503971`) address the immediate symptoms; this is the longer-term discipline that prevents the next class of drift.

title: Add get_schema daemon op (topology export for diagram/architecture)
description:
Filed 2026-05-11. T2 of decade `daemon-typed-wire`, thread `missing-ops`.

## Context

mache's `serve_diagram.go` type-asserts a `schemaProvider` interface to retrieve the schema topology (the cross-tier dependency map LLO ships with). `SQLiteGraph` implements it; `udsGraph` doesn't, so the diagram-by-name path silently degrades in `--control` mount.

Today the schema topology lives in mache itself (built from `Topology` at startup). But LLO is the owner of the source-of-truth dependency graph at parse time, so the daemon should be the one exposing it.

## Work

Add `get_schema` op that returns LLO's parsed schema topology — the cross-tier dependency map (ll-core → ll-open relationships, plus any extension layer DDLs registered via `DaemonExt`).

### Schema (`daemon.capnp`)

```capnp
struct GetSchemaRequest {}

struct SchemaTier {
  name   @0 :Text;        # "ll-core", "ll-open", extension-defined names
  crates @1 :List(Text);  # crate basenames owned by this tier
}

struct GetSchemaResponse {
  ok    @0 :Bool;
  tiers @1 :List(SchemaTier);
}
```

### Handler

`op_get_schema(ctx)` reads from a static topology source (likely `rs/ll-core/schema/` or a config blob). No DB query needed; schema is parse-time-known.

### Acceptance

- `get_schema` in `base_op_names`
- Returns the same shape mache's local `schemaProvider` returns today
- A-1 drift gate has `get_schema.json` fixture entry
- Integration test
- Regen Go bindings; task ci green

## Downstream

Mache `udsGraph.Schema()` implementation in a separate mache-side bead (gated on this LLO bead + tag).

## Why MEDIUM priority (not P1 like find_callees)

Diagram degrades silently — users don't see errors, just less informative output. Useful but not blocking the `--control` mount itself.

comments.text: Closing — shipped. `"get_schema"` is in `BASE_OP_NAMES` (`wire.rs:84`) with `op_get_schema` handler in `ops.rs`. Live as of v0.4.8.

title: Ingest copies every file's bytes three times; two are removable and one is on the serial critical path
description:
cmd_parse.rs, the monorepo-scale ingestion path.

Each file's verbatim bytes are materialized three times per parse:
1. std::fs::read(abs_path) -> owned Vec<u8> `content` in the rayon worker. Unavoidable.
2. cmd_parse.rs:2607 `let source_blob_bytes = content.to_vec();` — a full copy, forced only because parse_file_pure takes content as &[u8] and therefore cannot move it. `content` has no use after this line inside the function, and the caller has no use after the call, so the signature can take Vec<u8> by value and move it.
3. cmd_parse.rs:1259 `source_blob_buf.push(pf.content_hash.to_vec(), pf.source_blob_bytes.clone())` — a second full copy, on the SERIAL main-thread insert loop. `source_blob_bytes` has exactly one use in the whole loop (this line), `pf` is owned by-value from the Vec, and SourceBlobBatch's generated push takes `blob_bytes: Vec<u8>` BY VALUE. The clone is gratuitous.

The field's own doc comment already describes the intended behavior and does not match the code: 'verbatim file bytes as read from disk by the rayon worker, MOVED INTO source_blobs.blob_bytes on the main-thread insert loop.' It is cloned, not moved.

Scale: on a Linux-kernel-shaped corpus (28M LOC / 75K files) this is roughly two extra full-corpus memcpys per ingest, one of them serialized behind the single-threaded insert loop.

Related but NOT in scope here: cmd_parse.rs:1369 `pf.pointer_blob_hash.to_vec()` runs inside the per-AST-entry loop, so it allocates a 32-byte Vec per node (~4.8M allocations at kernel scale). Fixing that means changing the batch row type from Vec<u8> to [u8; 32] through the rusqlite ToSql binding layer — a real refactor, filed separately if worth it.

comments.text:
Acceptance met by PR #355, merged to main in the #361 promotion.

parse_file_pure now takes content BY VALUE and its last statement moves it into source_blob_bytes; the insert loop moves rather than clones both source_blob_bytes and pointer_blob_bytes. F1s passes and task ci was green (receipt ac165e79).

Measured, interleaved A/B against the pre-change binary on kibana TypeScript slices, min-of-2 per cell: wall -2.4% at 2000 files and -3.6% at 8000. Row counts byte-identical (1397557 / 6301699), which is the result that actually mattered — the change provably does not alter the projection.

Recording the measurement honestly: a first, NON-interleaved run reported -8/-10%, which was wrong. Baseline and branch had run under different memory states (an earlier 32k run left 8.3 GB of swap in use). The interleaved number is the real one.

title: T8: Capnp schemas as producer/consumer contract for Σ event log
description:
Thread under decade ley-line-open-9d30ac (Σ Merkle-CAS Substrate).

**Motivation.** ADR-0013 Step 1 shipped `_lsp_refs.referrer_node_id` as a SQL column. The producer (LLO `lookup_referrer_node_id` at project.rs:507) and the consumer (mache canonical views) both implement "given (uri, line, col), find the smallest enclosing AST node" — coupled through a SQL schema that has no schema-evolution story. be6136 (closed at 9fb993f) was caused exactly by this: a one-byte path mismatch (/tmp vs /private/tmp) made every JOIN miss. The SQL schema is acting as a cross-process protocol, and SQL is the wrong tool for that.

**The flip** (per L2/L3 synthesis 2026-05-08): capnp messages are the data plane, not the wire format on top of one. SQLite is a *projection* of the capnp event log. LLO emits capnp `BindingRecord`/`AstNode`/`SourceFile` events; LLO's `_ast`/`_lsp_refs` are local SQL projections; mache's canonical views are also local projections; control-room (Swift) gets the same primitives via capnp codegen — single source of truth, schema-evolved, language-agnostic.

**Deliverable arc.**
- T8.1 schema crate scaffold + Rust bindings (foundation)
- T8.2 BindingRecord capnp schema + LLO producer-side dual-write (dissolves the be6136 class of bugs)
- T8.3 AstNode + SourceFile capnp schemas + LLO producer-side dual-write (`_ast` becomes a projection)
- T8.4 TS bindings + mache consumer migration (multi-runtime payoff; mache reads capnp, not SQL)
- T8.5 Σ integration — capnp segments hashed → content-addressed → drive Σ root advance (ties to T2/T3)
- T8.6 ADR-0014 — capnp-as-protocol, schema evolution rules, versioning policy

**Why under Σ decade.** Σ is the substrate; T8 is the *typed wire format* of that substrate. Σ defines content-addressed event logs; T8 defines what's *in* an event. Without T8, the "event log" is implicit (raw SQL writes); with T8, it's typed, evolveable, and consumable by any language with a capnp runtime (Rust, TS, Swift, Go).

**Channels.** T8.1–T8.5 = `final`. T8.6 = `analysis` (ADR).

**Cross-repo touch:** mache (../mache) needs T8.4 to retire its SQL canonical views. control-room (../control-room) gets bindings as a side benefit. cloister (../cloister) inherits the schema for capnp termination at workerd.

comments.text:
**Thread topology** (decomposed 2026-05-08, post-be6136 closure):

```
T8.1 (cd8811) capnp schema crate scaffold + Rust bindings
  ├─→ T8.2 (cdcae2) BindingRecord schema + LLO dual-write   (P1; dissolves be6136 class)
```

title: T8.2: BindingRecord capnp schema + LLO producer-side dual-write
description:
Bead 8.2 of T8 under decade ley-line-open-9d30ac. Channel: final.

**Why this first.** be6136 (closed at 9fb993f) was a SQL-coupling bug between LLO `_lsp_refs` writes and mache canonical-view JOINs. Fixing it locally was correct, but the underlying contract — "two SQL processes agree on column names" — has no schema-evolution story. Capnp `BindingRecord` is the typed alternative.

**Schema** (`schemas/binding.capnp`):
```
@0xb1ndcap;  # generated capability ID

using Common = import "common.capnp";

struct BindingRecord {
  # Stable identity of the ref site.
  refSite @0 :Common.NodeRef;       # (sourceId, range)
  refToken @1 :Text;                 # textual lemma at ref site
  
  # Resolved targets (LSP gave us these).
  targets @2 :List(Common.NodeRef);  # 0 = unresolved (use mention path)
  
  # Producer-side AST resolution: smallest enclosing construct
  # at the ref site. Replaces _lsp_refs.referrer_node_id.
  referrer @3 :Common.NodeRef;       # NULL-equivalent: empty node_id
  
  # Causality: the parse run that emitted this record.
  parseGen @4 :UInt64;
}

struct NodeRef {
  sourceId @0 :Text;                 # _source.id (relative path)
  nodeId @1 :Text;                   # _ast.node_id
  range @2 :Common.Range;            # for unresolved/lookup-only refs
}
```

**Producer-side dual-write** in `rs/ll-open/lsp/src/project.rs::project_references`:
- Continue writing to `_lsp_refs` (consumers not yet migrated)
- *Also* emit a `BindingRecord` capnp message to a content-addressed event log (initially: append-only file at `${ctrl}.bindings.capnp`; T8.5 promotes to ll/CSS-distributed segment)
- Hash each record (BLAKE3) — that hash IS the record's content address

**Out of scope:**
- Mache consumer migration (T8.4)
- Σ root advance integration (T8.5)
- `_lsp_refs` removal (later — keep dual-write until consumers migrated)

**Acceptance:**
- `cargo test -p leyline-lsp` includes a round-trip test: `project_references` → emit capnp → read back → field-equal asserts
- `_lsp_refs` rows still produced (existing tests still pass)
- New event-log file exists at `${ctrl}.bindings.capnp` after enrich

comments.text:
Empirical input from end-to-end validation of the post-be6136 .db (mache-side, ADR-0013 closeout):

## What works ✅

- Schema columns populate. `_lsp_refs.referrer_node_id` is non-NULL for 9/9 rows in a 9-line gopls-enriched fixture.
- Falsifiability A (skip-list ablation, mache-3509aa) **passes** on a real LLO-built mache self-build: 0 newly-flagged-dead defs when dropping the dead_code skip-list. Means the alive-check binding arm — `r.target_node_id = d.node_id` — is firing correctly. ADR-0013's headline design works empirically.

## What revealed a node-id format question 🟡

Falsifiability B (π_{1→0} round-trip, mache-354464) reports **20/20 (100%) discrepancies** on the same .db. The harness asks: for each `_lsp_refs` row, does `(referrer_node_id, ref_token)` appear in `node_refs`? Answer is no, because the two columns use **different node-id shapes**:

```
_lsp_refs.referrer_node_id (LLO post-be6136):
  pkg/auth.go/function_declaration/parameter_list/parameter_declaration_0/type_identifier
  pkg/auth.go/function_declaration/block/statement_list/return_statement/expression_list/call_expression/selector_expression/field_identifier

node_refs.node_id (LLO leyline parse, call extractor):
  pkg/auth.go/function_declaration/block/statement_list/return_statement/expression_list/call_expression
```

LLO's `lookup_referrer_node_id` returns the **smallest enclosing AST node** at the reference site — leaf identifier (field_identifier, type_identifier). LLO's call extractor for `node_refs` records the **call-expression** node. They're at different AST depths.

Implications:
- For `dead_code` (uses `target_node_id`, NOT `referrer_node_id`): unaffected. Falsifiability A passes.
- For `find_callers` MCP / "where did this come from?" queries: the leaf-identifier path is less useful than a construct-level (function/method) reference would be. Agents asking about a caller want the function name, not the AST node.
- For Falsifiability B's projection: 100% mismatch — the soundness check isn't usable as designed.

## Recommendation for T8.2

The BindingRecord capnp schema should commit to a clear convention. Three options:

1. **Construct-level**: `referrer_node_id` = the smallest enclosing `function_declaration` / `method_declaration` (or equivalent in other languages). Aligns with what `node_refs.node_id` records for call-extraction-shaped rules. Best for `find_callers` UX.
2. **Reference-bearing-node**: `referrer_node_id` = the `call_expression` / `selector_expression` containing the reference. Matches `node_refs.node_id` exactly — Falsifiability B's projection becomes a tight equality check.
3. **Leaf-identifier (current)**: `referrer_node_id` = the leaf `(type_)?identifier` token. What LLO ships today. Most precise but least aligned with `node_refs`.

Whichever wins, the SQL columns and capnp `BindingRecord.referrerNodeId` should agree, AND `node_refs.node_id` should be normalized to the same level (currently records call_expression nodes; if the design picks construct-level, the call extractor needs to walk up too).

If T8.2 picks option 1 or 2, mache's Falsifiability B harness needs no change. If T8.2 stays with option 3, the harness needs to walk up the LLO-emitted AST path to compare at a shallower level, OR the harness becomes "for each ref, does the enclosing call_expression appear in node_refs?" which adds tree-walking on the consumer side.

Test harness in mache:
- `cmd/falsifiability_lsp_projection_test.go::TestFalsifiabilityB_IntegrationOnLeylineParse` (gated on `MACHE_FALSIFIABILITY_INTEGRATION=1`)
- `cmd/falsifiability_skip_list_ablation_test.go::TestFalsifiabilityA_IntegrationOnLeylineParse` (same gate, currently passing)

Filing this here rather than as a separate bead because the resolution naturally lives in T8.2's BindingRecord schema definition.

title: KrunWorkerBackend::start can block forever in Command::spawn — hangs CI with no timeout
description:
Observed live on 2026-08-17 during `task ci` on branch fix/perf-gate-env-race. The run wedged for 1h33m with zero log output and 0.0% CPU until killed (CI_EXIT=201 is the kill, not a result).

## Process tree at the hang

    34766  target/debug/deps/krun_worker_backend-30f21cbcde0c22f9      1h33m  0.0% CPU
    34774   |- /bin/sh $TMPDIR/.tmpW1VsFR/leyline-krun-worker \
                 --cas-root ... --libkrun .../libkrun.dylib --run-root .../runs/leyline-run-xkIihw

## Stack (macOS `sample`, saved to scratchpad/hang-sample.txt)

Test thread `the_hijack_opt_in_reaches_the_worker_and_is_absent_by_default`:

    krun_worker_backend.rs:476
      -> leyline_runtime::backends::libkrun::backend::KrunWorkerBackend::start  (Backend::start)
        -> std::process::Command::spawn
          -> std::sys::process::unix::Command::spawn
            -> read  (libsystem_kernel)

Blocked in the CLOEXEC error-reporting pipe read INSIDE Command::spawn — the
parent blocks there until the child execs (pipe closes) or reports an error.

A second thread spawned by the same Backend::start:

    std::io::copy(BufReader<ChildStderr>, Sink) -> read

draining the stub worker's stderr, which never reaches EOF because the stub is
still alive.

## Why it is a P1 rather than a flake

There is no timeout on the spawn/readiness path. The sibling test
`backend_enforces_the_wall_clock_limit_and_cleans_up` passes, so the backend
does have a wall-clock limit — but it applies to the RUN, after start() returns,
and here start() never returns. A hang is worse than a failure: on GitHub Actions
this consumes the full job timeout instead of failing fast, and locally it wedges
`task ci` silently.

## Intermittency

Not caused by the branch under test: the diff was two test files plus CHANGELOG,
nothing near the execution backend, and the same test passed on the same machine
90 minutes earlier (scratchpad/ci-rebased.log:5319, zero-copy branch run).

## Related

Bead ley-line-open-c6101e called this shape out explicitly: 'Waiting for a
process/daemon to become ready ... these need a real readiness predicate, i.e.
poll-until-condition with a generous ceiling that only fails on genuine hang.'
That burn-down covered sleeps in tests; this is the same defect in the backend's
own start path.

comments.text:
Sharpened diagnosis. The original report said "start() blocks in Command::spawn
with no timeout", which is where the stack pointed but not WHY. Reading the code
narrows it considerably, and rules out the first two theories.

## Ruled out: the readiness wait is already bounded

backends/libkrun/backend.rs:258 does

    let line = match event_rx.recv_timeout(self.config.ready_timeout) { ... }

with ready_timeout = 15s in the tests (krun_worker_backend.rs:17) and an
explicit "timed out waiting for libkrun worker readiness" error at :281. So the
readiness phase cannot account for a 93-minute hang. Whatever blocked was
BEFORE the recv_timeout — i.e. in the spawn itself at :196, which matches the
sample.

## Ruled out: the env-lock/fork interaction

Rust's Command::spawn takes an internal env lock around fork. There is no
set_var/remove_var anywhere in ll-open/runtime (grep is clean), and each test
binary is its own process, so no sibling test in krun_worker_backend was racing
the environment. This is NOT the same defect as ley-line-open-f07c20.

## Most probable mechanism

backend.rs:194 calls configure_process_group(&mut command) immediately before
:196 command.spawn(). configure_process_group installs a pre_exec hook
(backends/process.rs:35-62).

Installing ANY pre_exec hook makes posix_spawn ineligible, so std falls back to
fork(). The parent then blocks reading the CLOEXEC error pipe until the child
either execs (pipe closes) or writes errno. That read is unbounded by
construction -- there is no timeout parameter on Command::spawn.

fork() in a MULTITHREADED process gives the child a memory image in which any
lock held by another thread at fork time is held forever, by a thread that does
not exist in the child. cargo's harness runs the tests in this binary on
parallel threads, and many of them spawn workers, so concurrent fork() from a
multithreaded parent is the normal case here, not an edge one. A child that
deadlocks on an inherited lock before reaching exec never closes the pipe, and
the parent waits forever at 0% CPU.

That matches every observed fact: 0% CPU on both processes, no log output, and
intermittency (the same test passed on the same machine 90 minutes earlier --
scratchpad/ci-rebased.log:5319).

The pre_exec body itself is not the bug. It calls only setpgid and allocates
nothing, and its SAFETY comment is accurate. The hazard is the fork path that
installing the hook forces, not the hook's contents.

## Note on the stub workers

Every stub in krun_worker_backend.rs ends in /usr/bin/tail -f /dev/null, and
several begin with /bin/cat reading stdin to EOF. Those make grandchildren that
outlive the shell and hold stderr open, which is consistent with the second hung
thread the sample showed (io::copy(BufReader<ChildStderr>, Sink) never reaching
EOF). That is a real lifecycle wart, but it cannot by itself explain a block
INSIDE Command::spawn, which happens before any of that script runs.

## Fix options, with the trade

1. Drop pre_exec so posix_spawn is used again, and set the process group from
   the PARENT after spawn. Removes the fork path entirely. The catch: a parent
   setpgid(pid, pid) races the child's exec and returns EACCES once the child
   has exec'd, so the group is not reliably established -- and
   terminate_process_group's kill(-pid) depends on it. Would need the
   direct-pid fallback promoted from fallback to primary.

2. Keep pre_exec but bound the spawn: perform it on a watchdog thread with a
   timeout. Honest about the failure, but a timed-out spawn leaks the blocked
   thread and the half-forked child, so it converts a hang into a leak.

3. posix_spawnattr_setpgroup via POSIX_SPAWN_SETPGROUP is exactly the right
   primitive and is what std would need to expose; not reachable through
   std::process::Command today without dropping to libc for the whole spawn.

Not attempting a fix here. This is process supervision on the confinement path
(ADR-0035), the failure is intermittent so a speculative change cannot be
validated by one green run, and option 1 changes the guarantee
terminate_process_group relies on. Wants execution-boundary-adversary review and
a reproduction harness (spawn under deliberate multithreaded allocator pressure,
in a loop) before code moves.

## Interim mitigation worth considering independently of the fix

The GitHub Actions job has no timeout-minutes, so this consumes the full 6-hour
default ceiling instead of failing. A timeout-minutes on the CI job caps the
blast radius from 6 hours to the job budget while the real fix is designed.
comments.author: rsry-cli

comments.text:
CORRECTION to the mechanism in the previous comment. Do not implement a fix
against it as written.

The previous comment concluded: installing a pre_exec hook forces the fork()
path, and a child that deadlocks on a lock inherited from the multithreaded test
harness never reaches exec, so the parent blocks forever on the CLOEXEC error
pipe. That reading does not survive the code.

## The contradiction

`KrunWorkerBackend::start` runs, in order:

    let mut child = command.spawn()?;               // (1)
    let mut stdin = child.stdin.take();
    serde_json::to_writer(&mut stdin, request)?;
    stdin.flush()?;
    drop(stdin);                                    // stdin IS closed
    let stderr = child.stderr.take();
    std::thread::spawn(move || {
        let result = read_readiness_line(&mut reader);
        let _ = event_tx.send(result);
        let _ = std::io::copy(&mut reader, &mut std::io::sink());   // (2)
    });
    let line = event_rx.recv_timeout(self.config.ready_timeout)     // bounded

The `sample` output showed one thread at (1) and another at (2). (2) cannot run
until (1) has returned, so those two frames cannot belong to the same start()
call. The single-call story is therefore wrong.

Also disproved by the same read: the earlier note speculated that the stub's
`/bin/cat` never sees EOF. It does — `drop(stdin)` closes the pipe explicitly.

## The reading that does fit

cargo runs the tests in this binary on parallel threads, and many of them spawn
workers. So the two frames belong to DIFFERENT concurrent start() calls: one
past spawn and draining stderr, another still inside spawn.

That makes the likely mechanism fd inheritance across concurrent spawns rather
than a lock deadlock: Command::spawn creates a CLOEXEC error pipe, and a
concurrently-forking sibling can inherit the write end. It closes at that
sibling's exec — but every stub worker in this suite ends in
`/usr/bin/tail -f /dev/null`, a grandchild that outlives the shell, so there is a
long-lived process able to hold the fd. The parent then reads a pipe whose write
end is never closed, forever, unbounded by construction.

pre_exec still matters: it makes posix_spawn ineligible and forces the fork
path where this is possible at all. But it is a precondition, not the cause.

## Status: NOT reproduced, so NOT fixed

25 isolated runs at --test-threads=8: no hang. A heavier attempt (60 runs at
--test-threads=16 under saturating CPU load) is running.

Deliberately not implementing a fix. The last fix would have been built on a
mechanism the code contradicts, and the three candidate fixes have real costs on
the confinement path (parent-side setpgid races the exec and weakens what
terminate_process_group depends on; a spawn watchdog converts a hang into a
leaked thread plus a half-forked child; POSIX_SPAWN_SETPGROUP is not reachable
through std::process::Command). Guessing again is worse than waiting.

What would settle it, in order:
1. A repro harness that spawns concurrently from many threads with a
   long-lived grandchild, run in a loop. If fd inheritance is the mechanism it
   will show up without needing the rest of LLO.
2. `lsof` on the blocked parent at hang time, to see who holds the pipe's
   write end. That is the direct evidence and it was not captured.
3. execution-boundary-adversary review before any change lands, since this is
   process supervision on the ADR-0035 confinement path.

## Release-blocking assessment

This is NOT a regression from any of the current in-flight work — the code
predates it and none of PRs #355/#356/#357/#358/#359 touch this path.
Observed once, in a full `task ci` run, and not reproduced in 85 attempts since.
CI blast radius is already capped at 30 minutes by #358.

Recommendation: do not gate a release on it. Gate the NEXT release on either a
repro or a reviewed fix, and keep this bead P1 rather than promoting it.

    cargo build --tests -p leyline-runtime --test krun_worker_backend
    BIN=$(ls -t rs/target/debug/deps/krun_worker_backend-* | grep -v '\.d$' | head -1)
    for j in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do (while :; do :; done) & done      # saturate CPU
    for i in $(seq 1 200); do timeout 180 "$BIN" --test-threads=16 || echo "RUN $i"; done

CPU saturation is required. Rates measured on an M-series mac:

    25 runs, --test-threads=8,  no load   -> 0 failures
    60 runs, --test-threads=16, saturated -> 1 failure  (run 33)
    80 runs, --test-threads=16, saturated -> 1 failure  (run 69)
    220 runs, --test-threads=16, saturated -> 4 failures

So roughly 1-2% under load and effectively zero idle, which is why it presents
as a CI-only intermittent.

## Observed failure

    thread 'backend_cleanup_handles_guest_created_restrictive_directories'
    panicked at ll-open/runtime/tests/krun_worker_backend.rs:286:31:
    ready worker: ExecutionError { code: BackendFailed, retryable: false,
      detail: "timed out waiting for libkrun worker readiness" }

## HYPOTHESIS 1 — REFUTED: pre_exec forces fork(), child deadlocks pre-exec

The earlier comment claimed the parent blocks forever in Command::spawn's
CLOEXEC error-pipe read because the forked child deadlocks on a lock inherited
from the multithreaded harness.

Refuted by reading start(): the `sample` output showed one thread inside
Command::spawn AND another inside io::copy(ChildStderr, Sink). The second only
runs after the first returns, so they cannot belong to one start() call — they
are different concurrent tests. The single-call story does not hold.

## HYPOTHESIS 2 — REFUTED BY EXPERIMENT: the readiness ceiling was too tight

READY_TIMEOUT was 15s. The theory: under saturation a stub worker
(/bin/sh + /bin/cat + one printf) legitimately needs longer, so the ceiling was
a startup budget wearing a hang-detector's clothes — the shape bead
ley-line-open-c6101e burned down elsewhere.

Raised it to 120s (8x) and re-ran under identical load:

    before (15s):  2 failures / 140 runs  = 1.4%
    after (120s):  4 failures / 220 runs  = 1.8%

No improvement. The change is NOT being committed.

The refutation is informative: if an 8x larger budget does not help, readiness
is not late — it never arrives. The timeout only ever controlled when we give
up. So the defect is upstream of the wait: either the stub never emits its
line, or start() never reaches the point of listening.

Note this also means the earlier 80-run clean sweep was a false negative. At a
1.4% base rate, P(0 failures in 80) is about 0.32, so a third of such sweeps
look like a fix. Any future verification of this bug needs 200+ loaded runs
before "no failures" means anything.

## Where to look next

Upstream of `event_rx.recv_timeout`, in order:

1. Does the stub ever run? `/bin/cat >/dev/null` requires stdin EOF; start()
   does `drop(stdin)` so it should get it, but that has not been observed
   directly under load. Instrument the stub to touch a file before and after
   the cat, and check which side is missing on a failing run.
2. Does `Command::spawn` itself return? Timestamp around it. This is where
   hypothesis 1 pointed, and while its MECHANISM was wrong the SITE may not be.
3. Is stderr the right channel under load? readiness is read from the child's
   stderr while a second thread later drains the same pipe; check for a race
   between `read_readiness_line` and the drain loop taking over.
4. lsof on a stuck parent to see who holds the pipe write end.

## Relationship to the ORIGINAL symptom

The 1h33m wedge at 0% CPU that opened this bead is NOT this flake. A 15s
timeout fails at 15s; it cannot wedge for 93 minutes. Two distinct symptoms,
one now reproducible and one not. Do not close this bead on the flake alone.

## Release posture unchanged

Pre-existing; not a regression from PRs #355/#356/#357/#358/#359, none of which
touch this path. CI blast radius capped at 30 minutes by #358. Recommend not
gating the current release on it.

comments.text:
SITE PROVEN. Live sample of a wedged process, not inference. Mechanism still
open; do not implement against a guess.

## Reproduction (deterministic enough to iterate on)

    cargo build --tests -p leyline-runtime --test krun_worker_backend
    BIN=$(ls -t rs/target/debug/deps/krun_worker_backend-* | grep -v '\.d$' | head -1)
    for j in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do (while :; do :; done) & done     # saturate CPU
    # run in a loop; poll for a run exceeding ~45s; `sample` that pid

Hit on run 130 of 250 with READY_TIMEOUT at its original 15s.

## The stack (sample, pid 9132, wedged 45s+)

Wedged test thread — backend_rejects_a_duplicate_run_id_without_replacing_the_live_worker:

    KrunWorkerBackend::start   (Backend::start)
      std::process::Command::spawn
        std::sys::process::unix::Command::spawn
          read   (in libsystem_kernel.dylib)

A SEPARATE thread, belonging to a different test that already got past spawn:

    Backend::start's spawned closure
      std::io::copy(BufReader<ChildStderr>, Sink)
        read

Only one test thread was live in the sample. 13 of 14 tests had completed.

## What this settles

1. The block is `Command::spawn`'s CLOEXEC error-pipe read. That read is
   unbounded BY CONSTRUCTION — std has no timeout parameter — which is why a
   93-minute wedge is possible at all.

2. It is NOT the readiness wait. `event_rx.recv_timeout(ready_timeout)` is
   never reached. This is independently confirmed by the original CI incident:
   93 minutes with READY_TIMEOUT = 15s. A 15s wait cannot produce that.

3. The two frames in the ORIGINAL sample (spawn + io::copy) belong to DIFFERENT
   concurrent tests, not one call. That reconciliation was reasoned earlier and
   is now observed.

4. Raising READY_TIMEOUT 15s -> 120s does not help (4 failures / 220 loaded
   runs vs 2 / 140), and makes the failure mode WORSE: a bounded panic becomes
   a longer wedge. Not committed.

## Mechanism: still unproven

Consistent with the site: a concurrently-forking sibling inherits this spawn's
CLOEXEC pipe write end during the window between pipe creation and the
sibling's exec. Under CPU saturation that window widens, which fits the
load-dependence exactly (~1-2% saturated, ~0% idle).

What is NOT yet explained is why the fd is held FOREVER rather than until the
sibling execs. Every stub in the suite ends in `/usr/bin/tail -f /dev/null`, so
long-lived grandchildren exist and are the obvious suspects, but CLOEXEC should
close at each exec. That gap is the remaining unknown.

Missing evidence, and the single most valuable next step: `lsof -p <parent>`
plus `lsof` across the worker tree AT HANG TIME, to identify which process
holds the write end. The repro loop above can be extended to capture it.

## Candidate fixes, none implemented

- Serialize spawns behind a process-wide lock. Closes the pipe-creation/fork
  race directly; spawn is rare so the cost is negligible. A global lock in a
  library needs deliberate scoping.
- Drop `configure_process_group`'s pre_exec so posix_spawn becomes eligible and
  the fork+CLOEXEC-pipe protocol is bypassed. Costs the process-group
  guarantee that `terminate_process_group`'s `kill(-pid)` depends on.
- Bound the spawn with a watchdog. Converts a hang into a leaked thread plus a
  half-forked child; honest but not clearly better.

This is process supervision on the ADR-0035 confinement path and I have now
been wrong about the MECHANISM twice while being right about the SITE once.
Wants execution-boundary-adversary review, with the lsof evidence in hand,
before code moves.

## Release posture

Unchanged: pre-existing, touches none of PRs #355/#356/#357/#358/#359, and #358
caps CI cost at 30 minutes. Recommend not gating the current release on it.
